confidence_note: Count the spots: exactly 7 black spots on scarlet-red wing cases is diagnostic. 3 on each side plus 1 shared spot at the midline.
summary: Britain's most familiar beetle. Exactly 7 black spots on bright scarlet wing cases. A single adult eats 50–60 aphids per day — one of the most important natural pest controllers in Britain.
full_description: The 7-Spot Ladybird (Coccinella septempunctata) is Britain's most familiar beetle and one of the most recognisable insects in the world. At 7–8mm long, it has hemispherical, bright scarlet-red wing cases (elytra) bearing exactly seven black spots: three on each wing case plus one shared spot at the midline between them. The pronotum (the plate behind the head) is black with two small white spots at the front corners. The bright warning colouration (aposematism) deters predators — when threatened, ladybirds can secrete a bitter, toxic yellow fluid from leg joints (reflex bleeding) that is highly effective at deterring birds. They are among the most important natural pest controllers in Britain: a single adult can eat 50–60 aphids per day, and the larvae — which look completely unlike the adult, being spiky and black with yellow or orange spots — are even more voracious, consuming 100–150 aphids over their development. One of the gardener's and farmer's greatest allies.
native_info: Native to the UK and common throughout Britain. Populations can be temporarily displaced by the invasive Harlequin Ladybird in some areas, but the 7-Spot remains widespread.
wildlife_value: An essential natural pest controller. Reduces aphid populations without chemical intervention. Presence in a garden or field indicates a healthy, pesticide-free environment. Adults and larvae are also food for insectivorous birds, spiders, and ground beetles, making them part of the wider food chain.

life_stages.description: In autumn, 7-Spot Ladybirds seek sheltered sites for winter dormancy — under bark, in dense leaf litter, in hollow stems, or in crevices in walls. They often congregate in groups of dozens or more. They remain dormant through cold weather, relying on fat reserves built up during autumn feeding. On warm late-autumn or early-spring days they may briefly emerge before returning to shelter.

Active adults emerge from hibernation in March or April as temperatures rise. They feed on aphids, pollen, and nectar before mating in April–May. Adults are strong fliers and may travel considerable distances between aphid colonies. The distinctive scarlet and black pattern serves as a warning to predators that they are toxic and unpalatable. A freshly emerged adult after hibernation is as bright as ever — the colours do not fade with age.

photos.caption: 7-Spot Ladybird — the classic view showing all 7 black spots on scarlet wing cases
7-Spot Ladybird on vegetation
7-Spot Ladybird — spot pattern clearly visible
7-Spot Ladybird on plant, April

life_stages.description: Females lay clusters of 10–50 upright, yellow, oval eggs on plants where aphids are abundant — the hatching larvae will immediately have a food source. A female can lay up to 400 eggs over her lifetime, though many are eaten by other insects before hatching. Eggs hatch within 5–8 days depending on temperature.

Ladybird larvae look completely different from the adults and are often not recognised for what they are. They are elongated, dark grey or black, with bright yellow or orange spots, and carry small spiky projections along their backs. They are extremely mobile, walking long distances across plants in search of aphids. A single larva can eat 100–150 aphids during its 3–4 week development, making them even more valuable pest controllers than the adults.

photos.caption: 7-Spot Ladybird larva — black with yellow spots, very different from the adult
Ladybird larva on leaf showing the spiky, spotted appearance
Newly hatched 7-Spot Ladybird larva

life_stages.description: The larva attaches itself to a leaf or stem and pupates, forming a yellow-orange pupal case. The pupa is stationary and non-feeding — inside, the larva undergoes complete metamorphosis (holometabolism) into the adult form. The pupal stage lasts about 1–2 weeks. The adult that emerges is initially pale yellow, hardening and developing its full red colour within a few hours.

photos.caption: 7-Spot Ladybird pupa on a plant stem

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are native ladybird species on British plants
similar_species.key_difference: The 2-Spot Ladybird has only 2 black spots (one per wing case). It is also slightly smaller (4–6mm) and more variable in colour — some forms are black with red spots. Count the spots: 2 vs 7 makes identification straightforward.

similar_species.similarity_note: An invasive species now common in Britain
similar_species.key_difference: Harlequin Ladybird is larger (6–9mm), more domed, and extremely variable — it can have 0–22 spots in different colour combinations (red, orange, black). The most common form has many small spots. If a 'ladybird' looks unusually large or has an unusual spot pattern, it may be a Harlequin.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Harlequin is active March–October, as is 7-Spot

confidence_note: A large, oval sett entrance (20–30cm wide) with a substantial spoil heap of soil and old bedding material. Wide footprints with 5 toes and long curved claw marks. Dung pits (small holes containing droppings) at territory edges.
summary: Badgers live near Old Down, and their signs are unmistakeable once you know them — large oval sett entrances with massive spoil heaps, wide footprints with long claw marks, and scratch marks on trees. The sett itself may have been in the same spot for hundreds of years.
full_description:
Badgers (Meles meles) are the UK's largest native land carnivore, and their signs are distinctive and substantial. The sett — the underground burrow system — is the key feature: a large oval entrance (20–30cm wide) with a substantial mound of excavated soil in front of it. Old, well-established setts can have dozens of entrances and the spoil heaps in front of them can be enormous — accumulated over decades or even centuries of occupation. The same sett may be used continuously for hundreds of years.

Look for badger bedding being brought to the surface and aired on warm spring mornings — dry grass, dead leaves, and moss dragged out and left near the entrance before being taken back in. This is one of the most reliable signs that a sett is actively occupied. Badger footprints are wide and bear-like, with 5 toes and prominent long curved claw marks — very different from fox prints. They are often seen in soft mud near the sett entrance or along regular paths.

Badgers are strictly protected by law (the Protection of Badgers Act 1992): it is illegal to disturb a badger sett, harm a badger, or block a sett entrance. Observe from a distance and do not approach active setts.
native_info: Native throughout Britain. Common in a wide range of habitats. Fully protected by the Protection of Badgers Act 1992.
wildlife_value: Badger setts create extensive underground habitat used by Rabbits, Foxes, and many invertebrates when badgers are not occupying every tunnel. The regular disturbance of soil at sett entrances creates important habitat for bare-ground invertebrates and plants. Badgers are major predators of wasp nests, bumble bee nests, and hedgehog-sized prey.

life_stages.description: A large oval hole (20–30cm wide, wider than tall) with a substantial spoil heap of soil and old bedding material. Old setts have massive accumulated spoil. Look for bedding (hay, grass, leaves) aired near entrances on warm spring mornings.

photos.caption: Badger sett entrance — large oval opening with spoil heap
Badger sett — note the wide, low oval shape and accumulated spoil

life_stages.description: Badger footprints are wide (4–5cm), kidney-shaped, with 5 toes and very long (1–2cm) straight claw marks. Look in soft mud near the sett. Badgers use regular paths through vegetation — these run in straight lines and are wider and more definite than rabbit runs.

confidence_note: The lip of the flower mimics a bumblebee so convincingly that it's unmistakeable — there is nothing else like it in the UK.
weather_note: Numbers at any one site vary enormously from year to year — a hillside with dozens one summer may have almost none the next. Likely linked to soil moisture in the preceding autumn.
summary: The most astonishing wildflower in Britain — its lip has evolved to look exactly like a bumblebee, complete with fuzzy texture and patterning. Each flower is a tiny masterpiece.
full_description:
The Bee Orchid is arguably the most extraordinary wildflower in Britain. Each flower has evolved to mimic a female bumblebee in extraordinary detail — the velvety brown-and-yellow lip, the patterning, even the texture, all designed to fool male bees into attempting to mate with it, and in doing so transfer pollen. There's a twist, though: the bee species involved (Eucera long-horned bees) don't live in Britain. So the UK's Bee Orchids are unable to attract pollinators at all — and simply self-pollinate instead. They've kept the disguise but lost the purpose.

Bee Orchids appear first as a flat rosette of oval leaves in autumn, which persists through winter and spring. The flowering spike emerges in June, growing to 15–45cm, and carries 2–7 flowers. The three sepals are pink, and behind them the extraordinary lip — a rounded, velvety lobe coloured warm brown with yellow and cream markings — is unmistakeable. Each flower is a perfect miniature puzzle: the more you look, the more detail you see.

Bee Orchid numbers at Old Down will vary considerably from year to year — some summers may bring dozens, others just a handful. This natural variability is normal and is not cause for concern. They love short, well-drained chalk turf that is not too competitive, and often appear in disturbed ground or near path edges where the sward is kept open.
native_info: Native to southern and central England and Wales. Has spread to disturbed ground and road verges in recent decades. Requires well-drained, low-fertility soil — cannot compete with rank grassland.
wildlife_value: Self-pollinates in the UK (the bee-mimicry attracts no actual pollinators here). However, Bee Orchids are associated with rich chalk grassland ecosystems that support many insects, and their presence indicates the correct management — short, unfertilised turf. The rosette leaves provide shelter for small invertebrates through winter. The flowers produce no nectar, so bees visiting (if they do) get nothing — the orchid is a pure deceiver.

life_stages.description: Bee Orchid spends most of the year as a flat rosette of smooth, oval, grey-green leaves at ground level. These appear in autumn and persist through winter. If you know where Bee Orchids grow at Old Down, look for the rosettes from September onwards — they're easy to find once you know the leaf shape.

The flowering spike emerges rapidly in June, reaching 15–45cm. It carries 2–7 flowers, each with three pink or white sepals and the extraordinary lip that mimics a bumblebee. Look very closely at the lip — you'll see the velvety texture, the 'H' or 'U'-shaped marking, and the overall uncanny resemblance to an insect. After flowering, the plant sets seed and dies back completely.

confidence_note: Smooth, silver-grey bark is distinctive — like an elephant's leg. Oval leaves with slightly wavy edges and silky hairs when young. Triangular nuts in prickly cases (beech mast).
summary: The most graceful of British trees — smooth silver-grey bark, a soaring straight trunk, and a canopy that turns copper-gold in autumn. Beech woodland at Old Down is one of the most magical habitats on the site.
full_description:
Beech is a tree of superlatives. Its bark is the smoothest and most silver-grey of any British tree — people can't resist touching it, and unfortunately can't resist carving initials into it either, which is why so many old beeches carry old love-carvings that stretch and distort as the tree grows. The canopy is dense and domed, and the leaves emerge in spring as the most delicate, translucent pale green — then turn deep glossy green in summer, and finally copper, orange, and gold in autumn. Old beech trees in autumn are one of the best sights in the British countryside.

Beech casts such dense shade that almost nothing grows beneath it — the woodland floor is often bare brown leaf litter. This is sometimes called a 'beech desert,' though it is not truly dead: fallen leaves rot slowly and the deep leaf layer provides habitat for fungi, invertebrates, and small mammals. In autumn, beech produces triangular nuts called mast, held in spiky four-lobed husks. In a mast year (heavy seed production, which happens every few years), the woodland floor can be carpeted with them. Wood mice, Grey Squirrels, Chaffinches, and even Badgers gorge on them.

The smooth bark is a favourite surface for Nuthatch and Treecreeper to search for insects. Look for the distinctive screw-shaped holes where woodpeckers have been working, and feel the bark for the tiny channels and bumps where fungi are fruiting. Beech is native to southeast England and parts of Wales but was widely planted across Britain in the 18th and 19th centuries.
native_info: Probably native to SE England and parts of Wales; widely planted elsewhere. A dominant tree of chalk and limestone woodland in southern England.
wildlife_value: Beech mast is a vital high-calorie food for squirrels, mice, voles, pigeons, and Chaffinches in autumn and winter. The dense leaf litter supports a rich fungal community, including mycorrhizal fungi that live on beech roots. Smooth bark is searched by Nuthatch and Treecreeper for invertebrates. Old beech trees develop cavities used by bats and hole-nesting birds.

life_stages.description: In April–May, beech buds are the most elegant of any tree — long, pointed, and copper-brown, like tiny cigars. As they burst, the new leaves emerge pale green and translucent, edged with silky white hairs. Look up through a newly leafed-out beech canopy against a blue sky for one of the great sights of spring.

photos.caption: Beech leaves in spring — translucent pale green with silky edges

life_stages.description: By summer the leaves are deep glossy green and the canopy is dense. The smooth silver-grey bark and tall, straight trunk are the best ID features at any time of year.

photos.caption: Mature beech tree with characteristic smooth grey trunk
Beech bark — smooth and silver-grey, like elephant skin

life_stages.description: In autumn the canopy turns copper and gold, and the tree drops beech mast — small triangular brown nuts inside spiky four-lobed husks. In a mast year, the forest floor is carpeted with them. Grey Squirrels, Chaffinches, and mice all exploit this seasonal feast.

photos.caption: Old Beech in Epping Forest — a classic mature beech
Beech leaves in spring

summary: Small but enormously important — this is the only food plant for Small Blue caterpillars. The bright yellow flowers tipped with orange-red give it the nickname 'Eggs and Bacon'. Grow on the chalk slopes and search carefully for the tiny black eggs laid on the flower buds.
full_description:
Bird's-foot Trefoil (Lotus corniculatus) is a low-growing member of the pea family, rarely reaching more than 30cm tall. It has small trefoil (three-leaflet) leaves with two additional leaflets at the leaf base — technically making it five-leafed. The bright yellow flowers are held in clusters of 2–7 and are streaked or tipped with orange-red, giving the plant its vivid nickname. When the seed pods ripen they spread in a claw-like pattern, like a bird's foot — the origin of the other common name.

At Old Down, Bird's-foot Trefoil is one of the most ecologically critical plants on the site. It is the sole larval food plant for the Small Blue butterfly — the only plant the caterpillars will eat — and also used by Common Blue caterpillars. Without good populations of Bird's-foot Trefoil on the chalk slopes, neither butterfly could survive here. It grows in low, well-drained turf and thrives where rabbit grazing keeps the grass short — which is one reason rabbits are so important to the ecology of Old Down.

The flowers are excellent for watching insects: bumblebees, particularly the long-tongued Garden Bumblebee, feed on the nectar, and several moth species use it as a caterpillar food plant. On warm summer days, Small Blue adults can often be found nectaring on the very plants their caterpillars depended on the previous year.
native_info: Native throughout the UK in short grassland, especially on well-drained and chalk soils. Common on roadsides, meadows, and coastal cliffs. Thrives in low-nutrient conditions.
wildlife_value: A critical chalk grassland plant for insects. The primary larval foodplant for Common Blue butterfly caterpillars, and also used by the Six-spot Burnet Moth caterpillar. The flowers are a rich nectar source for bumblebees, solitary bees, and many other insects. The seed pods explode when ripe, scattering seeds several metres. Its nitrogen-fixing root nodules improve soil fertility, making it an important part of the grassland ecosystem.

life_stages.description: Low spreading mats of trefoil leaves emerge in spring. The leaves are small, bright green, and slightly hairy. The plant grows close to the ground, spreading outward from a central taproot.

Clusters of 2–7 pea-like flowers appear from June through August. Each flower is yellow, often tipped or streaked with orange-red, held on a thin stem above the leaves. Look carefully at open flower buds — Small Blue butterflies lay their tiny eggs directly on the flower buds. The eggs are minute white spheres, visible with good eyes or a hand lens.

photos.caption: Bird's-foot Trefoil showing the classic yellow-and-orange flowers
Bird's-foot Trefoil flowers in chalk grassland

life_stages.description: After flowering, the seed pods develop as slender dark brown pods that spread in a claw or bird's-foot pattern. The pods pop open when ripe and can be heard cracking on hot dry days.

similar_species.similarity_note: A closely related species sometimes growing in the same area
similar_species.key_difference: Greater Bird's-foot Trefoil (Lotus pedunculatus) is taller, up to 60cm, with hollow stems and prefers damp grassland, marshes, and fens rather than dry chalk. Common Bird's-foot Trefoil has solid stems and grows in drier conditions.

photos.caption: Bird's-foot Trefoil — critical food plant for Small Blue caterpillars
Bird's-foot Trefoil flowers in close-up

weather_note: White blossom appears before the leaves and can open anywhere from late February in warm years to late April in cold springs. 'Blackthorn winter' is the cold spell that sometimes returns when Blackthorn is in bloom.
summary: The shrub that turns pure white before it even has leaves in spring — the blossom appears on black, bare spiny branches, creating one of the most dramatic sights in the early hedgerow. Then in autumn the same branches are covered in dark blue-black sloe berries.
full_description:
Blackthorn (Prunus spinosa) is a dense, thorny shrub or small tree that is one of the most important components of chalk grassland hedgerows and scrub. It can grow to 5m tall and spreads by suckers, forming impenetrable thickets. The branches are very dark, almost black, with stiff sharp spines — the 'blackthorn' of its name, contrasting with the white-barked Hawthorn. The leaves are small, oval, and finely toothed, appearing after the blossom.

The timing of Blackthorn blossom is one of the most dramatic events in the spring hedgerow. Before a single leaf has opened, the bare black branches become smothered in pure white 5-petalled flowers in March or April, creating a cloud of white visible from a distance. This cold, bright-blossomed period is often called a 'Blackthorn winter' because a cold spell frequently accompanies or follows the blossom. The timing varies significantly year to year — by several weeks — depending on spring temperatures.

In autumn, the transformation is equally dramatic: the blossom positions are replaced by sloe berries — dark blue-black, heavily bloomed (with a waxy powder coating), and very astringent if eaten raw. After the first frosts, the sloes soften and become less sharp, and are the basis of sloe gin. Thrushes, Fieldfares, and Redwings eat sloes enthusiastically in autumn. The dense, thorny thickets provide nesting sites for Yellowhammer, Whitethroat, and Linnet at Old Down.
danger_note: The thorns are sharp and can cause deep puncture wounds. Blackthorn thorns are known to cause infection if they break off under the skin. Handle with care when working near these shrubs.
native_info: Native throughout the UK in hedgerows, woodland edges, scrub, and chalk and limestone downland. One of the most important native shrubs for wildlife.
wildlife_value: Provides critical early pollen and nectar for queen bumblebees, mining bees, and early butterflies when few other plants are in flower. Sloe berries are a major food source for thrushes (Fieldfare, Redwing, Blackbird) in autumn and winter. Dense thorny thickets provide safe nesting for Yellowhammer, Whitethroat, and Linnet. Caterpillars of Brown Hairstreak butterfly feed exclusively on young Blackthorn shoots.

life_stages.description: In winter, Blackthorn is a stark dark shrub of nearly black bare spiny branches. The darkness of the stems is distinctive and gives the plant its name. The very dark stems contrast sharply with the grey-white bark of Hawthorn in the same hedgerow.

One of the most spectacular events in the early hedgerow — pure white 5-petalled flowers covering the bare black branches before a single leaf has appeared. Each flower is 1–1.5cm across with prominent yellow stamens. The blossom can appear as early as late February in warm years. This is the most reliable time to identify the plant with certainty.

photos.caption: Blackthorn in full blossom on bare branches — one of spring's most dramatic hedgerow sights
Blackthorn blossom close-up showing the characteristic pure white flowers

life_stages.description: After blossom, small oval, finely toothed leaves appear. The shrub is now green, denser and less distinctive. Look for the sharp spines — these are true spines (modified branches) and are very stiff and sharp. In summer, developing sloe berries can be seen as small hard green spheres.

The berries turn from green to dark blue-black and develop a waxy bloom (pale grey powder coating). Ripe sloes in October are beautiful — dark, round, and covered in this misty bloom. They are very astringent raw, but after the first frosts (or a night in the freezer) the flesh softens slightly. Thrushes, Fieldfares, and Redwings descend on ripe sloe bushes in October.

photos.caption: Ripe sloe berries with characteristic waxy bloom

similar_species.similarity_note: Both thorny shrubs growing in the same hedgerows at Old Down
similar_species.key_difference: Hawthorn flowers after its leaves appear (May), while Blackthorn flowers before any leaves (March–April). Hawthorn has grey-brown bark and red berries (haws). Blackthorn has very dark nearly black bark and blue-black berries (sloes).
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Blossom timing is the clearest separation: Blackthorn = March–April, bare branches; Hawthorn = May, with leaves

photos.caption: Blackthorn blossom on bare black branches — a sign of very early spring
Blackthorn blossom close-up
Ripe sloe berries with waxy blue-black bloom

summary: The acrobatic jewel of the hedgerow — a Blue Tit can hang completely upside down from the thinnest twig while it picks off insects and larvae. The vivid blue-and-yellow combination makes it one of Britain's most colourful small birds.
full_description:
The Blue Tit (Cyanistes caeruleus) is one of Britain's most colourful and familiar small birds — bright blue cap, wings and tail, yellow breast, white cheeks with a dark eye stripe, and a thin dark line running down the yellow belly. Males are slightly brighter than females, but the difference is subtle. Blue Tits are tiny — just 12cm long and about 11 grams — but they are energetic and acrobatic, able to hang upside down on the thinnest twigs to access food.

Blue Tits are particularly important predators of caterpillars in spring. A breeding pair with a nest full of chicks can collect up to 1,000 caterpillars per day from the surrounding trees — and they time their breeding to coincide with the peak of caterpillar emergence from oak trees. If the spring is warm and caterpillars emerge early, but the tits start nesting on the traditional date, they may miss the peak. This timing mismatch, driven by climate change, is one of the most studied ecological problems in British birds.

At Old Down, Blue Tits are most visible in the hedgerows and scrub around the site perimeter. In autumn and winter they join roving mixed-species flocks with Great Tits, Long-tailed Tits, and Treecreepers, moving through the hedgerow together. The loud, scolding 'tsee-tsee-tsee' alarm call and the 'churring' contact notes are distinctive once learned.
native_info: Resident and abundant throughout England, Wales, and Scotland. Most common in woodland and woodland edge, but adapts well to gardens, hedgerows, and urban areas. One of Britain's most numerous birds.
wildlife_value: Major predator of caterpillars, aphids, and other small invertebrates. A single breeding pair may remove tens of thousands of invertebrates from an area during the breeding season. Nest holes used after abandonment by other species including some insects. Seeds of sunflowers and teasels eaten in winter.

life_stages.description: Vivid blue cap, wing-coverts and tail; bright yellow breast with a faint dark line down the centre; white cheeks with a dark eye stripe. The blue of the cap can appear almost electric on a sunny day. Both sexes are identical in general appearance, though males tend to be slightly brighter blue on the cap.

photos.caption: Blue Tit adult showing vivid blue cap and yellow breast

life_stages.description: Eggs are laid in April–May in a nest box or tree hole. Chicks hatch after two weeks and fledge at about three weeks. Juveniles have yellow-green on the face and breast (replacing the white cheeks) and duller blue. They are often seen in family groups in July, noisily following parents through hedgerows.

photos.caption: Juvenile Blue Tit — yellow-green where the adult is blue, streaky head
Blue Tit parent feeding chicks at the nest hole

similar_species.similarity_note: Closely related, often in the same flocks
similar_species.key_difference: Great Tit is larger (14cm vs 12cm), has a bold black stripe running down a yellow breast, a black head with white cheeks, and no blue on the cap or wings. The Great Tit's song is the familiar 'tea-cher tea-cher' repeated call.

photos.caption: Blue Tit — one of Britain's most colourful small birds
Juvenile Blue Tit — yellow-green where the adult is blue, streaky head
Blue Tit parent feeding chicks at the nest hole

confidence_note: All flowers hang to one side of the drooping stem. Petals curl back at the tips. Cream (not yellow) anthers inside. Sweet, distinctive scent. Leaves are long and strap-like. The Spanish Bluebell (invasive) has flowers all round the upright stem.
weather_note: Peak flowering varies by several weeks depending on spring temperatures — as early as late March in warm years, as late as mid-May in cold ones.
summary: A carpet of bluebells in an ancient woodland in late April is one of the most iconic sights in British nature. The UK holds about half of the world's population of native Bluebell — it's a genuinely global responsibility.
full_description:
The Bluebell is one of the most celebrated wildflowers in Britain, and the country has a remarkable global responsibility: the UK holds around 50% of the entire world's population of native Bluebell (Hyacinthoides non-scripta). The sight of a bluebell wood in late April — a shimmer of violet-blue through the bare grey trunks, and the sweet, honey-like scent hanging in the cool air — is one of the most evocative experiences in British nature.

Native bluebell is quite different from the Spanish Bluebell (H. hispanica) introduced from gardens. Native bluebells have all their flowers on one side of a drooping stem (so the tip hangs over), creamy-white anthers inside each flower, and a sweet scent. Spanish Bluebells have flowers all round an upright stem, blue-violet anthers, and little scent. Hybrids between the two exist and are a conservation concern — if you have Spanish Bluebells in your garden near woodland, consider removing them.

Bluebells are spring ephemerals: they do all their growing and flowering while the woodland canopy is still open and light reaches the ground. By midsummer the leaves have died back completely and the plant survives underground as a bulb through summer and autumn. The bulbs contain toxic starch and were used historically to glue feathers onto arrows. All parts are toxic if eaten in quantity. They are protected by law: it is illegal to dig up wild bluebells.
danger_note: All parts of the Bluebell are toxic if eaten — the bulbs are particularly so. Skin contact with the sap can cause irritation in sensitive individuals. Wash hands after handling.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. The UK holds approximately 50% of the world's native Bluebell population. Protected by the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 — illegal to dig up wild bulbs.
wildlife_value: An important nectar source for early bumblebees emerging from hibernation, particularly Garden Bumblebee and Early Bumblebee. Long-tongued bees can reach the nectar; short-tongued bees sometimes bite through the base of the flower to steal it. The spring flowering before canopy closure makes it crucial for early pollinators. Dense carpets indicate ancient, undisturbed woodland — they spread very slowly and cannot recolonise disturbed ground quickly.

life_stages.description: Bluebells emerge from underground bulbs in February–March, with long, strap-shaped leaves appearing before the flowers. In a bluebell wood, the ground is green before it turns blue.
Flowers appear in April–May. Each stem droops at the tip and carries all its flowers on one side. Petals curl back to reveal cream anthers. The sweet scent is strongest in still air in the morning.

Bluebell carpet in ancient woodland
Bluebell woodland — the UK holds half the world's population of this species
Common Bluebell
Bluebell carpet in woodland
Bluebell woodland

confidence_note: Unmistakable — hooked thorns, compound leaves, and either white-pink flowers or red/black berries at different times of year.
weather_note: Climate change is causing earlier fruiting by 2–3 weeks compared to historical norms. In warm springs, you may find ripe black berries from late July rather than the traditional August. Berries tend to be sweeter in warm autumns.
summary: Flowers in May–June, berries August–October. One of the most ecologically important plants in Britain — feeds over 100 insect species and dozens of bird and mammal species. Also yields the finest free food the British countryside has to offer.
full_description: Bramble, or Blackberry (Rubus fruticosus agg.), is a collective name covering hundreds of closely related microspecies within a complex aggregate. A scrambling, arching shrub growing 1–2m tall, it sprawls through hedgerows and scrub on long canes covered in hooked, backward-curving thorns that catch clothing and skin. The compound leaves usually have 3 (sometimes 5) oval, toothed leaflets. Bramble is effectively evergreen in mild winters, retaining some leaves year-round. In May–June, clusters of five-petalled white or pale pink flowers appear, intensely visited by pollinators. The familiar blackberries follow: each is a compound fruit made up of many small drupelets. Starting green and hard in July, they turn red, then ripen to glossy black in August–October. Bramble is ecologically one of the most important plants in Britain: flowers feed over 100 insect species, berries sustain birds and mammals through autumn, dense thorny growth shelters nesting birds, and leaves feed dozens of moth caterpillar species.
danger_note: Hooked thorns can cause scratches and snagging. Take care when picking berries in dense stands.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. One of the most common plants in Britain, found in virtually every hedgerow, woodland edge, and scrubby area.
wildlife_value: Flowers visited by over 100 insect species including bees, butterflies, hoverflies, and beetles. Berries eaten by Blackbird, Robin, Song Thrush, Waxwing, Wood Mouse, Fox, Badger, and Hedgehog. Dense thorny canes provide nesting sites for Whitethroat, Blackbird, and Wren. Many moth species use Bramble leaves as caterpillar food.

life_stages.description: In winter, Bramble stands as a tangle of woody arching canes with hooked thorns visible along their length. Some leaves remain (Bramble is semi-evergreen), often tinged red or purple in cold weather. The bare canes show the plant's structure clearly — long, arching stems that root where their tips touch the ground, gradually spreading the clump outward.

New bright green shoots emerge from the base of the plant and from existing canes. The fresh compound leaves are lighter green than the older leaves. Flower buds begin forming at the tips of the new growth. The plant expands rapidly in spring, new canes sometimes growing several centimetres per day in warm weather.

Bramble flowers from May to July (sometimes later), producing clusters of five-petalled flowers in white or pale pink. Each flower is 2–3cm across and sweetly scented. The extended flowering period — sometimes lasting 8–10 weeks — makes Bramble one of the most valuable nectar sources of the British summer. Bumblebees, honeybees, and many butterfly species visit constantly on warm days.

photos.caption: Bramble flowers — white five-petalled blossoms in clusters, UK
Bramble flowers close-up showing the five petals and stamens

life_stages.description: As flowers fade, berries begin to form. Initially the small drupelets are green and hard, gradually swelling. They then turn red — at which point they are very sour and astringent. On the same cane you may find both open flowers and berries at different stages of development, as Bramble flowers over such a long period.

photos.caption: Bramble with developing berries — green turning red

life_stages.description: Through August, the berries ripen from red to deep glossy black. When fully black and slightly soft to the touch, they are sweet and ready to eat. A natural sugar spike makes ripe brambles excellent forage for wildlife — and people. The Bramble picking season typically runs from mid-August to late September, though this is shifting earlier due to climate change.

photos.caption: Bramble berries ripening — mix of red and black on the same cane
Ripe blackberries — glossy black and ready to pick

life_stages.description: By September the berries are at their peak — deep black, soft, and sweet, with the best flavour after a warm summer. This is prime season for picking. Wildlife competition is intense: Blackbirds, Robins, Fieldfares, Waxwings, Wood Mice, Foxes, Badgers, and Hedgehogs all feed heavily on ripe brambles. By late October the remaining berries over-ripen and shrivel.

photos.caption: Fully ripe blackberries — peak picking season

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are thorny Rubus species with similar compound leaves
similar_species.key_difference: Wild Raspberry has much finer, less hooked thorns, thinner and more delicate stems, and produces red (not black) berries. The berries are also hollow when picked (they come off the central plug), unlike Bramble berries which are solid.

photos.caption: Bramble flowers
Ripe blackberries
Bramble flower close-up
Bramble unripe berries
Bramble ripening
Mature blackberries

confidence_note: Male is brilliant sulphur yellow — the most vivid yellow of any UK butterfly. Female is a very pale greenish-white and can be confused with Large White, but the distinctive leaf-shaped wing outline and orange spot on each wing identify both sexes.
weather_note: One of the earliest butterflies of the year — can emerge on warm days in January or February. Emergence timing varies with winter temperature. Often the first butterfly of the year.
summary: The canary-yellow male Brimstone is one of the most vivid sights of early spring — often the first butterfly of the year. The word 'butterfly' may actually come from this species: 'butter-coloured fly.'
full_description:
The Brimstone is one of Britain's longest-lived butterflies — adults live for up to 13 months, overwintering as adults tucked into ivy or Holly, and emerging on the first warm days of late winter or spring. On a mild February afternoon, a flash of vivid sulphur yellow along a hedgerow is the classic first-Brimstone-of-the-year moment. The male is the most intensely yellow butterfly in Britain — nothing else comes close. The female is a pale, almost white greenish-cream and is regularly mistaken for a Large White at first glance.

Both sexes have a distinctive wing outline — the wings are shaped like leaves, with a small hook at the tip of the forewing. When at rest with wings closed, the leaf-vein pattern and leaf-green colouring of the underside makes both sexes effectively invisible against ivy or leafy vegetation. An orange spot sits at the centre of each wing, visible on both surfaces.

The caterpillars feed exclusively on Buckthorn and Alder Buckthorn — neither of which is particularly common at Old Down, so Brimstones seen there are likely adults that have moved in from nearby woodland or hedgerow rather than being bred on site. Adults are powerful fliers and can travel significant distances.
native_info: Native throughout England and Wales; scarce in Scotland. Requires Buckthorn or Alder Buckthorn for breeding. Adults are long-lived and mobile.
wildlife_value: As one of the earliest butterflies to appear in spring, Brimstones are early pollinators of spring flowers — they particularly favour Primrose, Lungwort, and Bugle. The caterpillars are entirely dependent on Buckthorn species. The overwintering adults' leaf-shaped, leaf-coloured wings are a remarkable example of camouflage adaptation.

life_stages.description: The caterpillar is plain green with a white stripe along the side — perfectly camouflaged on a Buckthorn leaf. It feeds on Buckthorn (Rhamnus cathartica) or Alder Buckthorn (Frangula alnus). It pupates in a leaf-shaped green chrysalis attached to a stem.

The male is brilliant sulphur yellow — possibly the origin of the name 'butterfly' (butter-coloured fly). Each wing has an orange central spot. The leaf-shaped outline is apparent at rest, and when wings are closed the green underside makes him nearly invisible.

photos.caption: Male Brimstone — vivid sulphur yellow with leaf-shaped wings
Brimstone pair — male (yellow) and female (pale green-white) courting in flight
Male Brimstone butterfly
Male and female Brimstone in flight

confidence_note: Flat, fast-moving, shiny brown-orange arthropod with 15 pairs of legs (30 legs total). The first pair of legs are modified as venomous fangs. Much flatter and faster than a millipede. Found under stones and logs. Antennae and legs about the same length.
summary: The fastest animal under a log — centipedes sprint across the ground the moment you lift a stone. They are predators: the first pair of legs are modified into fangs. Not dangerous to people, but great to watch.
full_description:
Centipedes are ancient, fascinating, and completely harmless to people in Britain. The Brown Centipede (Lithobius forficatus) is the most commonly encountered species — flat, shiny, reddish-brown, about 2–3cm long, with 15 pairs of legs (exactly 30 legs). It moves with surprising speed when a stone is lifted, scurrying for cover. This speed is essential: centipedes are hunters, chasing and catching invertebrate prey using their speed and modified front legs.

The front pair of legs in centipedes has evolved into venomous fangs (forcipules) used to seize and paralyse prey — primarily insects, worms, and other invertebrates. In theory the fangs can pierce human skin, but in practice this almost never happens with British species, and even if it did, the sensation would be no worse than a mild bee sting. British centipedes are entirely harmless to handle.

A useful distinction for children: centipedes have ONE pair of legs per body segment and are flat, fast predators. Millipedes have TWO pairs of legs per body segment, are rounder, much slower, and eat dead plant material. Lift a log and you may find both; the centipede sprints, the millipede ambles.
native_info: Native throughout Britain and Ireland. Very common everywhere under logs, stones, and in leaf litter.
wildlife_value: An important predator of soil invertebrates, insect larvae, worms, and slugs. Centipedes are eaten by Robins, Blackbirds, Hedgehogs, Shrews, and many other predators. They are a key part of the soil food web.

life_stages.description: Found under logs, stones, and in leaf litter year-round. Lift a log and watch it sprint for cover — the speed is remarkable. Count the legs to confirm it's a centipede (30 legs = 15 pairs, one per segment). Compare with a millipede under the same log — completely different movement.

photos.caption: Brown Centipede — 15 pairs of legs, fast predator under logs and stones
Brown Centipede — flat, shiny, reddish-brown
Brown Centipede
Brown Centipede

confidence_note: Buff-tailed Bumblebee can be confused with White-tailed Bumblebee (Bombus lucorum), which is very similar but has a cleaner white tail and brighter lemon-yellow bands. The tail colour — buff-orange vs white — is the key difference, but is not always easy to judge in the field.
summary: One of Britain's largest and most important bumblebees. The queen emerges in early spring — sometimes even in January in mild winters — and is enormous compared to other insects at that time of year. Watch Cowslips and Knapweed flowers at Old Down for the constant movement of workers collecting pollen and nectar.
full_description:
The Buff-tailed Bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) is one of the most abundant and widespread bumblebees in Britain. Queens are very large — up to 22mm long — with a yellow band on the thorax, a second yellow band on the abdomen, and a buff-orange tail. Workers are similar but smaller (11–17mm). Males are smaller still, with a more extensive yellow pattern and a yellow-tipped face. The tail colour varies and can be quite pale in worn individuals, making separation from the White-tailed Bumblebee tricky in the field.

Queen Buff-tailed Bumblebees are among the very first insects to emerge in spring, sometimes flying in January or February in mild weather. After hibernating in a small underground cell, the queen must feed intensively to build up energy reserves before finding a suitable nest site — typically an old mouse hole, compost heap, or underground cavity. She then builds a colony of 200–400 workers through spring and summer, which fan out to forage across a large area. A single worker will visit thousands of flowers per day.

At Old Down, Buff-tailed Bumblebees are among the key pollinators of Cowslip, Bird's-foot Trefoil, Knapweed, and Bramble. Their workers also visit Red Clover, Vetch species, and a wide range of other flowers. Other bumblebee species also occur at Old Down, including the Red-tailed Bumblebee (Bombus lapidarius) — unmistakable with an all-black body and red tail — and the Early Bumblebee (Bombus pratorum), which is smaller and has an orange tail even earlier in the year.
danger_note: Female bumblebees can sting if handled or if their nest is disturbed, but are not aggressive when foraging on flowers. Unlike honey bees, bumblebees can sting multiple times. Leave nests undisturbed.
native_info: Native throughout England, Wales, and southern Scotland. One of Britain's most common bumblebees, present in almost all habitats from gardens to chalk grassland. Colony size 200–400 workers.
wildlife_value: One of the most important pollinators in Britain, visiting a huge range of wildflowers. Essential for the pollination of Bramble, White Clover, Bird's-foot Trefoil, and many other plants at Old Down. The long-tongued workers can reach nectar in deeper flowers including Cowslip. Colonies provide food for Badgers who excavate nests for larvae and honeypot stores.

life_stages.description: The queen is the first sign of Buff-tailed Bumblebee in the year — a large, heavy bee appearing in February–April, flying low over the ground looking for a nest site, or feeding intensively on early flowers like Willowherb, Dandelion, and Blackthorn. She is noticeably larger than any worker bee. One yellow band on the thorax, one on the abdomen, and a buff-orange tail.

photos.caption: Buff-tailed Bumblebee queen foraging — note the large size and buff tail

life_stages.description: Workers are much smaller than the queen but share the same yellow-and-buff pattern. They visit flowers constantly, often carrying visible orange pollen baskets (corbiculae) on their hind legs. Watch a Knapweed or Bramble flower at Old Down and workers will pass through every few seconds on a warm day.

photos.caption: Buff-tailed Bumblebee worker on a flower

similar_species.similarity_note: Very similar species, often in the same habitat
similar_species.key_difference: White-tailed Bumblebee (Bombus lucorum) has a pure white tail (vs buff-orange), brighter lemon-yellow bands, and is generally slightly smaller. The difference in tail colour can be subtle in faded or worn individuals. Both species occur at Old Down.

similar_species.similarity_note: Another common bumblebee at Old Down
similar_species.key_difference: Red-tailed Bumblebee (Bombus lapidarius) is completely distinctive — all-black body with a vivid red-orange tail. No yellow bands on the thorax or abdomen.

photos.caption: Buff-tailed Bumblebee queen — note large size and buff-orange tail
Buff-tailed Bumblebee worker foraging

confidence_note: Whorls of 6–8 narrow leaves around the square stem. Covered in tiny hooked hairs that stick to clothing and fur. Tiny white four-petalled flowers. Round sticky seeds that cling to anything. Completely unmistakeable once you know it.
summary: Britain's best throwing plant — Cleavers sticks to jumpers, dog fur, and anything else it touches. It's every child's favourite, but it's also a serious plant with a clever seed-dispersal trick.
full_description:
Cleavers, sticky weed, sticky willy, goosegrass — this plant has more folk names than almost any other wildflower, most of them reflecting its most famous characteristic: it sticks to everything. The entire plant is covered in tiny hooked hairs (like microscopic velcro), and the round seeds are especially sticky. Children throughout history have thrown clumps of it at each other's backs and watched it cling — it's an irresistible plant.

Cleavers is an annual that scrambles up through hedgerow shrubs and tall vegetation, using its sticky stems to grip other plants for support. The leaves are arranged in whorls of 6–8 around a square stem. In late spring it produces tiny white four-petalled flowers, followed by the distinctive round paired seeds that cling to animal fur, bird feathers, and clothing — a very effective method of seed dispersal that takes seeds far from the parent plant.

In herbal medicine, young Cleavers shoots were eaten as a spring salad green or made into juice — it's edible if cooked or prepared, though rather rough to eat raw. The roasted seeds were once used as a coffee substitute. Despite its humble appearance, Cleavers is ecologically important: its dense scrambling stems provide structure for hedgerow insects, and the seeds are eaten by some birds.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. Extremely common in hedgerows, woodland edges, and disturbed ground. One of the most familiar annual weeds.
wildlife_value: The seeds are eaten by some finches. The dense scrambling stems provide structural complexity in hedgerow bases. The tiny flowers are visited by small insects. The sticky seeds disperse by adhering to animal fur — this means the plant's seeds travel with deer, rabbits, foxes, and domestic animals, linking habitats across the landscape.

life_stages.description: Cleavers scrambles up through other vegetation, supported by its sticky stems. Pull a piece off a hedge and feel it — the tiny velcro-like hooks are remarkable under a magnifying glass.

Tiny four-petalled white flowers appear, followed by round paired seed-pods covered in hooked hairs. These stick firmly to fur, feathers, and clothing. Press one onto your sleeve and it won't come off easily.

photos.caption: Cleavers scrambling up through hedgerow vegetation
Cleavers flowers — tiny white four-petalled flowers
Cleavers — whole plant showing whorled leaves and scrambling habit
Cleavers — whorled leaves and sticky stems in natural habitat
Cleavers — tiny white flowers and the sticky stems

confidence_note: The deeply notched, ragged wing edges are unique among British butterflies — no other species has this shape. Orange-brown with dark spots. Underside looks like a dead leaf with a small white comma-shaped mark (the species name 'c-album' = white C).
weather_note: Overwinters as adult, emerging on warm days from February onwards.
summary: The butterfly with the most extraordinary camouflage in Britain — close wings and it becomes a dead leaf, complete with ragged torn edges and a pale comma-mark like a leaf blemish. Named for that tiny white comma underneath.
full_description:
The Comma's outline is unlike any other British butterfly: the wing edges are deeply cut and notched, like torn, weathered leaves. Combined with the streaked brown underside and tiny white comma mark, a resting Comma with closed wings is one of the most convincing leaf mimics in nature. It sits on woodland edge vegetation with wings closed and vanishes. Open the wings and it's a different creature: bright orange-brown with dark spots, very similar to a Small Tortoiseshell but with more ragged edges.

The Comma has an interesting conservation history. It nearly disappeared from Britain by the early 20th century, surviving only in the Welsh borders, then recovered spectacularly through the 20th century and is now widespread and common, even expanding northwards — possibly a response to climate change. It is one of the few UK butterflies that is genuinely increasing.

Two colour forms of the summer brood exist: 'hutchinsoni' (pale orange-yellow, producing autumn adults) and the darker form (producing overwintering adults). All forms overwinter as adults. Larvae feed on Stinging Nettles, Hop, and Elm — the nettle connection means it shares habitat requirements with Peacock and Small Tortoiseshell.
native_info: Native throughout England and Wales. Spreading northwards. Has increased significantly in the last 50 years.
wildlife_value: Adult pollinators of late-summer flowers and ivy (October). Caterpillars feed on nettles, eaten by insectivorous birds.

life_stages.description: The ragged wing outline is the instant ID feature — no other British butterfly has this notched shape. The underside is a superb dead-leaf mimic with a tiny white comma mark. Look for the comma mark when the butterfly lands with wings closed.

photos.caption: Comma — the ragged wing edges and orange-brown colour are diagnostic
Comma showing the deeply notched wing outline — unique among British butterflies

similar_species.similarity_note: Both orange, both overwinter as adults
similar_species.key_difference: Small Tortoiseshell has smooth wing edges. Comma's deeply notched, ragged wings are unmistakeable.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Often found feeding on the same flowers in August–September

photos.caption: Comma Butterfly
Comma showing ragged wing edges

confidence_note: Males are unmistakable — electric bright blue with black border and white fringe. Females are mostly brown with variable blue scales near the body and orange spots near the wing margin, and can be confused with Brown Argus or Small Blue females. Both sexes have diagnostic orange spots on the undersides of all wings.
summary: The male is an electric metallic blue that seems to glow in sunlight — one of the most beautiful sights of British grassland summer. Both sexes have lovely orange-spotted undersides. The caterpillars feed on Bird's-foot Trefoil, so finding the butterfly at Old Down means the chalk grassland is in good shape.
full_description:
The Common Blue (Polyommatus icarus) is the most widespread blue butterfly in Britain and among the most beautiful. Males have vivid sky-blue upperwings with a narrow black border and white fringe, and seem to glow in sunlight — a blue that is almost impossible to describe in writing. Females are predominantly brown with variable amounts of blue near the wing base and orange spots along the outer margins. Both sexes share the same distinctive underside: pale grey-buff with black spots and a row of vivid orange-red spots near the wing margins — this pattern is the reliable ID feature for both sexes.

The Common Blue has two broods at Old Down in a good year — the first flies May to June, the second July to September. The caterpillars feed primarily on Bird's-foot Trefoil (Lotus corniculatus), with some use of related legumes. Eggs are laid singly on the upper surface of trefoil leaflets. The caterpillars are green and well-camouflaged, and are tended by ants — the caterpillars have a special gland that produces a liquid the ants drink, and in return the ants protect the caterpillar from predators.

At Old Down, Common Blue is typically more numerous than Small Blue, and is a strong indicator of chalk grassland quality. On warm sunny days in July, it is possible to see males spiralling upward in territorial chases, females nectaring on Knapweed and Marjoram, and both sexes roosting with wings closed on tall grass stems in the evening.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. The most common and widespread blue butterfly in Britain. Most abundant on chalk and limestone grassland, coastal dunes, and brownfield sites where Bird's-foot Trefoil grows.
wildlife_value: Caterpillars are specifically dependent on Bird's-foot Trefoil, making this butterfly a reliable indicator of good chalk grassland. Caterpillars are tended by ants — a mutualistic relationship. Adults are prey for spiders and birds. The presence of Common Blue at Old Down indicates a healthy population of its food plant.

life_stages.description: Eggs are tiny, disc-shaped, and pale green-white, laid singly on the upper surface of Bird's-foot Trefoil leaflets. They are very difficult to spot without a hand lens. Newly hatched caterpillars eat the egg shell before starting on the leaf.

Green, slug-like caterpillar with a darker line along the back and pale sides — excellent camouflage on the trefoil leaves. Look for small black ants attending the caterpillar: the caterpillar has a gland on its back that produces a sweet secretion that ants drink, and the ants guard the caterpillar in return.

Electric sky-blue upperwings with a narrow black border and white fringe. The blue has a slightly violet tone in certain lights. Underwing is pale buff-grey with black spots and vivid orange spots near the margin. Males are territorial and can be seen chasing other males on sunny days.

photos.caption: Common Blue male upperside — the vivid electric blue is unmistakable on a sunny day
Common Blue showing diagnostic orange-spotted underside

life_stages.description: Brown upperwings with variable amounts of blue scaling near the wing base (some females are almost as blue as males, others almost entirely brown). Orange spots along the outer wing margin. The orange-spotted underside is the same as the male and is the most reliable identification feature.

photos.caption: Common Blue mating pair — male (blue, left) and female (brown, right)

similar_species.similarity_note: Both blue butterflies occurring at Old Down
similar_species.key_difference: Small Blue is much smaller with a wingspan of 16–27mm (Common Blue 28–36mm). Male Small Blue is not blue — it is sooty grey-brown with a dusting of blue scales near the body. Underside is pale grey with black dots and NO orange spots.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both fly May–August at Old Down

similar_species.similarity_note: Another blue butterfly sometimes seen at Old Down
similar_species.key_difference: Holly Blue underside is distinctive — plain silvery-blue with tiny black dots and no orange spots. Holly Blue flies earlier in spring (April) and tends to fly high around Holly and Ivy, rather than low over grassland.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Holly Blue first brood April–May; Common Blue May–September

photos.caption: Common Blue male — one of Old Down's most beautiful summer butterflies
Common Blue showing the diagnostic orange-spotted underside
Common Blue mating pair — male blue (left), female brown (right)

confidence_note: Short antennae (shorter than body length). Brown, green, or purple-grey with hairy underside. Males produce a series of short chirps (6–10 per second) in a warm afternoon sun. Jumps strongly when disturbed. Hind legs much longer than front legs.
weather_note: Only sings in warm sunshine — a cool cloudy day will produce silence even in peak season. The song is warmth-dependent.
summary: Close your eyes on a warm August afternoon at Old Down and listen — that rapid chirping from the grass is the grasshopper's song. Males rub their hind legs against their wings to 'stridulate'. Grasshoppers are ancient: they've been singing like this for 300 million years.
full_description:
The Common Field Grasshopper is the most frequently heard grasshopper on dry chalk grassland in southern England. On a warm, still August afternoon at Old Down, their song — a series of short, buzzy chirps, each burst lasting 1–2 seconds, repeated every few seconds — is one of the defining sounds of the site. To produce it, the male rubs a row of tiny pegs on his inner hind femur against a hardened vein on the forewing — a process called stridulation. Different grasshopper species produce different songs; with practice they can be identified by ear alone.

Grasshoppers belong to a group called Orthoptera, which also includes crickets. The key difference: grasshoppers have short antennae (shorter than the body), are active by day, and produce song by rubbing leg against wing. Crickets have very long antennae, are mostly nocturnal, and produce song by rubbing the wings together. Grasshoppers have been on Earth for over 300 million years — they were singing on ancient fern forests long before the dinosaurs existed.

The Common Field Grasshopper is highly variable in colour — the same species can be brown, green, purple, or striped. This polymorphism may help individuals match their specific patch of ground. Adults overwinter as eggs laid in soil, with nymphs hatching in May and reaching adulthood by July.
native_info: Native throughout Britain. The most common grasshopper on dry chalk and limestone grassland in England.
wildlife_value: Grasshoppers are an important food source for Kestrel, Skylark, Yellowhammer, and many invertebrate predators including spiders and ground beetles. Their grazing helps maintain short-turf structure. Chalk grassland grasshopper populations are indicators of site quality.

life_stages.description: Nymphs hatch in May from overwintered eggs in soil. They look like miniature adults but with developing wing buds and no adult wings. They moult several times as they grow.

Adults reach full size by July. On warm sunny days, males sing from prominent grass stems. Try to spot one singing — watch for the rapid up-down movement of the hind leg. The song stops immediately if the grasshopper spots you approaching.

photos.caption: Common Field Grasshopper — short antennae and strong hind legs for jumping
Field Grasshopper — colour varies widely from brown to green

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are green jumping insects found in grassland
similar_species.key_difference: Bush crickets have very long antennae (longer than the body), are mostly nocturnal, and call at night. Grasshoppers have short antennae and call by day.

photos.caption: Common Field Grasshopper
Field Grasshopper

confidence_note: Smooth moist skin, dark mask through the eye, long back legs for jumping. Distinguished from Common Toad by smooth skin (toad is warty) and jumping rather than walking.
summary: Britain's most familiar amphibian. The life cycle — from jelly spawn to tadpole to froglet to adult — is one of nature's most dramatic transformations and an iconic sign of spring.
full_description: The Common Frog (Rana temporaria) is Britain's most widespread amphibian and one of the most beloved signs of spring. Adults are 5–9cm long with highly variable colouring — typically brown, olive, or grey with darker mottling, though reddish and yellowish forms also occur. The dark 'mask' running from the nostril through the eye to the shoulder, prominent golden-yellow eyes with horizontal slit pupils, and smooth but moist skin help distinguish frogs from the similar Common Toad. Frogs have powerful hind legs for jumping (50cm+ in a single leap) and are generally slimmer than toads. Their lifecycle is one of the most dramatic in nature: from jelly clumps of spawn in February–March, through free-swimming, algae-grazing tadpoles, to froglets emerging from the pond in June–July, to fully terrestrial adults that must nonetheless stay near water to keep their permeable skin moist. Adults return faithfully to their natal pond each spring, sometimes travelling hundreds of metres across roads and fields to breed.
native_info: Native throughout the UK and Ireland. One of the most common and widespread amphibians in Britain. Numbers have declined locally due to pond loss, drought, and disease (Ranavirus), but the species remains common.
wildlife_value: Tadpoles feed on algae (helping control algal blooms) and are food for newts, dragonfly larvae, diving beetles, and fish. Adults are important predators of slugs, snails, insects, and earthworms — of significant benefit in gardens and farms. Adults are themselves prey for herons, egrets, grass snakes, otters, and pike. A healthy frog population indicates a clean freshwater ecosystem.

life_stages.description: Frog spawn is laid in large gelatinous clumps in shallow, still water — ponds, ditches, or even large puddles and bird baths. Each clump can contain 1,000–3,000 black eggs, each surrounded by clear jelly that swells in water. The jelly protects the eggs and acts as a lens to warm them in weak spring sunlight. Multiple females often spawn in the same pond, creating vast aggregations. Spawn laid in too-shallow water or exposed to frost can be killed. The eggs hatch in 2–4 weeks, depending on temperature.

photos.caption: Common Frog spawn — black eggs in clear jelly clumps
Frogspawn in pond — a classic early spring sight
Frog spawn close-up showing individual eggs in jelly

life_stages.description: Tadpoles hatch as tiny, dark grey or black creatures with a large rounded head and a long, flattened tail for swimming. They breathe through feathery external gills at first, then internal gills as they develop. Tadpoles are primarily herbivores, grazing on algae using a specialised rasping mouth. They grow over 8–12 weeks from tiny hatchlings to fully formed tadpoles up to 3–4cm long. They are highly vulnerable to predation — newts, dragonfly larvae, diving beetles, and fish take enormous numbers.

photos.caption: Common Frog tadpoles feeding — dark bodies with long tails
Tadpoles in pond, feeding on algae
Frog tadpoles grazing

life_stages.description: After 8–12 weeks, the tadpole begins metamorphosis. Hind legs appear first, then front legs. The tail is gradually reabsorbed as the animal's digestive system switches from algae-grazing to insect-hunting. For a brief period the froglet has both legs and a tail — an extraordinary intermediate stage. Tiny froglets (just 1–2cm long) emerge from the pond in large numbers in June–July, often during or after rain, spreading into surrounding grassland and hedgerows. They must keep their skin moist and find shelter quickly.

photos.caption: Froglet at the final larval stage — legs developed, tail being reabsorbed

life_stages.description: Adult frogs live primarily on land in damp habitats — meadows, gardens, woodland floors — but must stay near water to keep their permeable skin moist. They breathe through both lungs and their moist skin. Adults hunt by sight, catching slugs, snails, worms, flies, and other small invertebrates with a rapid tongue strike. In autumn they seek damp, sheltered spots to hibernate through winter — under log piles, in compost heaps, or in pond mud. They emerge again in late winter (sometimes February in mild years) and make their way back to the breeding pond to spawn.

photos.caption: Common Frog adult — showing the dark eye mask and moist skin
Common Frog in profile showing typical brown colouring
Adult Common Frog — the colour pattern is highly variable
Adult Common Frog in grassland habitat

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are widespread British amphibians often found in the same habitats
similar_species.key_difference: Common Toad has warty, dry-looking skin (not smooth and moist). It is stockier, walks rather than hops, and has copper-coloured eyes (not golden). Toads are also generally larger (7–15cm vs 5–9cm for frogs).
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both spawn in spring, but Toads breed slightly later than Frogs (March–April vs February–March)

similar_species.similarity_note: A rarer British amphibian with similar colouring
similar_species.key_difference: Natterjack Toad has a distinctive yellow stripe running down the centre of its back — diagnostic and unmistakable. Also much rarer, mainly confined to sandy coasts and heathland. Extremely loud call.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Natterjack breeds later in spring than Common Frog

summary: Deep purple thistle-like flowers that attract an extraordinary range of butterflies to Old Down in summer. Watch a patch of Knapweed on a warm July day and you might count six or seven butterfly species in an hour.
full_description:
Common Knapweed (Centaurea nigra) is one of the most ecologically valuable wildflowers of chalk grassland. Reaching 30–90cm tall, it has stiff branched stems, slightly rough oblong leaves, and produces tough, brush-like purple flower heads from July through September. The flower head has a distinctive blackish-brown papery base (the 'knap'), giving the plant its name. Flowers are deep reddish-purple, resembling a small thistle but with no spines on the leaves.

At Old Down, Common Knapweed is one of the signature plants of high summer. On warm days in July and August, single clumps can attract Marbled White, Meadow Brown, Common Blue, Small Skipper, and Gatekeeper butterflies simultaneously — along with dozens of bumblebees and hoverflies. The flowers produce abundant nectar accessible to many insects, and the ripe seed heads are important food for Goldfinches in late summer and autumn.

Common Knapweed is sometimes confused with Greater Knapweed (Centaurea scabiosa), which also grows at Old Down. Greater Knapweed has conspicuous outer florets that spread out in rays around the flower head — like a crown — and deeply divided, feathery leaves. Common Knapweed has a simpler, brush-like flower head with no ray florets, and less divided leaves.
native_info: Native and common throughout England and Wales in meadows, grasslands, and roadsides, especially on well-drained soils including chalk. One of the signature species of lowland meadow and chalk grassland habitats.
wildlife_value: One of the most important nectar plants at Old Down. Visited by Marbled White, Meadow Brown, Common Blue, Gatekeeper, and Small Skipper butterflies, as well as multiple bumblebee species and hoverflies. Seed heads are eaten by Goldfinch and other finches. Caterpillars of several moth species feed on the leaves and stems.

life_stages.description: Knapweed grows as clumps of rough, oblong leaves in spring. The leaves are slightly grey-green with a rough texture. Stems begin to elongate in May–June before flowering begins.

The classic reddish-purple flower heads open from July, each on a tough stiff stem. The blackish-brown bracts at the base of each flower head are diagnostic — squeeze one gently and feel the stiff papery scales. At peak flowering a single established plant can carry 10–20 flower heads simultaneously.

photos.caption: Common Knapweed flowers in chalk grassland
Common Knapweed close-up showing the distinctive blackish bracts

life_stages.description: After flowering, the heads become papery seed heads that Goldfinches prize highly in autumn. Each seed has a small tuft of bristles and is spread by wind. The dried stems persist through winter, providing structure in the landscape.

similar_species.similarity_note: Both Centaurea species growing in the same habitats at Old Down
similar_species.key_difference: Greater Knapweed (Centaurea scabiosa) has larger flowers with conspicuous spreading outer ray florets forming a fringe, and deeply divided, feathery leaves. Common Knapweed has a simpler brush-like flower head with no rays, and less divided leaves.

confidence_note: The smallest British bat — about the size of a thumb. Dark brown fur with a dark face, ears, and wing membrane. Jerky, twisting flight low over vegetation and water. Emerges 20–30 minutes after sunset. Echolocates at 45kHz (a bat detector makes them audible as a rapid ticking).
weather_note: Only active in warm weather above about 8°C. Not seen in cold or wet conditions.
summary: Britain's most common bat — tiny, fast-flying, and acrobatic at dusk. A single Pipistrelle eats up to 3,000 midges and gnats per night. Stand by a hedgerow at sunset and watch them emerge to feed.
full_description:
The Common Pipistrelle is Britain's most abundant bat and most people's first bat sighting. It is tiny — weighing just 3–8g, about as heavy as a two-pence coin — but astonishingly agile. It emerges from its roost about 20–30 minutes after sunset and can often be watched feeding along hedgerows and woodland edges, making sharp twisting turns as it catches small moths, midges, and gnats on the wing. A single bat eats up to 3,000 insects per night.

Pipistrelles navigate and hunt by echolocation — they emit bursts of ultrasound at around 45kHz (well above human hearing) and listen to the echoes to build a 3D picture of their surroundings. A bat detector converts the calls to an audible clicking or ticking sound. If you have one, bring it to Old Down at dusk — the calls are very distinctive. The closely related Soprano Pipistrelle calls at 55kHz and is identified by bat detector only.

Bats are strictly protected under UK and EU law — it is illegal to disturb, handle, or harm a bat, or to block, damage, or destroy a roost (even when the bats are not present). If you find an injured bat on the ground, do not handle it with bare hands; contact the Bat Conservation Trust helpline.
danger_note: Do not handle bats with bare hands — although bat bites are very rare, bats can carry European Bat Lyssavirus. If you find a grounded bat, call the Bat Conservation Trust helpline (0345 1300 228) rather than handling it directly.
native_info: Native throughout Britain and Ireland. The most common bat species in the UK. Fully protected.
wildlife_value: A single Common Pipistrelle consumes up to 3,000 insects per night, providing significant pest control. Bats are important predators of moths (including some pest species), midges, and gnats. Pipistrelle roosts in buildings and trees are protected — loss of roost sites is a major conservation issue.

life_stages.description: Females gather in maternity roosts (often in roof spaces) in June–July to give birth. Each mother has a single pup. Pups are born naked and helpless, gaining fur within two weeks. They start flying at about three weeks. Maternity colonies can number hundreds of bats.

photos.caption: Pipistrelle pup — born blind and helpless, gaining fur within two weeks

life_stages.description: Watch for fast, jerky, twisting flight at dusk along hedgerows, woodland edges, and over water. Emerges 20–30 minutes after sunset. Tiny — barely larger than a large moth. The flight pattern is distinctive: rapid direction changes unlike any bird.

confidence_note: Spotted leaves are the key feature — look for dark purple blotches in rings or streaks. Flowers vary from almost white to deep pink-purple, which can cause confusion.
summary: Britain's most common orchid, but no less beautiful for it — pale pink flowers with intricate dotted patterns, and the distinctive spotted leaves that give it its name.
full_description:
The Common Spotted Orchid is the most widespread orchid in Britain, found in a huge range of habitats from chalk downland to woodland rides, road verges, and even garden lawns. The key ID feature is the spotted leaves: each leaf has dark purple blotches, rings, or streaks — no other common UK orchid has this combination of spotted leaves with pale pink flowers. The flower spike grows 20–50cm and carries many flowers, each one a delicate pale pink to deep pink-purple with darker spots and streaks on the three-lobed lip.

The flowers are pollinated by a range of bumblebees and solitary bees, attracted by both the colour and a mild vanilla-like scent. Unusually, the flowers produce nectar (unlike some related orchids that offer nothing and rely on deception). Plants grow from a pair of underground tubers and can live for many years, though they may not flower every season.

Common Spotted Orchid is highly variable: the flower colour ranges from almost white to vivid pink-purple, and the lip pattern varies enormously. This makes identification tricky in some cases, but the spotted leaves are always the clincher. Like all native orchids it is protected by law and should never be picked or uprooted.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. The most common and widespread British orchid. Found in a wide range of habitats but most abundant on neutral to calcareous soils.
wildlife_value: Produces nectar and is pollinated by a range of bumblebees and solitary bees. The flowers are also visited by hoverflies. As a perennial of unimproved grassland, its presence indicates that the site has not been fertilised or heavily disturbed. All native orchids are protected by the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

life_stages.description: The spotted leaves emerge before the flower spike, making this the best time to find and identify young plants. Look for 4–8 shiny leaves arranged in a spiral, each marked with dark purple blotches.

photos.caption: Common Spotted Orchid spotted leaves — the key ID feature

life_stages.description: The flower spike rises to 20–50cm with dozens of pale pink to deep pink flowers. Each flower has a three-lobed lip marked with darker pink or purple dots and lines. The spike flowers from the bottom upward, so bottom flowers are fully open while the top is still in bud.

photos.caption: Common Spotted Orchid in full flower, showing the variable pink colouring

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are pink orchids of chalk grassland
similar_species.key_difference: Pyramidal Orchid has unspotted leaves and a tight pyramid-shaped flowerhead. Common Spotted has spotted leaves and a more cylindrical spike.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Common Spotted flowers slightly earlier — May to July vs Pyramidal's June to August

photos.caption: Common Spotted Orchid in flower
Common Spotted Orchid spotted leaves

confidence_note: Yellow and black banded abdomen, narrow waist, and smooth (not fuzzy) body. Four wings. The yellow face has a characteristic anchor or dagger-shaped black mark — use this to distinguish from German Wasp (which has three dots). In flight, legs hang down.
summary: Wasps are misunderstood — all summer they are ferocious hunters of caterpillars and flies, doing a huge amount of pest control. Only in late summer, when the colony collapses and workers go sugar-seeking, do they become a nuisance. They sting only in defence.
full_description:
The Common Wasp has an image problem. Most people associate wasps with late-summer nuisance — crawling over jam sandwiches, buzzing aggressively around picnics, and stinging unprovoked. But this behaviour happens only for a few weeks at the end of the colony's life. From April to August, wasps are beneficial predators: they catch caterpillars, flies, aphids, and other insects by the thousand to feed their larvae, doing enormous amounts of pest control in gardens and crops.

A Common Wasp nest is a masterpiece of engineering. Starting from scratch each spring, the queen builds a nest from chewed wood fibre (paper) — she chews bark and dead wood, mixes it with saliva, and applies it as a paste that dries to a papery material. Workers expand the nest through summer until a colony may contain 10,000 workers. The hexagonal cells are used for raising larvae.

In late summer, the new queens and males are produced, the colony collapses, and the workers — suddenly without larvae to feed — look for sugar instead. This is when they become a nuisance. Stay calm near wasps, cover food and drink, and resist swatting — a crushed wasp releases an alarm pheromone that makes nearby wasps aggressive.
danger_note: Wasps sting in self-defence when they feel threatened. The sting is painful but not medically significant for most people. However, some people are allergic to wasp venom — a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is a medical emergency. People with known allergies should carry an EpiPen.
native_info: Native throughout Britain and Ireland. Very common everywhere.
wildlife_value: A major predator of caterpillars, flies, aphids, and other insects in summer — providing significant pest control. Wasps also act as pollinators of some flowers and fig species. Nest wood-pulp building recycles dead wood. Wasp nests are raided by Badgers and Green Woodpeckers for the larvae.

life_stages.description: Newly-mated queens emerge from hibernation in March–April and begin building a new nest alone. She raises the first workers entirely by herself. Queens are larger than workers with the same colour pattern.
Workers (sterile females) hunt insects to feed the larvae and expand the nest. In late summer, look for workers feeding on ripe fruit, sap runs, and any sweet food source as the colony winds down.

Common Wasp — bold yellow and black stripes, smooth body (not fuzzy like a bee)
