confidence_note: Easily confused with Hemlock (Conium maculatum), which is extremely toxic. Always check for plain green stems and no smell.
summary: Tall, lacy white-flowered plant that foams along hedgerows and roadsides in spring. One of the most abundant wildflowers of the English countryside — and easily confused with the deadly Hemlock.
full_description: Cow Parsley (Anthriscus sylvestris) creates frothy white drifts along hedgerows, field margins, and woodland edges from April to June. Reaching 40–100cm tall, it has hollow green stems (never purple-blotched), finely divided feathery leaves in a triangular outline, and flat-topped white flower heads (umbels) — each a compound of smaller umbrellas branching from the central stem. The plant has no distinctive smell when leaves are crushed, which is an important contrast with the similar-looking but extremely toxic Hemlock. Cow Parsley belongs to the carrot family (Apiaceae), named for the characteristic umbrella-shaped flower heads. It is a biennial or short-lived perennial, dying back in winter and re-emerging vigorously in spring from a taproot.
danger_note: The plant itself is harmless, but it closely resembles Hemlock (Conium maculatum), which is extremely toxic. Cow Parsley has plain green stems and no smell. Hemlock has purple-blotched hollow stems and a musty unpleasant smell. Never eat any white-flowered umbellifer without expert verification.
native_info: Native throughout the UK and common in most habitats, particularly in fertile soils along roadsides, hedgerows, and woodland edges.
wildlife_value: An important early food source for many insects. The open flower structure makes nectar easily accessible to hoverflies, beetles, and small bees. Several moth species use Cow Parsley as a larval food plant, and hollow dead stems provide nesting sites for solitary bees over winter.

life_stages.description: In early spring, Cow Parsley emerges with fresh bright green feathery leaves. Already recognisable by its distinctive finely divided, triangular leaf shape at 10–30cm tall. The stems are distinctly hollow and plain green — look closely and you can see they are not solid. No flowers yet, but the plant is growing rapidly in the warming hedgerow.

The iconic white flower heads appear in spring, creating lacy clouds along hedgerows. Each flower cluster is a flat-topped umbrella shape (umbel) typical of the carrot family. Multiple smaller umbels branch from the central stem to form a compound umbel. The plant is now 60–100cm tall. Hoverflies, bees, and beetles visit constantly on sunny days. If you crush a leaf it should smell faintly green but pleasant — never musty or unpleasant.

life_stages.description: After flowering, the plant develops characteristic paired seeds — two elongated, ribbed seeds joined together, hanging in clusters where the flowers were. The seeds turn brown and disperse by wind or catching on passing animals. The brown seed heads are less showy than the flowers but still recognisable. The plant dies back from the lower stems upwards through July.

similar_species.similarity_note: Very similar appearance — another white-flowered umbellifer of hedgerows
similar_species.key_difference: Rough Chervil has hairy, solid stems with reddish spots or blotching, and slightly smaller flower heads

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are white-flowered umbellifers appearing from late spring. Wild Carrot is particularly easy to confuse with Cow Parsley in early season before it develops its key features.
similar_species.key_difference: Wild Carrot has a single red/purple flower in the centre of the umbel and leaves that smell distinctly of carrot when crushed. The seed head curls inward forming a characteristic 'bird's nest' shape.

confidence_note: The drooping yellow flower clusters with orange/red spots inside are distinctive. Could be confused with Primrose, but Primrose flowers face upwards and are paler yellow.
summary: Golden yellow drooping flower clusters on chalk grassland — an indicator of ancient, undisturbed meadows. The orange spots inside each flower are diagnostic.
full_description:
Cowslips (Primula veris) are charming low-growing plants of chalk and limestone grasslands, old meadows, and field edges. Reaching only 10–25cm tall, they emerge in early spring as a rosette of wrinkled, oblong leaves before sending up flowering stems in April. The golden yellow flowers droop in characteristic one-sided clusters — each bell-shaped bloom has five notched petals and, crucially, orange or red spots at the petal base. Those spots are the best diagnostic feature, distinguishing Cowslips instantly from the similar Primrose. A sweet, light fragrance hangs over good patches on warm spring afternoons.

Cowslips are a reliable indicator of ancient, undisturbed chalk grassland. They cannot survive fields that have been ploughed or heavily fertilised, so large populations — like those at Old Down — tell you the grassland has been relatively undisturbed for many decades. At Old Down, Cowslips appear in April as one of the first great wildflower events of spring, sometimes carpeting entire slopes in golden yellow before most other flowers have opened.

The relationship between Cowslips and the Duke of Burgundy butterfly is one of nature's most specific partnerships: caterpillars feed almost exclusively on Cowslip and Primrose leaves, making good Cowslip populations essential for this nationally scarce butterfly, historically recorded at Old Down. The long-tongued Bombus hortorum (Garden Bumblebee) can reach nectar deep in the narrow flower tube that shorter-tongued insects cannot access, giving it a private food source in early spring.
native_info: Native throughout England and Wales, preferring chalky or limestone soils. Scarce in Scotland and north England. Common at Old Down and similar chalk grassland sites.
wildlife_value: A critical early nectar source for insects emerging from winter dormancy. Visited by early bumblebees, honeybees, Orange-tip butterflies, and hoverflies. The Garden Bumblebee (Bombus hortorum) has a tongue long enough to reach nectar deep in the flower tube. The leaves are the sole larval food plant for the Duke of Burgundy butterfly, a nationally scarce species historically recorded at Old Down.

life_stages.description: Cowslips emerge from winter dormancy as clusters of wrinkled, oval leaves lying flat against the ground in a rosette. Even at this stage, the distinctive leaf texture — wrinkled like crumpled paper, with a slightly rough surface — helps identify them from other early-spring plants. The leaves are 5–10cm long with a slightly irregular, wavy margin.

Flower stems begin to rise from the centre of the leaf rosette. The stems are slightly hairy and pale green. You can see the developing round buds forming in a cluster at the top of each stem. The buds are slightly darker yellow-green before they open.

Cowslips produce their iconic drooping clusters of golden yellow flowers. Look inside each flower — the orange or red spots at the petal base are diagnostic of this species. The nodding flower heads give the plant a distinctive bowing character quite unlike the upward-facing Primrose. At this peak stage, a single patch can contain dozens of flowering plants, creating a haze of golden yellow across the grassland. Each plant can have 2–5 flower stems.

Cowslip in chalk grassland habitat
Cowslip flowers close-up — note the drooping, bell-shaped blooms
Cowslip — golden yellow flowers on tall stems

life_stages.description: After flowering, the petals fall and seed pods form at the top of the stalks. The pods are oval capsules that split open when ripe to release small, round seeds. The plant then begins to die back as summer arrives, with the leaves yellowing and shrinking before disappearing until the following spring.

similar_species.key_difference: False Oxlip has upward-facing flowers like Primrose but on tall stems like Cowslip. Less common than either parent.

summary: One of Britain's most important wildflowers — not a weed. Golden flowers in early spring are a lifeline for queen bumblebees just waking from winter. The round white clock seed heads are irresistible to blow and each one carries seeds that can travel kilometres on the wind.
full_description:
The Dandelion (Taraxacum officinale agg.) is one of the most ecologically valuable and overlooked wildflowers in Britain. What looks like a single golden flower is actually a composite head of 100–200 tiny individual flowers, each containing both pollen and nectar. The deeply toothed leaves — 'dent de lion' (lion's tooth in French) is the origin of the name — grow in a flat rosette, with the teeth pointing back towards the centre. All parts produce a milky white latex sap when broken. Plants can grow 5–40cm tall.

In early spring, Dandelions are one of the first flowers to open after winter, often by February in mild weather. At this time they provide an absolutely critical food source for queen bumblebees that have recently emerged from hibernation and need energy before they can establish their new colonies. Without early-flowering plants like Dandelions, queen bumblebees may fail. They are also one of the first nectar sources for Orange-tip and Small Tortoiseshell butterflies. Dandelions continue flowering sporadically through summer and autumn, with a second peak in late summer.

The seed clock — a perfect sphere of parachuted seeds — is an engineering masterpiece. Each seed has a parachute of fine bristles (a pappus) that generates a vortex ring in the air, allowing seeds to stay aloft far longer than their weight would suggest. A single plant can produce 200 seeds per head, with several heads per plant. Goldfinches and other finches eat the seeds before they fully disperse. Note: Dandelion is technically an aggregate species — there are actually hundreds of micro-species within the Taraxacum group, distinguishable only by specialists.
native_info: Native throughout the UK in almost every habitat. Abundant in meadows, lawns, roadsides, and disturbed ground. One of the most widespread plants in the northern hemisphere.
wildlife_value: Critical early nectar and pollen source for queen bumblebees emerging from hibernation in February–March. Visited by over 100 species of insect including many specialist mining bees. Seeds eaten by Goldfinch, Linnet, and Greenfinch. Leaves eaten by many moth caterpillars and by rabbits. One of the most important plants for urban and rural wildlife alike.

life_stages.description: The deeply toothed, strap-shaped leaves form a flat rosette at ground level, present all year in mild conditions. The lobes of each leaf point backwards towards the base — run your finger from tip to base and feel them pointing back like the teeth of a lion (dent de lion). Snap a leaf and white milky latex sap oozes out.

photos.caption: Dandelion leaves showing the deeply toothed 'lion's tooth' lobes

life_stages.description: The hollow, leafless flower stems rise from the rosette, each topped with a single golden flower head made up of 100–200 individual ray florets. Flowers close at night and in dull weather. On sunny days they open fully and are covered in insects. The first flowers can appear as early as February in mild years.

photos.caption: Dandelion flower in full bloom

life_stages.description: After flowering, the golden head closes for a day or two before reopening as the perfect spherical seed clock — a globe of white parachuted seeds, each attached to a single seed by a stalk of fine bristles. The whole structure is 3–5cm across. On still days seeds drift slowly upward; on windy days they can travel hundreds of metres. Count the puffs it takes to blow all the seeds off — and check the time!

photos.caption: Dandelion clock — perfect sphere of parachuted seeds
Dandelion seed head close-up showing parachute bristles

similar_species.similarity_note: Both produce yellow dandelion-type flowers in grassland
similar_species.key_difference: Cat's-ear (Hypochaeris radicata) has branched flower stems (Dandelion stems are unbranched), solid stems (Dandelion stems are hollow), and smaller rougher leaves with rounder lobes. Cat's-ear also has small scale-like leaves on the stem.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both flower spring–autumn, Cat's-ear peaks June–September

photos.caption: Dandelion — one of Britain's most important early wildflowers
Dandelion clock — perfect sphere ready for dispersal
Dandelion seed parachutes close-up
Dandelion leaves — deeply toothed like a lion's teeth

confidence_note: Large (2–3cm), all-black, elongated rove beetle with very short wing cases (elytra) leaving most of the abdomen exposed and flexible. When threatened, raises the tail upward like a scorpion and opens its large jaws. Unmistakeable in this defensive posture.
summary: The most dramatic beetle in Britain — when threatened it curls its tail up like a scorpion and opens its fangs. Completely harmless to people, but a ferocious predator of slugs, worms, and other invertebrates.
full_description:
The Devil's Coach Horse is a rove beetle (family Staphylinidae) — a family characterised by very short wing cases that leave most of the abdomen exposed and flexible. This gives the Devil's Coach Horse a scorpion-like appearance, especially when threatened: it raises the tip of its abdomen upward, opens its large, powerful jaws, and releases a foul-smelling chemical from glands at the tail tip. This defensive display is dramatic but entirely harmless to people.

The Devil's Coach Horse is a nocturnal predator, hunting under logs, stones, in leaf litter, and along garden paths at night. It eats slugs, worms, fly larvae, and other invertebrates — making it a genuine garden and woodland ally. It moves fast and purposefully, and can bite if handled carelessly (its mandibles are surprisingly strong), though the bite is no worse than a small pinch.

In Irish folklore, the Devil's Coach Horse was believed to be a manifestation of evil and could supposedly absorb sins by chewing them. Medieval Europeans thought it could curse people with a glance. In reality it is one of the most beneficial beetles in the garden.
danger_note: The defensive display (raised abdomen, open jaws) looks alarming but is harmless. The bite from the large mandibles is a mild pinch only. The chemical secretion from the tail tip smells unpleasant but is not toxic. Do not handle unnecessarily.
native_info: Native throughout Britain and Ireland. Very common in a wide range of habitats.
wildlife_value: An important nocturnal predator of slugs, worms, fly larvae, and other invertebrates. Significant in controlling slug populations. The larvae are also predatory, living in soil and leaf litter.

life_stages.description: Look under logs, stones, and in leaf litter. At night it hunts actively on paths and in hedgerow bases. If disturbed it adopts the scorpion posture — tail raised, jaws open — then scurries away fast. The short wing cases (elytra) leave the flexible abdomen completely exposed.

photos.caption: Devil's Coach Horse in defensive posture — tail raised like a scorpion
Devil's Coach Horse — large black rove beetle, completely harmless to people
Devil's Coach Horse in defensive posture
Devil's Coach Horse

confidence_note: Small, moth-like, brown-grey butterfly that rests with wings held flat like a moth. Dark grey-brown with faint white spots. Often mistaken for a moth but note the characteristic clubbed skipper antennae. Flies very fast and low.
weather_note: Flies only in warm sunshine. On cloudy days it rests with wings spread flat on warm bare ground or stones — surprisingly easy to find when not flying.
summary: Don't be put off by the name — the Dingy Skipper is a Red List species and one of Old Down's most special butterflies. Find it in May–June along south-facing slopes where Bird's-foot Trefoil grows, resting flat-winged on bare chalk.
full_description:
The Dingy Skipper suffers badly from its name — 'dingy' is deeply unfair. Yes, it is brown and grey, but it is a UK Red List butterfly (population declined by over 50% since the 1970s), a specialist of high-quality chalk and limestone grassland, and an exciting find at Old Down. It is one of the indicators that the site is genuinely special for chalk grassland invertebrates.

The Dingy Skipper is a member of the skipper family, which are small, rapid-flying butterflies with a distinctive thickset body and hooked antenna tip. Dingy Skippers rest with wings held flat (like a moth) rather than folded vertically, often on bare warm soil or stone. The grey-brown chequered pattern is intricate at close range. On cold or cloudy days they roost in dead flower heads, holding the wings wrapped tightly around themselves.

The sole larval foodplant is Bird's-foot Trefoil (Lotus corniculatus). Eggs are laid singly on the leaves. Caterpillars live inside a rolled leaf tied with silk. The species overwinters as a caterpillar inside a rolled grass stem, then pupates in spring. There is one brood per year, flying May to June. The decline is linked to loss of chalk grassland and abandonment of traditional management that kept swards short and open.
native_info: Native throughout England and Wales. UK Red List — population declined over 50% since 1976. Mainly southern England.
wildlife_value: A specialist chalk grassland species whose presence reliably indicates high-quality, traditionally managed habitat. The caterpillars feed only on Bird's-foot Trefoil. Finding Dingy Skippers at Old Down confirms the quality of the chalk grassland management.

life_stages.description: Look along south-facing slopes with Bird's-foot Trefoil in warm sunshine in May–June. On cloudy days, find them roosting in dead knapweed or thistle heads, wings wrapped around the stem. On sunny days they fly fast and low, settling on bare chalk or soil with wings spread flat.

photos.caption: Dingy Skipper — grey-brown moth-like butterfly resting with flat wings
Dingy Skipper on chalk grassland — wings spread flat in typical resting posture
Dingy Skipper
Dingy Skipper resting flat

confidence_note: Large (3–5cm) pale pink or white five-petalled flowers in June–July. Arching thorny stems. Oval, toothed leaflets in groups of 5–7. Distinctive oval red rose hips in autumn.
summary: Britain's classic wild rose — delicate pink five-petalled flowers in midsummer, then brilliant red oval hips in autumn that are packed with vitamin C. The thorny arching stems make the best impenetrable hedgerows.
full_description:
The Dog Rose is the most familiar wild rose in Britain and one of the most beautiful hedgerow plants. In June and July, the long arching stems are studded with large, delicate flowers — typically pale pink fading to almost white, with five broad petals and a central boss of golden stamens, and a faint sweet scent. The plant scrambles up through hedgerow shrubs using its curved thorns as grappling hooks, sometimes reaching 3–5 metres.

The flowers last only a few days each, but a hedgerow of Dog Rose in full flower in late June is genuinely beautiful. By September the petals have long gone and the plant is dotted instead with bright red oval hips — the fruit, containing the seeds. Rose hips are famous for their vitamin C content (higher than most citrus fruits) and were widely gathered during WWII when citrus fruit was unavailable. They are an important winter food for birds, especially Blackbird, Song Thrush, Redwing, and Fieldfare, which swallow them whole and spread the seeds in their droppings.

The old name 'Dog Rose' is ancient: it may come from the belief that the root could cure a bite from a mad dog, or simply from 'dag' meaning a dagger, referring to the thorns.
danger_note: The hairy seeds (achenes) inside the hips are irritating if eaten directly. The hips themselves are fine but always remove the seeds before eating.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. Very common in hedgerows and scrub. The most widespread of the native wild roses.
wildlife_value: Flowers provide pollen and nectar for bumblebees, hoverflies, and solitary bees. The hips are eaten by Blackbird, Song Thrush, Redwing, Fieldfare, and small mammals. The dense thorny stems provide excellent nesting habitat for Dunnock, Whitethroat, and other hedgerow birds. Galls on Dog Rose ('Robin's pincushion', caused by the gall wasp Diplolepis rosae) are a mini-habitat for dozens of insect species.

life_stages.description: Large, elegant five-petalled flowers open in June–July. Each flower lasts only a few days. The colour varies from deep pink to almost white. The golden stamens in the centre attract beetles and bees.

photos.caption: Dog Rose flowers — five pale pink petals with golden stamens
Dog Rose in hedgerow

life_stages.description: Smooth, oval, bright red hips ripen September–October and persist into winter. They are a vital food for birds and are extremely rich in vitamin C. Look for the dried flower remnants at the tip of the hip.

photos.caption: Dog Rose hips in autumn — brilliant red and packed with vitamin C
Dog Rose flowers
Dog Rose in hedgerow
Dog Rose hips

confidence_note: Compound leaves with 5–7 pairs of toothed leaflets. Flat-topped cream flower clusters (corymbs) in May–June. Black elderberries in September. Crush a leaf and it has a distinctive unpleasant smell. Pithy hollow stems.
summary: The hedgerow's medicine cabinet and free larder — clusters of cream flowers for elderflower cordial in June, then drooping bunches of black berries for elderberry wine in September. A shrub with something for everyone.
full_description:
Elder is one of Britain's most distinctive hedgerow shrubs, and one of the most useful to both wildlife and people. In late May and June, it is smothered in flat-topped clusters of tiny cream flowers with a heady, sweet, slightly musty scent — elderflower cordial made from these is a genuine summer delicacy. By September, those flowers have become drooping clusters of small, shiny black berries (elderberries) — beloved of Blackbird, Robin, Starling, and countless other birds, and the basis of elderberry wine, jam, and cordial.

Elder grows fast on disturbed, nitrogen-rich soils — it loves old badger setts, rabbit warrens, and road verges. The bark is corky and rough, with a distinctive warty texture. The hollow pithy stems were used by country children for centuries to make peashooters and simple musical instruments. The leaves have a very distinctive unpleasant smell when crushed — this immediately distinguishes elder from other compound-leaved shrubs. The leaves, bark, and raw berries contain compounds that cause nausea if eaten in quantity; the cooked berries are safe and delicious.

Despite its modest size, elder is one of the most wildlife-rich shrubs in the hedgerow. The flowers attract over 50 species of insects; the berries are eaten by at least 30 species of bird; and the pithy stems are hollowed out by small solitary bees for nesting.
danger_note: Raw elderberries, leaves, and bark can cause nausea and vomiting if eaten in quantity. Cooked berries are safe and widely used. Do not eat any part of this plant raw.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. Very common in hedgerows, woodland edges, and disturbed ground. Fast-growing and opportunistic.
wildlife_value: The flowers attract over 50 insect species including hoverflies, bees, and butterflies. The berries are eaten by Blackbird, Robin, Starling, Blackcap, and many other birds in autumn — a crucial high-energy food source for migrant and resident birds alike. Hollow stems are used by some solitary bees for nesting. The dense growth provides cover for nesting birds and small mammals.

life_stages.description: Large, flat-topped clusters of tiny cream flowers cover the shrub in May–June. The sweet, heady scent is one of the characteristic smells of early summer. Each flat head (corymb) can be 10–20cm across.

photos.caption: Elder flowers — flat cream corymbs with a heady summer scent
Elder flowers close-up

life_stages.description: By August–September, the flower clusters have become heavy drooping bunches of small, shiny black berries. The ripe berries stain fingers purple. Birds strip them rapidly — a loaded elder bush may be stripped within a day or two in autumn.

photos.caption: Elderberries — black, drooping clusters in autumn
Elder — mature leaves and ripening elderberries on the branch
Elder flowers
Elderberries in autumn
Elder — mature leaves and ripening elderberries on the branch

confidence_note: Deeply lobed leaves with tiny ear-lobes (auricles) at the base. Acorns on long stalks (2–8cm) — this is the key feature that separates it from Sessile Oak, where acorns are stalkless.
summary: Britain's most famous tree — the English Oak supports more wildlife than any other native tree, with over 500 species of insects alone. Look out for oak galls: strange alien-looking growths made by tiny wasps.
full_description:
The English Oak may be Britain's most iconic tree. It can live for over a thousand years, its ancient specimens providing shelter and food for an extraordinary community of creatures. Oak supports more species of insects — around 500 — than any other native British tree, and through these insects it supports bats, birds, and small mammals in a cascading web of life. An oak is not just a tree; it is a habitat.

The leaves are deeply lobed with distinctive ear-shaped lobes (auricles) at the base where the leaf stalk meets the blade. Acorns appear in September–October and are held on long, thin stalks — this is how to tell English Oak from the similar Sessile Oak, whose acorns sit directly on the twig without a stalk. The bark of young oaks is smooth and greyish, becoming deeply furrowed and ridged on old trees.

Oak galls are extraordinary structures created when tiny gall wasps lay their eggs in the tree's tissue. The tree responds by growing a protective swelling around the egg. The most dramatic is the oak apple (a spongy green/brown ball, 2–3cm across) and the marble gall (a hard, round, pea-sized growth caused by Andricus kollari). Each gall species is made by a different wasp species, and each is a tiny world of its own.
native_info: Native throughout England, Wales, and parts of Scotland. One of the commonest British trees. The dominant tree of lowland oak woodland.
wildlife_value: Supports around 500 species of insects, including many specialist oak-feeders. The caterpillars of moths that feed on oak leaves are the primary food source for Blue Tit and Great Tit chicks in spring. Acorns are a critical food for Jays (who cache thousands per year, effectively planting oaks), squirrels, Wood Pigeons, deer, and mice. Oak galls are home to dozens of specialist gall wasps and their parasitoids. Old oaks with cavities provide roost sites for bats and nest holes for owls and woodpeckers.

life_stages.description: In April–May, oak produces both new leaves and long drooping catkins (male flowers) at the same time. The new leaves are pale, reddish-bronze. Look for the round female flowers — tiny, on separate stalks — that will become acorns.

photos.caption: English Oak leaves and structure

life_stages.description: From late spring through autumn, look for oak galls — strange swellings on leaves, twigs, and buds. Each is made by a different species of tiny gall wasp. Marble galls (round, hard, 1–2cm) are the most common; oak apples (spongy, 2–4cm) appear in early summer. They are completely harmless — just extraordinary miniature worlds.

photos.caption: Oak marble galls — each one contains the larva of a gall wasp

life_stages.description: Acorns ripen from green to brown in September–October. English Oak acorns are held on long stalks (2–8cm) — this is the most reliable way to tell it from Sessile Oak. A productive oak drops thousands of acorns, most of which are eaten by squirrels, Jays, and mice.

photos.caption: English Oak acorns on long stalks — the key ID feature
English Oak
English Oak acorns on stalks
Oak marble galls

confidence_note: Fox prints are oval, with 4 toes in a diamond pattern and a triangular central pad. Claws pointing forward. Usually in a straight line (foxes 'register' — hind foot falls in front foot print). Scat is twisted, tapered at one end, placed on prominent spots.
summary: Finding fox signs is easy once you know what to look for — but telling fox prints from dog prints trips up even experienced trackers. The key is the neat diamond toe arrangement, straight walking line, and pointed twisted scat on prominent spots.
full_description:
Foxes leave abundant signs throughout their territory, and learning to read them is a satisfying skill. The most reliable sign is the footprint: four toes arranged in a rough diamond around a triangular central pad, with claw marks pointing forward. The key difference from a domestic dog is the tight, neat arrangement of the toes (you can draw an imaginary 'X' between the central toes and the outer toes), and the fact that fox prints are usually in a very straight line — foxes walk efficiently and place their hind foot almost exactly in the print of their front foot (this is called 'registering'). Dog prints are more sprawling and irregular.

Fox scat (droppings) is one of the most distinctive signs: dark, twisted, pointed at one end, often with fur, feathers, or berry seeds visible. Crucially, foxes are conspicuous scent markers — they deliberately leave scat on prominent spots: on top of molehills, on stones, on the middle of paths, on fence posts. This is territorial advertisement. Fresh fox scat has a strong, sharp, earthy-musky smell. The smell of fox is also often noticeable near an earth (den) — a sweet, musky undertone often described as distinctive.

Other signs include: the earth itself (a large hole, often with a well-worn path and scattered bones/feathers nearby), flattened grass 'runs' through hedgerow bases, and in winter, prints in snow showing the characteristically straight walking gait.
native_info: Signs found throughout the UK wherever foxes are present — essentially everywhere.
wildlife_value: Fox scent marks and signs are important ecological signals. The presence of fox territory depresses rabbit activity in an area, which in turn reduces grazing pressure on vegetation. Reading fox signs helps build a picture of the invisible world of nocturnal wildlife at Old Down.

life_stages.description: Look for oval prints with 4 toes in a diamond pattern and clear claw marks pointing forward. Best seen in soft mud, wet soil, or snow. Fox prints appear in a very straight line — the hind foot registers almost exactly into the front foot print. Measure the print: 5–6cm long × 4–4.5cm wide.

photos.caption: Fox tracks in snow — oval prints in a straight, registering line

life_stages.description: Fox scat is dark brown-black, 7–10cm long, twisted, and pointed at one end. It is deliberately placed on prominent spots — on top of molehills, on stones at path junctions, on fence posts. Look for fur, feathers, berry seeds, or beetle cases in the scat. Fresh scat has a distinctive strong foxy smell.

The fox earth is a burrow, often in a bank, among tree roots, or dug into an old rabbit warren. The entrance is typically 20–25cm wide, with a well-worn path leading to it. Look for scattered bones, feathers, and fur nearby. A distinctive sweet-musky smell may be noticeable near the earth.

photos.caption: Fox tracks in snow — oval prints in a straight, registering line

confidence_note: Snails carry a spiral shell and leave a silver slime trail. Garden Snail: large (2.5–4cm), mottled brown. Banded snails (Cepaea): smaller, brightly coloured — yellow, pink, or brown with variable dark bands. Found on vegetation and damp paths after rain.
weather_note: Most active at night and after rain. In dry weather they seal their shell opening with dried mucus (aestivation) and wait for moisture.
summary: Two types to look for at Old Down — the familiar large Garden Snail on vegetation, and the beautiful colourful Banded Snails on chalk grassland. The banded snails are especially interesting: the colour and band pattern vary from snail to snail, even in the same patch.
full_description:
Old Down is home to two distinct groups of snails worth knowing about. The Garden Snail (Cornu aspersum) is the familiar large snail — mottled brown with a thick, globular shell — common on vegetation, paths, and in hedgerow bases. It is the classic 'snail with a shell' of the British garden and countryside.

More interesting ecologically are the banded snails (Cepaea species) found on chalk grassland. White-lipped Snail (Cepaea hortensis) and Brown-lipped Snail (Cepaea nemoralis) are both beautiful, colourful snails whose shells vary dramatically in colour and banding: yellow, pink, or brown, with anywhere from zero to five dark bands. This variation is genetic — it is one of the most studied examples of visible evolution in real time. The colour and banding pattern affects survival (camouflage against different backgrounds) and body temperature (darker shells warm up faster in cold conditions).

Snails are molluscs — related to slugs, mussels, and octopuses. Their muscular 'foot' glides on a carpet of mucus, leaving the silver trail. In dry weather they seal the shell opening with dried mucus and wait. In winter they hibernate under leaf litter. Song Thrushes are specialist snail predators, smashing shells on a favourite 'anvil' stone — look for a stone with broken shell fragments as a sign that a Song Thrush regularly hunts nearby.
native_info: Garden Snail is native/naturalised throughout Britain. Cepaea snails are native chalk grassland species.
wildlife_value: Song Thrushes are specialist snail predators — their distinctive 'anvil' behaviour (smashing snail shells on a favourite stone) is one of the clearest signs of a healthy snail population. Hedgehogs, Badgers, and ground beetles also eat snails. Chalk grassland Cepaea snails are an important food source for Song Thrush and are indicators of chalk grassland quality.

life_stages.description: Most active at night and after rain. In daytime find them resting under leaves, on walls, or sealed with dried mucus waiting for rain. After rain, walk the paths and look for the silver trails leading to snails feeding on low vegetation.

photos.caption: Garden Snail — the familiar large mottled-brown snail
Brown-lipped Banded Snail — colour and banding varies dramatically between individuals
White-lipped Snail (Cepaea hortensis) — chalk grassland species
Garden Snail
Brown-lipped Banded Snail
White-lipped Snail

confidence_note: Round, often brownish abdomen with a distinctive white cross or diadem of white spots on the top. Females are much larger than males. Builds a classic circular orb web with a spiral of sticky thread. Sits in the centre of the web, or hides in a retreat at the edge connected by a signal thread.
summary: The architect of the most beautiful structure in nature — the orb web, rebuilt every day. The dew-covered web on a September morning is one of Britain's iconic sights. Spiders are not insects — they have 8 legs and two body parts, not six legs and three.
full_description:
The Garden Spider builds one of nature's most impressive structures: a near-perfect circular orb web with a spiral of sticky thread radiating out from a central hub. The spider typically rebuilds this web every day or two — consuming the old web to recycle the protein, then spinning a new one in the small hours of the morning. A web may contain 20–60 metres of silk. On dewy September mornings, hundreds of webs glitter across hedgerows and grassland at Old Down.

The Garden Spider is a spider, not an insect — an important distinction to make with children. Spiders have 8 legs (insects have 6), two body parts — cephalothorax and abdomen — (insects have three), and fangs (chelicerae) rather than jaws. The Garden Spider's bite is not medically significant in the UK — it could theoretically pierce skin but almost never does, and the venom is not dangerous to people. They are completely harmless.

Females grow much larger than males over the summer, reaching 10–13mm by autumn compared to the male's 4–8mm. After mating in autumn, females lay a silk egg sac containing 300–900 eggs, often hidden in a crevice or under bark. The female dies after the first hard frost; the eggs overwinter and hatch in spring.
native_info: Native throughout Britain and Ireland. Very common everywhere.
wildlife_value: An important predator of flying insects including flies, wasps, moths, and beetles caught in the orb web. Garden Spiders are eaten by Blue Tits, Robins, and other insectivorous birds. The webs also trap many non-pest insects, but the ecological net effect is positive as a predator.

life_stages.description: Females reach full size by September — large, round-abdomened, with the distinctive white cross markings. They sit in the centre of the web waiting for prey, or hide in a curled leaf at the edge connected by a signal thread. September morning dew reveals dozens of webs in hedgerows.

photos.caption: Garden Spider in its orb web — look for the white cross mark on the abdomen
Garden Spider — round abdomen with distinctive white diadem spots
Garden Spider in web
Garden Spider

confidence_note: Black and white with red under the tail (both sexes). Male has a red patch on the back of his head; female has none; juvenile has a red cap. The drumming on dead wood in spring is unmistakeable. Undulating flight — a few wingbeats, then a brief fold.
summary: The pied woodpecker with the machine-gun drum — a rapid burst of hammering on a dead branch in spring that carries for hundreds of metres. Look for the bright red flash under the tail and, on the male, a red patch on the back of the head.
full_description:
The Great Spotted Woodpecker is the most common and widespread of Britain's three woodpecker species, and one of the easiest woodland birds to find. Its bold black and white plumage with a crimson-red patch under the tail is distinctive, and it is often heard before it is seen — either the sharp 'tchick!' alarm call, or the extraordinary rapid drumming in spring. Drumming is not pecking for food: it is territorial advertisement and mate attraction, like a song, created by hammering on a resonant dead branch 10–20 times per second. It carries far.

The bill is a remarkable tool. The woodpecker hammers into dead wood to extract beetle larvae and wood-boring insects from inside the trunk — a food source no other bird can reach. The tongue is extraordinarily long (much longer than the bill), barbed at the tip, and coated in sticky saliva; it can be extended to probe deeply into excavated chambers. In autumn and winter, Great Spotted Woodpeckers also eat seeds, extracting them from pine and spruce cones wedged into 'anvil' cracks in bark — look for the scattered cone debris at the base of a tree.

The nest hole is excavated by both male and female in a dead or dying tree, taking 2–3 weeks. The same hole is often used for several years, and old holes are taken over by Tits, Nuthatches, and Starlings. Look for the neat round holes in dead wood — much rounder and more precise than the ragged excavations made by feeding.
native_info: Native throughout mainland Britain. Common and increasing. Absent from Ireland.
wildlife_value: Great Spotted Woodpeckers excavate nest holes used by many secondary hole-nesters including Blue Tit, Great Tit, Nuthatch, Starling, and Pied Flycatcher. They are important predators of wood-boring beetle larvae in dead wood. In spring, they sometimes raid the nest holes of other birds for eggs and chicks — a less endearing but ecologically real behaviour.

life_stages.description: Juveniles have a red cap covering most of the crown — neither the male's red nape patch nor the female's plain black nape. They leave the nest in June and follow their parents closely for several weeks.

Bold black and white patterning with a red patch on the back of the neck (nape) — the male's distinguishing feature. Red under the tail in both sexes. Bill is strong and chisel-shaped. In spring the loud drumming carries through woodland.

Great Spotted Woodpecker on a branch — bold black, white, and red pattern
Great Spotted Woodpecker — male
Great Spotted Woodpecker on branch
Great Spotted Woodpecker

confidence_note: The brilliant emerald-green underside is unique — no other British butterfly shows this colour. The uppersides are plain brown, rarely seen as the butterfly almost always rests with wings closed. Tiny (26–34mm), fast-flying.
weather_note: Only flies in warm sunshine. Cold or cloudy days in May will show nothing; try warm, still, sunny mornings.
summary: A tiny jewel of a butterfly — the underside is a brilliant, iridescent emerald green, like a living leaf. It's one of Old Down's specialities: April–June only, warm sunshine only, and blink and you'll miss it darting between patches of Bird's-foot Trefoil and Gorse.
full_description:
The Green Hairstreak is the only butterfly in Britain with a green underside, and what a green it is — not muted or dull but a rich, bright emerald that seems almost to glow in sunlight. The uppersides are plain brown, almost never visible since the butterfly always rests with wings tightly closed, showing only the green underside against a leaf or stem. The combination of colour and habit makes it one of the most camouflaged butterflies in Britain: it disappears completely among green vegetation.

At Old Down, Green Hairstreak is an exciting find — an indicator of high-quality chalk grassland with the right foodplants and structure. It flies from late April to early June, with May being peak. Males are territorial: they choose a prominent perch (often on a particular bramble spray or gorse sprig) and dart out to investigate any passing butterfly or insect. Watch a favoured perch for a few minutes and the same male will often return repeatedly to the same spot.

The larvae feed on a range of chalk grassland plants — Bird's-foot Trefoil, Gorse, Broom, Bramble, and Rock-rose among others. Eggs are laid singly on the foodplant buds. The caterpillar is green and extraordinarily hard to find. The species has a single annual generation and overwinters as a chrysalis in the soil.
native_info: Native throughout Britain and Ireland. Widespread but always localised to suitable habitat. A good indicator of chalk grassland quality.
wildlife_value: Adults feed on nectar from Bird's-foot Trefoil, Gorse, and other chalk grassland flowers. The caterpillars are tended by ants in some studies. Their presence reliably indicates the right combination of chalk grassland structure, foodplants, and lack of disturbance.

life_stages.description: Look for tiny fast-flying butterflies along south-facing scrub edges. Males perch on prominent stems and dart out at rivals. Always resting with wings shut — the brilliant green underside is what you'll see. A white streak (the 'hairstreak') on the hindwing underside is sometimes visible at close range.

photos.caption: Green Hairstreak — the brilliant emerald-green underside is unique
Green Hairstreak at rest — wings always closed, showing only the green underside
Green Hairstreak
Green Hairstreak resting

confidence_note: Silver-grey fur with a buff or reddish tinge along the back. Large bushy tail with silver-grey hairs that have white fringes. Much bigger than a mouse or vole. The only squirrel most of us will see in England and Wales.
summary: The Grey Squirrel is one of Britain's most familiar animals — quick, curious, and an acrobatic climber. It was brought from North America in the 1870s and has since spread everywhere, sadly displacing the native Red Squirrel.
full_description:
The Grey Squirrel is everywhere in England and Wales, and in many parts of Scotland. It was introduced from North America in the 1870s by Victorian landowners who thought it would be an interesting addition to their estates. It has proven extremely successful — perhaps too successful. The Grey Squirrel carries a disease (squirrelpox) that is harmless to Greys but fatal to our native Red Squirrel (Sciurus vulgaris), and through this and competition for food, the native Red Squirrel has been reduced to just a few strongholds in northern Scotland, parts of northern England, and Ireland. This is one of the most significant and sad wildlife stories in Britain.

Despite this, the Grey Squirrel is a remarkable animal and genuinely entertaining to watch. It is an acrobatic climber, an expert food-hider (caching thousands of acorns and hazelnuts each autumn), and much cleverer than it might appear — experiments have shown Grey Squirrels can solve complex puzzles to reach food. Look for their drey high in the fork of a tree — a large messy ball of leaves, twigs, and bark, quite different from a bird's nest. It may be used year-round but is most visible in winter when leaves have fallen.

Grey Squirrels also strip bark from mature trees to reach the sweet sap — this can girdle and kill even large, old trees, and is a significant problem in commercial and ancient woodland.
native_info: Non-native. Introduced from North America in the 1870s. Now the dominant squirrel species in England and Wales. Invasive and responsible for the decline of the native Red Squirrel.
wildlife_value: Grey Squirrels cache thousands of acorns and hazelnuts each autumn and forget many of them — these forgotten caches become new trees. Jays do the same and are thought to be even more effective at planting oaks. Squirrel dreys are used by Tawny Owls and other species when abandoned. However, Grey Squirrels also predate bird nests and are a significant problem for woodland management. Their impact on Red Squirrel populations is serious and ongoing.
invasive_impact: Grey Squirrels carry squirrelpox virus, which is fatal to Red Squirrels. They out-compete Red Squirrels for food. They strip bark from trees, killing mature specimens. Their presence has caused the near-extinction of the Red Squirrel in England and Wales.

life_stages.description: Young squirrels are born twice a year — February–April and June–August — in a drey or tree hole. They are blind and helpless at birth, gaining fur at 3 weeks. They start to explore from the drey at about 7 weeks.

Adults are active all year — they do not hibernate. In autumn, watch them working systematically through woodland burying acorns and hazelnuts. The drey (large ball of leaves and twigs in a tree fork) is visible all year but most obvious in winter.

photos.caption: Grey Squirrel — silver-grey fur with a bushy plumed tail
Grey Squirrel in a tree — look for the large drey in the fork above
Grey Squirrel
Grey Squirrel in tree

confidence_note: Sharp thorns, deeply lobed leaves, and either white flower clusters or red berries make this unmistakable in most seasons.
summary: The backbone of the British hedgerow. White blossom in May, red haws in autumn. Supports over 300 invertebrate species and feeds dozens of bird species — one of the most ecologically vital trees in Britain.
full_description: Hawthorn (Crataegus monogyna) is possibly the most ecologically important tree or shrub in the British landscape. A thorny deciduous shrub or small tree reaching 6–15m, it dominates most traditional British hedgerows. The deeply lobed leaves (3–5 lobes, resembling small oak leaves) emerge early in spring, giving the plant its country name 'May' from its spectacular white flowering in April–May. The sweetly fragrant flowers attract enormous numbers of pollinators — bees, hoverflies, beetles, and butterflies. By September, the hedgerow blazes red with ripe haws: small apple-like berries packed with energy for migrating and resident birds. The sharp thorns (5–15mm, modified shoot tips) create impenetrable cover for nesting birds and sheltering small mammals. Hawthorn supports over 300 species of invertebrate and provides food for dozens of bird species including Fieldfare, Redwing, and Waxwing. Its role in the British countryside — ecologically, historically, and culturally — is irreplaceable.
danger_note: Sharp thorns can cause skin punctures. Take care when working near hawthorn hedges.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. The dominant hedgerow shrub in Britain and one of the most abundant native trees. An indicator of ancient hedgerows when found in combination with other shrub species.
wildlife_value: One of the most important plants in Britain for wildlife. Supports over 300 invertebrate species as caterpillar food plant or shelter. The dense thorny growth is the most sought-after nesting and roosting site for many hedgerow birds. Berries (haws) provide critical autumn and winter food for Fieldfare, Redwing, Waxwing, Robin, Blackbird, and many other birds. Flowering provides essential early-season pollen and nectar.

life_stages.description: In winter, Hawthorn stands as a thorny tangle of dark grey-brown branches. The sharp thorns are fully visible and act as an important reminder of the plant's identity even when leafless. Small growth buds at the twig tips are already formed, swelling slowly. The dense growth provides critical roosting shelter for birds in cold weather.

Hawthorn is one of the first hedgerow shrubs to come into leaf in spring — often showing green by late February in mild years. The fresh, pale green leaves have a distinctive deeply lobed shape (3–5 lobes) that gives the plant a lacy appearance. The thorns become more obscured as foliage thickens. This bursting of green is what gave Hawthorn its country name 'May', celebrated in Mayday traditions.

photos.caption: Hawthorn leaves showing the distinctive deeply lobed shape

life_stages.description: Hawthorn flowers create white clouds along hedgerows in late April and May. The clusters of small five-petalled white flowers are sweetly fragrant and provide essential nectar and pollen for an enormous range of insects. Flowers are sometimes faintly pink-tinged. The hawthorn's flowering is one of the great spectacles of the British spring.

photos.caption: Hawthorn flower clusters and buds
Hawthorn flowers in full bloom, May
Hawthorn in full bloom — the 'May blossom'
Hawthorn blossom close-up showing individual flowers

life_stages.description: After flowering, the petals fall and tiny green berries (haws) begin to form. They remain hard and green through the summer months, gradually swelling. At this stage they are very astringent and inedible. The deep green foliage provides dense shade and nesting cover during the breeding season.

photos.caption: Hawthorn showing leafy growth and developing fruit

life_stages.description: The haws ripen through August and September, turning from green to orange to deep red. They soften and develop a slightly sweet, mealy flesh around a hard stone. Birds begin visiting in earnest as soon as the berries ripen. A well-berried hawthorn in September is one of the most productive wildlife habitats in the British countryside.

photos.caption: Hawthorn berries (haws) ripening to red
Ripe haws in hedgerow, UK

life_stages.description: Deep red, fully ripe haws are soft and sweet. Thrushes (Fieldfare, Redwing, Blackbird, Mistle Thrush), Robins, Waxwings, and many other birds strip the berries enthusiastically. A large hawthorn may carry thousands of berries, providing critical fuel for migrating birds arriving from Scandinavia in October and November.

photos.caption: Hawthorn berries (haws) — fully ripe and red
Haws on a hawthorn hedge near Princes Risborough, UK

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are thorny hedgerow shrubs with white flowers
similar_species.key_difference: Blackthorn flowers much earlier (March) and always before its leaves emerge, producing white blossom on bare dark twigs. Hawthorn flowers when leaves are fully out. Blackthorn's fruits are purple-black sloes (not red haws).
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Blackthorn flowers March before leaves; Hawthorn flowers April–May with leaves

similar_species.similarity_note: The closely related Midland Hawthorn has very similar leaves and berries
similar_species.key_difference: Midland Hawthorn flowers earlier (April) and usually has deep pink or pale pink flowers; Common Hawthorn is usually white. Midland Hawthorn has less deeply lobed leaves and two seeds in each berry versus one in Common Hawthorn.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Midland Hawthorn flowers slightly earlier, April rather than May

confidence_note: Golden-yellow catkins ('lamb's tails') dangling from bare twigs in January–March are unmistakeable. In summer: round, slightly heart-shaped leaves with a pointed tip and toothed edge. Hazelnuts in a leafy husk in autumn.
summary: One of the first signs of spring — Hazel catkins dangle from bare branches in January, sometimes while there's still snow on the ground. In autumn the shrub produces hazelnuts that squirrels and dormice can't resist.
full_description:
Hazel is one of Britain's most familiar hedgerow and woodland-edge shrubs. It grows as a multi-stemmed bush rather than a single-trunked tree, and its most dramatic moment comes in the depths of winter: from January to March, long golden-yellow catkins dangle from every bare twig, releasing clouds of yellow pollen on warm days. These are the male flowers. Look carefully at the same time and you'll find the tiny female flowers — just a small swelling at a bud tip with red thread-like styles poking out, like a tiny crimson anemone.

Hazel has been managed by coppicing for thousands of years — cut it back to the ground and it regrows as multiple straight poles. Coppiced hazel was used for fencing, charcoal, hurdle-making, and basket weaving. This traditional practice created woodland edge habitat with the perfect mix of light and shade for dormice, woodland butterflies, and wildflowers.

The nuts ripen in September–October inside a leafy husk. Hazel Dormice (a Red List species and Old Down speciality) specifically need hazelnuts — they double their body weight eating them before hibernation. Grey Squirrels take nuts early (while still green); dormice wait for them to ripen. If you find a hazelnut shell with a neat round hole with smooth edges on the side, a dormouse made it. A rougher, more ragged hole is a mouse or squirrel.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. A common hedgerow and woodland-edge shrub. An ancient woodland indicator species.
wildlife_value: The nuts are a critical autumn food for Hazel Dormouse, Grey Squirrel, Wood Mouse, Nuthatch, and Jay. The catkin pollen is one of the earliest pollen sources for queen bumblebees emerging from hibernation. The multi-stemmed coppice structure provides nesting habitat for warblers and tits. Hazel Dormice are so dependent on hazel that their presence is almost always associated with it.

life_stages.description: Long, dangling golden catkins appear on bare branches from January — often the first sign that spring is on its way, even when it's cold. Shake a branch gently and a cloud of yellow pollen will drift off. Look closely at other buds for the tiny red female flowers.

photos.caption: Hazel catkins — golden 'lamb's tails' on bare winter twigs

life_stages.description: Round, slightly heart-shaped leaves with a pointed tip and toothed edge emerge in April. The surface is slightly rough and hairy. The bark of young stems is grey-brown with small pale lenticels.

photos.caption: Hazel leaves

life_stages.description: Hazelnuts ripen from green to brown September–October, each sitting in a distinctive leafy, fringed husk. Look for gnawed shells to identify which animal has been eating them — a neat round hole with smooth inner edges = dormouse; rougher hole = mouse; completely split or crushed = squirrel.

photos.caption: Hazelnuts ripening in their leafy husks
Hazelnuts — whole and cracked open to show the kernel
Hazelnuts in their husks
Hazel catkins in winter
Hazelnuts whole and cracked

confidence_note: Almost never seen directly as strictly nocturnal and spends most of its life in the canopy or in hibernation. Identification is almost always from signs: gnawed hazelnut shells (smooth round hole on the side with smooth inner edge), or the woven round nest of honeysuckle bark and grass. Any dormouse seen directly is unmistakeable — small, golden-orange, huge dark eyes, fluffy tail.
weather_note: Active only in warm weather. May enter torpor for days during cold spells even in summer. Hibernates October to April.
summary: Old Down's most secretive speciality — the Hazel Dormouse is strictly nocturnal, protected, and rarely seen. But its signs are distinctive: a gnawed hazelnut with a smooth round hole is a dormouse's calling card. The UK population has halved since the 1990s.
full_description:
The Hazel Dormouse is one of Britain's most charming mammals and one of its most threatened. Small, golden-orange, with enormous dark eyes and a thick fluffy tail, it looks almost too cute to be real. But it is also one of the hardest British mammals to see — strictly nocturnal, spending most of its time in the canopy or in hedgerow scrub, and hibernating for up to seven months (October to April). The UK population has declined by more than 50% since the 1990s.

Finding a dormouse sign is exciting and completely achievable. The key sign is a gnawed hazelnut shell: dormice make a smooth, round hole in the side of the nut (not at the top), with a smooth inner edge where the lower incisor has worked inward and slightly downward — leaving characteristic grooves around the inside of the hole. Wood Mice make a rougher, more ragged hole; squirrels split or crush the whole nut. If you find a shell like this in September or October under a hazel bush at Old Down, there's a dormouse living there.

The dormouse also makes a distinctive woven summer nest: a ball about the size of a tennis ball, woven from strips of honeysuckle bark and grass, placed 1–2 metres up in bramble, hazel, or other scrub. Hibernation nests are on or just below the ground. The dormouse is fully protected under Schedule 5 of the Wildlife and Countryside Act — it is illegal to disturb a dormouse or its nest.
native_info: Native to England and Wales. Red List — population declined over 50% since the 1990s. Legally protected under Schedule 5, Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.
wildlife_value: Dormice are specialist consumers of hazel nuts, honeysuckle flowers, pollen, insects, and berries. Their role in consuming and spreading hazel nuts is part of the woodland food web. Old nest structures are used by other small mammals. The species requires a continuous shrub layer linking hazel, bramble, and honeysuckle — making it an indicator of well-structured woodland edge habitat.

life_stages.description: The most reliable sign: a hazelnut shell with a smooth, round hole on the SIDE (not the top), with smooth, slightly inwardly-angled inner edges. Look under hazel bushes from September onwards. Compare with Wood Mouse holes (rougher, more ragged) and squirrel (smashed or split).

A woven ball nest about the size of a tennis ball, built from strips of honeysuckle bark and grass, placed 1–2m up in bramble, hazel, or other scrub. Much more tightly woven than a bird's nest. If you find one, observe from a distance only — do not disturb.

Golden-orange fur, large dark eyes, rounded ears, and a thick, furry tail (unlike other small rodents). Strictly nocturnal — if you ever see one in daylight it is likely sick or disturbed. Active from May to October, hibernating October to April.

confidence_note: Small bright pink five-petalled flowers. Deeply divided, feathery leaves that turn red in autumn or when stressed. Distinctive unpleasant smell when leaves are rubbed. Red-tinged stems. Hairy all over.
summary: A cheerful little plant that pops up in walls, hedgerow bases, and shady banks throughout the summer. The bright pink flowers and red-tinged feathery leaves are charming — but rub a leaf and there's that distinctive pong.
full_description:
Herb Robert is one of those plants that rewards a second look. At first glance it's a small, rather weedy plant in a shady hedgerow base — but look closely and you'll see delicate bright pink five-petalled flowers, feathery divided leaves with a reddish tinge, and hairy stems that are often entirely scarlet. The whole plant turns progressively redder as the season goes on, or when it's stressed by drought.

Rub a leaf and you'll immediately notice the distinctive smell — often described as nutty, musty, or just unpleasant. This is one of the best ID features. The plant is in the cranesbill family (Geraniaceae), and after flowering it produces long, pointed seed pods shaped like a crane's bill — hence the family name. When ripe, the pod splits open suddenly and flings the seeds several metres. Watch a seed pod carefully as it starts to split and you might catch this happening.

Herb Robert is one of the most shade-tolerant of common wildflowers, growing in walls, rocky places, hedgerow bases, and woodland floors where little else can manage. It's an annual — it dies each winter and regrows from seed, which it does prolifically. In folk medicine it had many supposed uses, now largely discredited.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. Very common in a wide range of habitats. An annual that seeds itself freely.
wildlife_value: Small-to-medium insects, particularly solitary bees and hoverflies, visit the flowers for nectar and pollen. The seeds are dispersed explosively from the long beak-shaped pods. The plant provides ground cover in hedgerow bases and woodland floors. Despite its smell, several moth species use it as a foodplant.

life_stages.description: Herb Robert germinates in spring, forming a small rosette of feathery divided leaves with reddish stems. It grows quickly.

Bright pink flowers (about 1cm across) with five petals appear from April through to October. The plant becomes increasingly red through the season — especially the stems and older leaves. Rub a leaf and smell your fingers for the distinctive musty Herb Robert scent.

photos.caption: Herb Robert flowers — small, bright pink, five-petalled
Herb Robert plant showing feathery leaves and red stems
Herb Robert flowers
Herb Robert plant

confidence_note: The only blue butterfly you are likely to see flying high around trees and shrubs rather than low over grassland. Bright sky-blue upperwings with very little dark edging in spring. Pale silver-blue undersides with small black dots (no orange spots).
summary: A sky-blue butterfly of woodland edges and scrub — the only blue you'll see flying up around holly, ivy, and shrubs rather than low over grass. Two generations each year, spring and late summer.
full_description: The Holly Blue (Celastrina argiolus) is the most widespread blue butterfly in the UK and the one most likely to be seen in gardens, parks, and woodland edges. Males are a vivid sky-blue above with narrow dark wing borders; females have broader dark borders that are more prominent in the second (late summer) generation. The undersides of both wings are pale silver-blue scattered with small black dots — quite different from the orange-spotted undersides of the Common Blue. Holly Blues fly higher than other blue butterflies, weaving around shrubs and trees rather than staying low over grassland. There are two generations per year: the first in spring (April–June) lays eggs on holly flower buds; the second in late summer (July–September) prefers ivy. The species is well known for dramatic population cycles — numbers boom and crash over several years, driven by a specialist parasitic wasp (Listrodomus nycthemerus) that attacks the caterpillars. Old Down's mix of scrub, woodland edge, holly, and ivy makes it excellent habitat.
native_info: Native to the UK. Common and widespread across England and Wales, less so in Scotland. Found in woodland edges, hedgerows, parks, and gardens wherever holly and ivy grow. Old Down's scrub and woodland edge provides ideal habitat.
wildlife_value: Adults nectar on a wide range of flowers including bramble, privet, and ivy. Caterpillars of the spring generation feed on holly flower buds and developing berries; the second generation feeds on ivy flowers. The caterpillars are tended by ants, which protect them in exchange for a sugary secretion — a relationship shared with several UK blue butterflies.

life_stages.description: Tiny, pale green, disc-shaped eggs are laid singly on the flower buds of holly (spring generation) or ivy (summer generation). They are very hard to spot without a hand lens. Eggs hatch within about a week.

Caterpillars are small, green, and slug-shaped — well camouflaged among flower buds and developing berries. Spring caterpillars eat holly flowers and unripe berries; summer caterpillars eat ivy flowers. Like many blue butterfly caterpillars, they secrete a sweet liquid that attracts ants, which in turn guard them from predators and parasitic wasps.
The chrysalis is small, pale brown, and formed low down on bark, leaf litter, or in crevices. The chrysalis of the second generation overwinters, not emerging until the following spring.

Spring adults (April–June) are brighter sky-blue with narrow dark borders, especially the males. Summer adults (July–September) have wider dark borders, particularly the females. Both generations have the distinctive pale silver-blue underside with small black dots. Watch for them flying high around holly and ivy bushes, often basking briefly on sunny leaves.

photos.caption: Holly Blue male, upperwing
Holly Blue underside showing silver-blue with black dots

similar_species.name: Common Blue
similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Common Blue flies low over grassland; Holly Blue flies higher around shrubs. Common Blue underside has orange spots near the wing edges; Holly Blue underside is plain pale blue with small black dots only.

similar_species.name: Small Blue
similar_species.how_to_tell_apart: Small Blue is much smaller (14–18mm vs 26–34mm), silvery rather than sky-blue, and restricted to chalk grassland with Kidney Vetch. Holly Blue is larger and found near holly and ivy.

photos.caption: Holly Blue male

confidence_note: Golden-brown with a fuzzy (hairy) thorax, clearly visible pollen baskets on the hind legs when foraging, and a pointed abdomen with yellow-brown and dark bands. Flies with a steady, purposeful hum. Smaller and less yellow than a bumblebee.
summary: The world's most famous pollinator — and a fascinating social insect. A single colony can contain 60,000 bees. Honey Bees communicate the direction and distance of flowers to each other by dancing.
full_description:
The Honey Bee is one of the most important insects on Earth — responsible, alongside other pollinators, for the production of a third of all human food. A single colony can contain 50,000–60,000 workers, all daughters of a single queen. The colony works as a single superorganism: workers build wax comb, raise larvae, collect nectar and pollen, guard the entrance, and regulate the temperature of the hive by fanning their wings.

Honey Bees communicate the location of flowers using the 'waggle dance' — a figure-of-eight dance performed inside the hive in which the angle of the waggle run relative to vertical indicates the direction of the food source relative to the sun, and the duration of the waggle indicates distance. This is one of the most sophisticated communication systems known in the animal kingdom.

The Honey Bee's sting is barbed — it stays in the skin after a sting, and the venom sac continues to pump venom for up to a minute. The bee dies after stinging. Remove the sting promptly by scraping (not squeezing) it out. Honey Bees are gentle compared to wasps — they sting only to defend the colony or themselves when pressed. Managed hives are kept by beekeepers; wild colonies nest in tree holes, old roofs, and other cavities.
danger_note: The sting is barbed and stays in the skin — scrape it out immediately (don't squeeze the venom sac). Sting is painful but not dangerous for most people. People with bee venom allergy should carry an EpiPen.
native_info: Native to Britain; the managed race (Apis mellifera mellifera) has been kept by beekeepers for thousands of years. Also present as wild colonies in tree holes and old buildings.
wildlife_value: One of the most important pollinators of wildflowers and crops. A colony visits millions of flowers per day. Honey Bee wax and honey support other wildlife; wax moth larvae feed in old combs. Swarms are eaten by opportunistic predators.

life_stages.description: Look for bees with orange or yellow pollen packed into the pollen baskets on their hind legs — bright orange or yellow blobs on each back leg. Workers visit hundreds of flowers per foraging trip, transferring pollen between plants.

photos.caption: Honey Bee landing — showing the fuzzy thorax and golden-brown colouring
Honey Bee foraging — note the orange pollen baskets on the hind legs
Honey Bee on flower — golden-brown with fuzzy thorax

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are golden-brown bees visiting flowers
similar_species.key_difference: Bumblebees are much larger, rounder, and much furrier all over. Honey Bees are slimmer with a pointed abdomen and only fuzzy on the thorax.

photos.caption: Honey Bee landing — showing the fuzzy thorax and golden-brown colouring
Honey Bee foraging
Honey Bee on flower

confidence_note: Evergreen, dark glossy leaves with 3–5 pointed lobes on climbing/creeping stems. Mature flowering stems have oval, unlobed leaves. Climbs using tiny root-like holdfasts.
summary: Far from being a pest, ivy is one of the most wildlife-rich plants in Britain. Its October flowers are the last great nectar feast for insects before winter, and the black berries sustain birds through the dark months.
full_description:
Ivy gets an unfair reputation. Many people think it's killing the trees it grows on, but in most cases ivy is simply using the tree as support — it feeds itself, rooting in the ground, and climbs with tiny adhesive rootlets rather than sending parasitic roots into the tree. Old ivy on an old tree is an ecosystem in its own right: the dense stems shelter moths, hibernating butterflies (Red Admiral, Comma, Brimstone), and hibernating bats, while the leaves provide year-round cover for birds.

Ivy has two distinct leaf forms. Juvenile stems — the climbing ones — have the familiar three-to-five-lobed dark glossy leaves. But once ivy reaches the top of a support and starts flowering, the leaves on those mature stems become oval and unlobed, completely different from the juvenile leaves. The flowers appear in October–November — clusters of small greenish-yellow umbels — and are one of the most important late-season nectar sources for queen wasps, Red Admiral butterflies, hoverflies, and bees. At a time when almost nothing else is flowering, a large ivy in full bloom buzzes with insects.

The black berries ripen in February–March — late in the season when other food is scarce — and are eaten by Blackbird, Robin, Blackcap, Woodpigeon, and Song Thrush. The berries are mildly toxic to humans (cause stomach upset) but are an important food source for birds.
danger_note: The berries and leaves contain compounds that are mildly toxic to humans, causing nausea and vomiting if eaten. The berries are fine for birds but should not be eaten by people. The sap can cause skin irritation in sensitive individuals.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. Extremely common in woodland, hedgerows, walls, and gardens.
wildlife_value: One of the most wildlife-rich plants in Britain. Late-flowering (October–November), providing nectar for queen wasps, Red Admirals, Comma butterflies, hoverflies, and late bumblebees when almost nothing else is available. Berries eaten by Blackbird, Robin, Blackcap, and Woodpigeon in late winter. Dense stems provide roosting and hibernating habitat for insects (including moths and butterflies), bats, and birds. Holly Blue butterfly caterpillars feed on ivy flowers and berries.

life_stages.description: Climbing stems have the familiar three-to-five-lobed dark, glossy leaves. Ivy climbs using tiny adhesive rootlets rather than twining — it glues itself to surfaces and does not damage stone, brick, or healthy bark. The stems are evergreen and provide year-round shelter.

photos.caption: Ivy climbing a tree — the lobed leaves of the juvenile climbing stems

life_stages.description: In October–November, mature ivy produces clusters of small greenish-yellow flowers. These are one of the last great nectar sources of the year — visit a large flowering ivy on a warm October day and listen to the buzzing of wasps, hoverflies, and the last bees of the season.

photos.caption: Ivy showing mature flowering stems with unlobed leaves

life_stages.description: Black berries ripen in late winter — February to March — when other food is scarce. They are an important food source for birds, particularly Blackcap and Robin. Berries are toxic to humans but safe for birds.

photos.caption: Ivy berries — black, late-ripening, toxic to humans but vital for birds
