Ivy climbing a tree
Ivy — mature flowering stems
Ivy berries in late winter

confidence_note: Pinkish-buff body, white rump (very conspicuous in flight), and a startling electric-blue wing panel with black barring. Black moustache stripe and black-and-white crest. Harsh, screaming 'skaaark!' call. Often heard before seen.
summary: The most colourful crow in Britain — a flash of electric blue and that harsh screaming call are the best ID clues. Jays are the oak woodlands' secret gardeners: each autumn one Jay buries thousands of acorns, forgetting many — and those forgotten acorns become oak trees.
full_description:
The Jay is a member of the crow family (Corvidae) — as clever and adaptable as its relatives, but far more colourful. The pinkish-buff body, white rump (brilliant white in flight), and electric-blue wing panel with fine black barring make it one of Britain's most striking birds. But it is shy: usually glimpsed flying through woodland or heard from dense cover, giving its explosive, harsh screaming call — 'skaaark!' — which is the most common sound of alarm in a beech or oak wood. Other woodland birds treat the Jay's alarm call as a general warning.

In autumn, Jays perform a remarkable behaviour: acorn-caching. A single Jay may collect and bury up to 3,000 acorns in a single autumn, each one buried individually in a separate hole 2–3cm deep. The Jay has a large sublingual pouch and can carry several acorns at once. It relocates its caches through memory — Jays have been shown to remember thousands of cache sites. But it inevitably forgets some, and those forgotten acorns germinate and become oak trees. Jays are one of the most important agents of oak forest regeneration in Britain — responsible for the spread of oak far faster than wind dispersal alone could achieve.

Jays are also accomplished mimics: they can reproduce the calls of Buzzard, Tawny Owl, and other species with surprising accuracy. In spring they become less secretive during courtship, and groups of 3–10 birds may be seen chasing through the treetops — a rare chance to see them well.
native_info: Native throughout England and Wales. Commoner in the south. Strongly associated with oak woodland but also found in mixed woodland, large gardens, and parks.
wildlife_value: Jays are the primary long-distance dispersers of oak acorns in Britain, responsible for the establishment of new oak trees far beyond the parent tree's crown. A single Jay may plant thousands of acorns in a season. They also eat beech mast, hazelnuts, invertebrates, and eggs and nestlings of other birds. Their loud alarm call functions as a warning system for many woodland species.

life_stages.description: Juveniles look similar to adults but have a softer, slightly streaky appearance. They follow parents and begin learning caching behaviour in their first autumn.

The electric-blue wing panel is unlike any other British bird. In flight, the brilliant white rump patch is the best field mark — it flashes as the bird bounces through trees. The harsh screaming 'skaaark!' call is the classic alarm sound of woodland.

photos.caption: Jay — pinkish body, blue wing panel, black moustache. The most colourful British crow.
Jay carrying an acorn — each autumn a single Jay buries thousands
Jay
Jay with acorn

summary: The hovering falcon — kestrels can hang motionless in the air while they use ultraviolet vision to track vole runs in the grass below. Old Down's open chalk grassland is perfect hunting ground. Watch the sky above the slope and you will nearly always spot one.
full_description:
The Kestrel (Falco tinnunculus) is Britain's most familiar bird of prey, and the one most likely to be seen hovering over roadside verges, motorway embankments, and open grasslands. Males have a striking blue-grey head and tail, chestnut-brown back with black spots, and a cream-buff breast with dark streaks. Females and juveniles are brown all over with barring on the back and tail. In flight, the long narrow pointed wings and long tail are distinctive; in a hover, the tail fans out and the wingtips vibrate rapidly while the head stays perfectly still — an extraordinary feat of aerodynamics.

Kestrels hunt primarily by hovering 10–30m above the ground, facing into the wind, with their eyesight focused on a remarkably small area of ground. They can detect ultraviolet light, which means they can see the urine trails left by voles — voles mark their runs with urine that reflects UV light strongly, effectively laying out a map of the best hunting spots. When prey is located, the kestrel drops in stages — hover, drop, hover again — before stooping rapidly to catch the prey in its talons.

At Old Down, Kestrels hunt the open chalk grassland and field margins throughout the year. Their main prey here is Field Voles, with occasional Shrews, large insects (especially in summer), and small birds. Breeding pairs nest in tree holes, cliff ledges, or old crow nests in trees around the site perimeter, with young fledging in June–July. Kestrel populations have declined significantly in lowland England since the 1970s, largely due to agricultural intensification reducing vole habitat — making chalk grassland sites like Old Down increasingly important.
native_info: Resident and widespread throughout the UK. Most common in open habitats including grassland, heathland, farmland, and motorway verges. Has declined by about 50% in lowland England since the 1970s.
wildlife_value: Controls Field Vole and Wood Mouse populations. Indicator species for open grassland habitat quality — a Kestrel hunting overhead means there is a healthy grassland invertebrate and small mammal community below. Also preys on large insects, helping regulate invertebrate populations.

life_stages.description: Blue-grey head and tail, chestnut-brown back with black teardrop spots, cream-buff underside with dark streaks. In flight from below, the tail is a clean blue-grey fan. This is the plumage most people associate with the Kestrel.

photos.caption: Male Kestrel showing blue-grey head and chestnut back

life_stages.description: The signature behaviour: head completely still while wings beat rapidly and tail fans open. The kestrel faces into the wind and maintains a fixed position in the air, scanning the ground below for movement. The head points downward at a slight angle. This behaviour is easier to see on windy days when less wing-flapping is needed.

photos.caption: Kestrel in classic hover — head perfectly still, wings and tail spread

life_stages.description: Young Kestrels leave the nest in June–July and look similar to adult females — brown with barring. They are often seen in late summer practising hovering, sometimes less smoothly than adults. The family group may remain loosely together for several weeks after fledging.

photos.caption: Juvenile Kestrels — streakier than adults, less rust-red. Fully grown but still learning to hunt.

similar_species.similarity_note: Both common raptors at Old Down
similar_species.key_difference: Sparrowhawk has short rounded wings and a long tail — it flies fast through woodland and hedgerows in a series of rapid flaps and glides, never hovering. Kestrel has long pointed wings and hovers regularly. Sparrowhawk has barred underparts.

photos.caption: Kestrel hovering — the behaviour that makes it instantly identifiable
Male Kestrel perched, showing blue-grey head and chestnut back
Juvenile Kestrels — streakier than adults, less rust-red. Fully grown but still learning to hunt.

confidence_note: The woolly white calyx and clustered flowerheads are distinctive. Flowers are usually yellow but can be orange, red, or cream — look for the fuzzy white 'cushion' around each cluster.
summary: A key chalk grassland plant and the sole foodplant for Small Blue butterfly caterpillars. The clustered flowerheads wrapped in woolly white calyces are unmistakeable once you know what to look for.
full_description:
Kidney Vetch is a low-growing chalk and limestone grassland plant with clusters of small flowers nestled in a distinctive woolly white or cream 'cushion' of sepals. The flowers are usually bright yellow but at Old Down you may also find orange-red or bicoloured forms — the whole plant can look remarkably different from one patch to the next. It grows in short, well-drained turf and is a strong indicator of ancient, unimproved chalk grassland. The leaves are divided into narrow leaflets and have a silvery sheen when young.

Kidney Vetch has one of the most important ecological relationships at Old Down: it is the sole larval foodplant of the Small Blue butterfly (Cupido minimus). The tiny female Small Blue lays her eggs directly on the flower buds, and the caterpillars feed inside the developing seed pods. No Kidney Vetch means no Small Blue — it's that simple. The Six-spot Burnet Moth caterpillar also feeds on it, alongside Bird's-foot Trefoil.

It also fixes nitrogen in the soil through root nodules containing symbiotic bacteria — the same trick legumes use — which helps maintain the low-fertility conditions that chalk grassland wildflowers need. The flowers are a favourite of bumblebees, particularly the short-tongued Buff-tailed Bumblebee which sometimes 'steals' nectar by biting a hole in the base of the flower.
native_info: Native throughout the UK on chalk, limestone, and coastal grassland. Most abundant in southern England.
wildlife_value: The sole larval foodplant of the Small Blue butterfly — one of the most specific ecological relationships in British entomology. Also used as a secondary foodplant by Six-spot Burnet Moth caterpillars and Common Blue caterpillars. The flowers are an important nectar source for bumblebees, solitary bees, and hoverflies. Root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen, helping maintain the low-fertility soils that chalk grassland specialists need.

life_stages.description: Kidney Vetch forms a low rosette of silky, divided leaves in spring. The leaves have a distinctive silvery-green sheen and feel soft to the touch.

Clusters of small pea-family flowers are held in a thick, woolly white or cream calyx that looks like a cushion. Flowers are usually yellow but can range from cream to deep orange-red. Look at the base of each cluster and you'll see the woolly sepals — this is the clincher for ID.

photos.caption: Kidney Vetch flowerhead showing the woolly white calyx
Kidney Vetch in flower, showing yellow flowerheads

life_stages.description: After flowering, the woolly calyces dry to a papery brown and contain small, kidney-shaped seeds. This is where the plant gets its common name.

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are yellow-flowered legumes of chalk grassland
similar_species.key_difference: Bird's-foot Trefoil has neat, un-woolly flowers and distinctive claw-shaped seed pods. Kidney Vetch always has a thick woolly white or cream calyx around each flower cluster.

photos.caption: Kidney Vetch — flowerhead close-up
Kidney Vetch in chalk grassland
Kidney Vetch — orange-red colour form

confidence_note: Male in summer has a striking crimson forehead and breast — look for the red patch as the key field mark. Both sexes have a white wing panel visible in flight. Females and winter males are streaky brown and can be confused with other small finches.
summary: A small finch of open countryside — the breeding male has a bright crimson forehead and breast that flash in the sun. Linnets love gorse and bramble scrub for nesting and feed on weed seeds on bare ground.
full_description:
The Linnet is a small, lively finch of heathland, scrub, and open farmland. The breeding male is one of the more attractive British finches: a warm brown back, pale underparts, and a vivid crimson forehead and breast that appear in spring and fade by autumn. The bill is stout and seed-cracking in shape. In flight, white wing panels and white sides to the tail flash conspicuously. Females and non-breeding males are streaky brown and much harder to identify — look for the wing panel as the most reliable feature in all plumages.

Linnets are social birds: you'll often hear them before you see them, giving a rapid, twittering song and a flight call that sounds like a musical 'chichichi.' They nest in loose colonies in dense scrub — gorse, bramble, and hawthorn are favourites — and several pairs may nest close together. The nest is a neat cup of grass and moss lined with hair and plant down.

Like the Yellowhammer, the Linnet is a Red List species whose UK population has declined dramatically. Both are specialist seed-eaters that depend on weedy arable fields, traditional hay meadows, and rough uncultivated ground that modern farming has largely eliminated. Their presence at Old Down indicates that the surrounding landscape still supports a seed-rich food supply.
native_info: Native resident and partial migrant. Widespread throughout the UK but declining. Red List species. Some birds move to coastal areas in winter.
wildlife_value: Linnets feed almost exclusively on seeds — especially the seeds of weeds like fat hen, chickweed, dandelion, and dock. They occasionally take small invertebrates to feed to chicks. Their foraging on bare and disturbed ground can help disperse seeds. As Red List species, Linnets are a priority for habitat management at sites like Old Down.

life_stages.description: In spring and summer the male develops a vivid crimson forehead and breast patch — these are the key ID features. The back is warm brown, the underparts pale. Look for the white wing panel in flight.

photos.caption: Male Linnet in breeding plumage — crimson forehead and breast

life_stages.description: The female is streaky brown with no red colouring — easily confused with other small finches. Look for the white wing panel (less bright than the male's), the small stout bill, and the warm brown tones rather than grey.

photos.caption: Female Linnet — streaky brown with no red

life_stages.description: In autumn and winter, Linnets form flocks, sometimes of hundreds, that roam over farmland and coastal marshes searching for seeds. The males lose their red colouring until spring.

photos.caption: Linnet in winter plumage
Male Linnet in breeding plumage
Female Linnet
Linnet, winter

confidence_note: Tiny pink, black, and white bird with an absurdly long tail — the tail is longer than the body. Moves through trees in a loose, chattering flock. High-pitched 'zee-zee-zee' contact call. Unmistakeable once seen.
summary: A tiny fluffy ball of pink and white with an impossibly long tail — Long-tailed Tits travel in family groups and fill the hedgerow with high-pitched contact calls. Their nest is one of the finest pieces of wildlife architecture in Britain.
full_description:
The Long-tailed Tit is one of the most charming birds in the British countryside. Tiny — the body is barely the size of a ping-pong ball — it has a tail that is longer than the body, giving it a lollipop silhouette unlike any other species. The plumage is a delicate mix of pink, black, and white, with a creamy-buff underside that almost glows in winter sunlight. It is almost never seen alone: Long-tailed Tits travel in family groups of 8–20 birds, keeping in constant contact with high-pitched 'zee-zee-zee' and 'tupp' calls as they bounce acrobatically through the outer twigs of trees and shrubs.

The nest is one of the most extraordinary structures built by any British bird: a deep, elastic, oval bag woven from moss and spider silk, attached to a fork in a thorny shrub (often Bramble, Hawthorn, or Gorse). The outside is studded with hundreds of flakes of lichen for camouflage. The inside is lined with up to 2,000 feathers — the builders collect feathers from the woodland floor over several weeks. The elastic spider-silk construction stretches as the chicks grow. The whole nest takes 3 weeks to build and is considered one of the finest structures in the animal kingdom.

In autumn and winter, Long-tailed Tits often join mixed feeding flocks with Blue Tits, Great Tits, Nuthatches, and Treecreepers, moving through woodland together. If you hear 'zee-zee-zee' from a hedgerow and wait, you may get a flock washing through at close range — watch them hanging upside down to reach the tiniest insects.
native_info: Native throughout Britain. Common and widespread in woodland edge, scrub, and hedgerow. Numbers increase in mild winters.
wildlife_value: Long-tailed Tits eat small insects, eggs, and larvae gleaned from outer twigs and buds — a feeding niche that complements rather than competes with other tit species. In cold weather, family groups roost huddled together for warmth. Their nests, once vacated, are not re-used but decompose slowly and the materials are recycled by other nest-builders.

life_stages.description: Pairs begin building their extraordinary oval nest from March. They collect moss, spider silk, and lichen for the outside, and feathers — sometimes over 2,000 — for the lining. The whole structure takes about three weeks. Look for them collecting material near Bramble and Hawthorn thickets.

After breeding, families join together in roving flocks of 8–20 birds. Listen for the constant high, thin 'zee-zee-zee' contact calls — then watch the hedgerow carefully for the tiny pink-and-white shapes bouncing along the outer twigs.

photos.caption: Long-tailed Tit — the tail is longer than the body
Long-tailed Tit — pink, white, and black with the signature long tail
Long-tailed Tit
Long-tailed Tit perched

confidence_note: Unmistakeable in all stages. Spring: large arrow-shaped leaves (often with dark spots). Flower: a hooded green-cream spathe enclosing a purple club-shaped spadix. Autumn: spike of brilliant scarlet-orange berries.
summary: One of the strangest and most dangerous plants in British woodland — the vivid scarlet berries are extremely toxic and look enticingly like berries in a children's story. The spring flower is just as bizarre: a hooded cowl over a purple club that generates its own heat.
full_description:
Lords-and-Ladies is one of the most extraordinary plants in Britain. The spring flowers are unlike anything else: a large, hooded cream-green spathe (the 'hood') wraps around a central purple club (the spadix). The spadix generates its own heat — measurably warmer than the air — and emits a faint unpleasant smell, both of which attract small insects down into the base of the spathe where they become temporarily trapped and pollinate the flowers. Once the flowers are pollinated the spathe withers, releasing the insects.

The berries are the most dangerous part. By August the stalk produces a dense spike of brilliant scarlet-orange berries that look exactly like something from a fairy tale — vivid, round, glossy, and clustered tightly together. They are one of the most dangerous wild plants for children in Britain. Eating just a few berries causes immediate intense burning and swelling of the mouth and throat, severe vomiting, and potentially serious breathing difficulties requiring medical attention. If you see a child pick these berries, act immediately.

The leaves also contain irritant crystals (calcium oxalate raphides) and cause burning and irritation if handled and then mouth touched. The arrow-shaped spring leaves are bright glossy green, often with dark purple blotches. They die back completely by midsummer, leaving the berry spike standing alone.
danger_note: HIGHLY TOXIC. The vivid scarlet-orange berries cause immediate severe burning and swelling of the mouth and throat if eaten, even in small quantities. The leaves and stems also contain irritant crystals that cause burning. If any part is eaten, seek medical attention or call 111 immediately. The berries are most dangerous to children as they look attractive and edible.
native_info: Native throughout England and Wales; scarcer in Scotland. Common in woodland, hedgerow bases, and shady banks.
wildlife_value: The spathe traps small flies (especially owl midges) as pollinators — a remarkable example of temporary insect imprisonment for pollination. The berries are eaten by Pheasants and some thrushes, which are not affected by the toxins. The large glossy leaves provide early ground cover in woodland.

life_stages.description: Large, shiny, arrow-shaped leaves emerge from January onwards in woodland. They are often spotted with dark purple blotches (some plants are unspotted). These are one of the first woodland plants to appear in the new year.

In April–May, a hooded cream-green spathe (the 'hood') unfolds to reveal the purple or brown club-shaped spadix inside. The spadix generates heat and smell to attract insects. Touch the inside of the spathe carefully — you may feel it is warmer than the air around it.

photos.caption: Lords-and-Ladies spathe and spadix — the purple club generates heat to attract insects

life_stages.description: By late summer the leaves have died away completely and the stalk is topped with a dense cluster of brilliant scarlet-orange berries. These are HIGHLY TOXIC — eating even a few causes severe burning in the mouth and throat. Never touch these and make sure children do not pick them.

photos.caption: Lords-and-Ladies berries — beautiful but HIGHLY TOXIC. Do not eat.
Lords-and-Ladies spathe and spadix
Lords-and-Ladies berries — HIGHLY TOXIC

confidence_note: The bold black-and-white chequered pattern is unique among British butterflies — nothing else looks like it.
summary: A stunning black-and-white chequered butterfly that looks like no other in Britain. Once you've seen one dancing over purple knapweed on a July afternoon, you'll never forget it.
full_description:
The Marbled White is one of Britain's most unmistakeable butterflies — its bold black-and-white chequered pattern is completely unique. Despite its name it is not related to the white butterflies at all, but belongs to the 'browns' family (Satyrinae), alongside Meadow Browns and Speckled Woods. It loves open chalk and limestone grasslands where it nectars eagerly on purple and pink flowers, especially knapweed, scabious, and thistles — you'll often see several together on a single knapweed flowerhead.

At Old Down, July is Marbled White month. On warm afternoons the hillside can be alive with dozens drifting lazily over the long grass, quite unlike the more jittery flight of other butterflies. Females do something unusual when egg-laying: rather than placing eggs carefully on a foodplant, they scatter them at random while flying, letting the eggs fall into the grass. The caterpillars feed on fine-leaved grasses including Red Fescue and Yorkshire Fog, so the rough, uncut areas of the site are crucial for the colony.

On cloudy days, Marbled Whites roost with wings spread open rather than folded — unusual for the brown family and a useful ID feature. If you find one roosting in the grass, look closely: the underside of the wings has a delicate pattern of grey, white, and black that is just as beautiful as the uppersides.
native_info: Native to southern and central England. A chalk and limestone grassland specialist. Has expanded its range northwards in recent decades, likely in response to climate change.
wildlife_value: Adults are important pollinators of chalk grassland wildflowers, especially knapweed, scabious, and thistles. The caterpillars feed on fine-leaved grasses including Red Fescue and Yorkshire Fog, making rough uncut grassland essential for breeding. A strong population of Marbled Whites indicates that the grassland is being managed well — not cut too early, not too heavily grazed.

life_stages.description: Females scatter creamy-white eggs at random into tall grass while flying — they don't place them carefully on a specific plant. The eggs hatch within 2–3 weeks.

The newly hatched caterpillar does something remarkable: it immediately goes to sleep. It hibernates through autumn and winter without eating, only waking in spring to feed on fine grasses. The caterpillar is green or brown, beautifully camouflaged, and feeds at night — so it's extremely hard to find.
The chrysalis forms in loose soil at the base of grass clumps, or in a thin silken hammock just above the ground. It is pale cream or green, well-hidden in the vegetation.

Adults fly from late June to August, peaking in July. Males and females look similar, though females tend to be slightly larger with more cream in the pattern. Both sexes are avid nectar feeders — look for them on knapweed, scabious, thistles, and marjoram. On cloudy days they roost with wings spread open in the grass.

photos.caption: Marbled White nectaring, showing the bold chequered upperwing pattern
Marbled White at rest on grass showing the underside wing pattern
Marbled White — bold chequered pattern
Marbled White at rest showing underside

confidence_note: Orange and black banding with double narrow black bands on the abdomen — the double bands are the key feature that separates it from many similar hoverflies. Much smaller and more slender than a wasp.
summary: One of Britain's most familiar hoverflies — orange and black striped, hovering perfectly still in mid-air before darting to a flower. It looks like a wasp but has no sting. Millions migrate here from mainland Europe every year.
full_description:
The Marmalade Hoverfly is probably the hoverfly most people have noticed — hovering motionless, then darting sideways, then hovering again. The orange and black banding mimics a wasp or bee well enough to deter many predators (this is called Batesian mimicry), but it is completely harmless. Look closely and you'll see the single pair of wings (flies have two wings; wasps and bees have four), the large fly-style eyes, and the short antennae — nothing like a wasp's.

Marmalade Hoverflies are migrants — every year, millions fly north from southern Europe and Africa to take advantage of the UK's summer flowers. Some years bring enormous numbers; on good days you can see them streaming in off the coast. Adults feed on nectar and pollen from flowers, while the larvae are voracious predators of aphids — a single larva can eat hundreds of aphids before pupating, making hoverflies important natural pest controllers.

The hover is extraordinary — the hoverfly maintains a fixed position in space with wingbeats of 120 per second, making tiny rapid adjustments for wind and air currents. It's one of the most impressive flying skills in the insect world. To see it best, watch one hovering over a flower on a warm, still afternoon.
danger_note: Despite resembling a wasp, hoverflies cannot sting. They are completely harmless.
native_info: Native to the UK and a migratory visitor in large numbers from mainland Europe. One of the most common hoverfly species in Britain.
wildlife_value: Adults are important pollinators — they visit a very wide range of flowers and can pollinate species that bees ignore. Larvae eat aphids, making hoverflies valuable natural pest controllers in gardens and crops. Migratory species like this one link ecosystems across Europe — the same individual may pollinate flowers in Spain, France, and England in a single season.

life_stages.description: The larva is a pale, slug-like maggot found among aphid colonies on plant stems. It is completely blind and moves by feel, but can eat hundreds of aphids. It pupates in a brown barrel-shaped pupa on or near the foodplant.

The adult is seen hovering over flowers or resting on leaves in sunshine. The orange and black banding is bright and contrasting. In flight, the hover is its most distinctive behaviour — it can hang motionless for extended periods, then dart sideways at speed.

photos.caption: Marmalade Hoverfly hovering — note the single pair of wings
Marmalade Hoverfly on flower

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are orange/black banded flying insects
similar_species.key_difference: Bumblebees are large and very furry; hoverflies are smaller and sleek. Bumblebees have four wings and longer antennae. Hoverflies hover motionless; bumblebees rarely do.

photos.caption: Marmalade Hoverfly hovering
Marmalade Hoverfly on flower

summary: One of Britain's most abundant grassland butterflies, and one of the few that will fly on dull, overcast days. Old Down can be carpeted with Meadow Browns in July and August. The single large eye-spot on the forewing is the key ID feature.
full_description:
The Meadow Brown (Maniola jurtina) is Britain's most abundant butterfly by population, and one of the most characteristic species of summer grassland. Males are dark brown with a small orange patch on the forewing containing a single black eye-spot with a white centre. Females are larger with a more extensive orange-brown patch on the forewing and a more prominent eye-spot. The underside of the hindwing is mottled buff-brown with a small cluster of spots — much paler and less patterned than many browns.

The Meadow Brown is unusual among British butterflies in that it will fly in overcast and even light rain, unlike most species that only fly in sunshine. This makes it one of the most reliably visible butterflies on visits to Old Down through the summer. It is single-brooded — one flight period from June through September — and the adults live for several weeks, nectaring on Knapweed, Bramble, Marjoram, and many other flowers. The caterpillars feed on a range of fine grasses, which is why the species thrives in both chalk grassland and rough grassland habitats.

At Old Down, Meadow Brown is typically the most numerous butterfly by count in summer, often hundreds visible simultaneously on a warm July day. It makes an excellent species for children learning to count butterflies — it is abundant, easy to spot, and lands frequently on flowers. Look especially on Knapweed, Bramble flowers, and Ragwort.
native_info: Native throughout England, Wales, and Ireland. One of the most abundant butterflies in Britain. Found in almost all grassland habitats, from chalk downland to coastal dunes to roadside verges.
wildlife_value: Caterpillars feed on common fine grasses, making this butterfly independent of specialist plants and very adaptable. Adults are important pollinators of Knapweed, Bramble, and Marjoram. Prey for bats, spiders, and birds. The abundance of Meadow Brown at Old Down provides a baseline indicator for grassland quality that is easy to monitor.

life_stages.description: The caterpillar hibernates over winter as a small larva, resuming feeding in spring on fine grasses. It is green with a pale stripe along each side, well camouflaged in the grass stems. By May it has grown to full size and pupates in a chrysalis close to the ground.

Dark brown wings with a small orange-brown patch on the upper forewing and a single black eye-spot (with one or two white pupils). Males tend to be darker than females. The underside of the hindwing is mottled brown and buff — much plainer than the Gatekeeper.

photos.caption: Meadow Brown male showing the dark brown wings and eye-spot on forewing

life_stages.description: Females are slightly larger than males with a more extensive orange-brown band on the forewing and a more prominent eye-spot. The orange colouring makes females look warmer and brighter than males when settled on a flower. Both sexes rest with wings closed when not in active flight.

photos.caption: Meadow Brown female — orange colouring more extensive than male

similar_species.similarity_note: Very similar brown butterfly often in the same habitat
similar_species.key_difference: Gatekeeper (Pyronia tithonus) is smaller, with two white pupils in the eye-spot (Meadow Brown has one or two but usually one), more orange on the forewing, and a distinctly patterned underside of the hindwing (Meadow Brown's is plainer). Gatekeeper prefers scrub-grassland edges and hedgerows rather than open grassland.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Gatekeeper flies July–August; Meadow Brown June–September

similar_species.similarity_note: Another brown grassland butterfly that can occur at Old Down
similar_species.key_difference: Ringlet is darker brown, almost sooty, with multiple cream-ringed eyespots on the underside of both wings. Meadow Brown is warmer brown with much plainer hindwing underside.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Ringlet flies June–August; Meadow Brown June–September

photos.caption: Meadow Brown — Britain's most abundant grassland butterfly
Meadow Brown male showing single eye-spot on dark forewing

confidence_note: Rounded heaps of fine, loose, dark soil — unmistakeable. In winter, the heaps may be larger and more frequent as moles dig deeper to follow earthworms into unfrozen ground.
summary: You'll almost never see a Mole — but you'll always see its work. Those neat conical heaps of fresh dark soil are the sign that a very remarkable animal is living just below your feet.
full_description:
The Mole is one of Britain's most extraordinary mammals — perfectly adapted for a life spent entirely underground. It is almost blind (eyes are tiny, covered by skin), has no visible ears, and a cylindrical body with massive, spade-like front feet that can shift loose soil with remarkable speed. A mole can dig a tunnel 3.5 metres per hour. The velvety fur is unique: it has no 'grain,' lying equally flat in any direction — essential for an animal that needs to reverse quickly in narrow tunnels.

Mole hills are the main sign at Old Down: rounded heaps of fine, loose, crumbled dark soil pushed up from below. A mole's tunnel network can extend across a huge area, and the hills mark the places where the mole has pushed excavated soil to the surface. Fresh hills are dark and damp; older ones are paler and may have grass starting to grow on them. In spring (March–April), the hills are larger and more frequent as the mole creates a special deep 'fortress' nest.

Moles eat almost exclusively earthworms, which they catch in their tunnels. They have a remarkable trick: they bite earthworms in the head to paralyse but not kill them, storing living worms in a 'larder' chamber to eat later. A single mole may store hundreds of paralysed earthworms. Despite their subterranean lives, moles occasionally come to the surface — usually young males dispersing in spring.
native_info: Native throughout mainland Britain. Absent from Ireland. Common in well-drained soils with good earthworm populations.
wildlife_value: Mole digging aerates and mixes soil, bringing subsoil to the surface. Mole hills create patches of bare soil that are important germination sites for short-lived plants, including some rare wildflowers. Mole tunnels are used by shrews, voles, and beetles. Moles are preyed upon by Tawny Owl, Buzzard, Stoat, and Heron.

life_stages.description: Rounded heaps of fine, crumbled dark soil are pushed to the surface from tunnel excavations. Fresh mole hills are dark and moist. Old ones pale and dry. In spring the mole builds a larger 'fortress' — a deeper chamber with a much larger heap above it.

photos.caption: Mole hills — the Mole's unmistakeable calling card
A fresh mole hill — dark, crumbled, fine soil
Mole hills on chalk grassland
Fresh mole hill

confidence_note: Male is unmistakeable — white with bright orange wingtips. Female is white with black wingtips and often confused with the white butterflies. Both sexes have a beautiful green-and-white marbled pattern on the underside of the hindwing.
weather_note: A true spring butterfly — numbers and timing vary with spring weather. Cold springs push emergence back; warm springs bring them out in April.
summary: The arrival of the Orange-tip is one of the classic signs that spring has truly arrived. The male's bright orange wingtips are unmistakeable — look for them dancing along hedgerows and wildflower verges in May.
full_description:
The Orange-tip is a spring butterfly — it emerges in April and May and is typically gone by June, with just a single brood per year. The male is one of the most distinctive British butterflies: white wings with a large patch of vivid orange at the tip of each forewing. There's no mistaking him when he flies past. The female is white with dark wingtips and no orange — she is regularly confused with Small White or Green-veined White, but the beautiful marbled green-and-white underside of the hindwing (visible when at rest or in flight) is present in both sexes and is the clincher.

The caterpillars feed on the flowers and seed pods of Garlic Mustard (Alliaria petiolata) and Cuckooflower (Cardamine pratensis) — plants that are usually found in damp meadows, hedgerow bases, and woodland edges rather than dry chalk grassland. At Old Down, look for Orange-tips flying along the hedgerow edges and in areas where damp ground or rank vegetation supports these foodplants.

One of the most remarkable things about Orange-tip caterpillars is that they are cannibalistic — if two caterpillars meet on the same plant, one will eat the other. This is why the female lays only a single egg per plant: if she laid more, they'd just eat each other.
native_info: Native throughout England, Wales, and southern Scotland. Common and widespread where foodplants grow. A single brood, flying April to June.
wildlife_value: Orange-tips are pollinators of spring wildflowers, including Cuckooflower and Garlic Mustard. The caterpillars feed on these plants' seed pods, making them dependent on damp, undisturbed ground where the plants grow. The adults are important nectar visitors to early-flowering plants including Bluebell, Dandelion, and Cuckooflower — all at a time when few other butterflies are flying.

life_stages.description: The female lays a single bottle-shaped egg on the flower stalk of Garlic Mustard or Cuckooflower — crucially, only one egg per plant, to prevent cannibalism. The egg starts white and turns orange as it develops, which can help you spot it.

The caterpillar is green-grey, almost perfectly matching the seed pods it feeds on. It is cannibalistic — if it meets another Orange-tip caterpillar, it will eat it. Look carefully along the seed pods of Garlic Mustard in June.

The chrysalis is remarkable — long, curved, and pointed, shaped like a curved thorn or leaf midrib. It is extremely well-camouflaged and attached along a stem. The butterfly overwinters inside and emerges the following April.

The male is brilliant white with a large orange patch covering the outer third of the forewing tip. Both sexes have a beautiful marbled green-and-white underside on the hindwing that looks like crinkled lichen — a perfect camouflage when at rest.

photos.caption: Male Orange-tip showing vivid orange wingtips
Male Orange-tip in flight

life_stages.description: When at rest with wings closed, both males and females show the green-and-white marbled underside of the hindwing — this is the best ID feature for the female, who has no orange above.

photos.caption: Orange-tip at rest showing the marbled green-and-white underside
Male Orange-tip butterfly
Orange-tip in flight
Orange-tip underside — marbled green and white

summary: Tall white daisies with golden yellow centres that stand above the summer grassland at Old Down in great drifts. One of Britain's most cheerful wildflowers — and a magnet for hoverflies, bees, and beetles.
full_description:
Oxeye Daisy (Leucanthemum vulgare) is one of the most recognisable wildflowers in Britain — the classic large daisy of summer meadows, with bright white ray petals surrounding a golden yellow disc. Plants grow 30–70cm tall, with slightly waxy toothed leaves that clasp the stem, and can form dense colonies in undisturbed grassland. Individual flowers are 3–5cm across, much larger than any other common white daisy, and held on long unbranched stems.

At Old Down, Oxeye Daisy produces spectacular displays across the chalk grassland from June through July. It thrives in the low-nutrient, well-drained chalk soil and is one of the easiest ways to spot ancient, unimproved meadow — it struggles where soil has been enriched with fertiliser. The flowers are open-structured and produce large amounts of pollen and nectar accessible to a wide range of insects, making patches of Oxeye Daisy some of the best places at Old Down to watch insects in summer.

Oxeye Daisy can be confused with similar-looking relatives like Scentless Mayweed, but is distinguished by its larger flowers, clasping stem-leaves, and taller growth. It is also noticeably scentless — crush the leaves and they have a faint, slightly aromatic smell, but nothing like the pineapple scent of Pineapple Mayweed.
native_info: Native throughout the UK in meadows, grasslands, roadsides, and disturbed ground, especially on well-drained and chalk soils. One of the most common meadow wildflowers where grassland is unimproved.
wildlife_value: One of the most visited flowers at Old Down in summer. The open disc provides abundant pollen and nectar accessible to hoverflies, solitary bees, bumblebees, beetles, and many butterfly species including Meadow Brown and Common Blue. Seed heads are eaten by finches in late summer.

life_stages.description: In spring, Oxeye Daisy grows as a flat rosette of deeply toothed, slightly waxy dark green leaves close to the ground. The leaves are spoon-shaped with rounded teeth. At this stage it can be confused with other rosette plants, but the leaf shape is distinctive.

Stems rise to 30–70cm and produce the large white-and-gold daisy flowers. At peak flowering in June–July, Old Down grassland can be dotted with hundreds of flowers simultaneously. Each flower head is 3–5cm across with 15–30 white ray florets surrounding the golden disc. Flowers close slightly in dull weather and fully at night.

photos.caption: Oxeye Daisy close-up showing white ray petals and golden disc
Oxeye Daisy in grassland habitat

life_stages.description: After flowering, the ray petals fall and the central disc forms a small seed head. Seeds are ribbed and cylindrical, dispersed by wind and animals. Plants die back in autumn but re-grow strongly the following spring.

similar_species.similarity_note: Both white-rayed daisies common in summer
similar_species.key_difference: Scentless Mayweed is smaller (1–2cm flowers), has very finely divided feathery leaves, and a hollow domed centre disc. Oxeye Daisy has larger flowers, solid stem, and clasping toothed leaves.

photos.caption: Oxeye Daisy — classic white and gold summer flower
Oxeye Daisy in chalk grassland

confidence_note: The four large peacock eye-spots on brick-red wings are completely unmistakeable. No other British butterfly looks anything like it. Even with wings closed the dark underside is distinctive.
weather_note: One of the first butterflies seen in warm spring sunshine, sometimes flying as early as February on mild days when it emerges from hibernation.
summary: The most spectacular butterfly in Britain — four vivid peacock eye-spots on brick-red wings that look almost artificial. It hibernates as an adult through winter, often in sheds or log piles, and is one of the first butterflies to appear in spring sunshine.
full_description:
The Peacock is justifiably one of Britain's most popular butterflies. The four large, vivid eye-spots — each mimicking the eye of an owl or larger predator — are an extraordinary defence mechanism. When a Peacock is resting with wings closed it is dark and nearly invisible, like a dead leaf. If disturbed by a small predator, it suddenly flips its wings open, revealing the four eyes and making a rustling hissing sound simultaneously — a startling double shock that gives the butterfly time to escape.

Unlike most butterflies, the Peacock overwinters as an adult — it hibernates in cool, dark places such as hollow trees, log piles, outhouses, and garden sheds. From October it enters hibernation, and on the first warm days of late winter (sometimes as early as February) it emerges to feed on early nectar sources before laying eggs. The caterpillars feed exclusively on Stinging Nettles, so patches of nettles in sunny locations are essential for breeding. The hairy black caterpillars live in groups inside a silk web on the nettle top, gradually dispersing as they grow.

At Old Down, Peacocks are most numerous in late summer when adults from the summer brood are feeding up on knapweed, thistles, and bramble to build fat reserves for hibernation. Look for them nectaring avidly on sunny days in August and September, sometimes with Red Admirals and Commas at the same flowers.
native_info: Native throughout Britain and Ireland. Common and widespread, particularly in the south.
wildlife_value: Adults are important pollinators of late-summer wildflowers including knapweed, thistles, Buddleia, and bramble. Caterpillars are an important food source for Blue Tit and Great Tit chicks in summer. The species depends on patches of Stinging Nettle in sunny locations for breeding.

life_stages.description: Spiky black caterpillars live communally in a silk web on Stinging Nettle tops. Up to 200 caterpillars per nest. Despite their threatening appearance they are harmless — they feed only on nettles. Look for the distinctive black tent-like webs on tall nettles in June–July.

photos.caption: Peacock caterpillars — black and spiky, living communally on nettles

life_stages.description: The four peacock eye-spots on brick-red wings are unmistakeable. At rest with wings closed the butterfly disappears — the dark underside is excellent camouflage against bark or dead leaves. If startled, it flips open its wings with an audible hiss.

confidence_note: Grey, armour-plated crustacean with 14 legs and two short tail appendages. When touched, the Pill Woodlouse (Armadillidium vulgare) rolls into a perfect ball. Common Woodlouse (Oniscus asellus) is flatter and cannot fully roll up. Both found under logs, stones, and damp material.
summary: Not an insect, not a spider — woodlice are actually crustaceans, more closely related to crabs and shrimps than to beetles. The pill woodlouse rolls into a perfect ball when touched. They breathe through gills, not lungs.
full_description:
The woodlouse is one of the most reliably findable creatures on a wildlife walk — lift almost any log, stone, or piece of bark in a damp spot and you'll find them. But woodlice are not insects. They are crustaceans — the same group as crabs, shrimps, and lobsters — and are one of the very few crustaceans to have adapted to life on land. They still breathe through gills, not lungs, which is why they need damp conditions: their gills must stay moist to function.

The most common species found in chalk grassland and woodland edge are the Pill Woodlouse (Armadillidium vulgare) — which rolls into a perfect sphere when disturbed, like a tiny armadillo — and the Common Woodlouse (Oniscus asellus), which is flatter, slightly shinier, and cannot fully roll up. Counting legs is useful: woodlice always have 14 legs (7 pairs), plus two tail-like uropods.

Woodlice are completely harmless and important decomposers — they eat dead plant material, helping break it down into nutrients. They are eaten by spiders, centipedes, ground beetles, shrews, and toads.
native_info: Native throughout Britain. Very common in damp habitats everywhere.
wildlife_value: Important decomposers of dead plant material — they break down leaf litter, dead wood, and organic debris, releasing nutrients back into the soil. Eaten by spiders, centipedes, ground beetles, shrews, toads, and slow-worms.

life_stages.description: Found under logs, stones, and damp bark year-round. When you find one, try gently touching a Pill Woodlouse (the round grey type) — it rolls into a perfect sphere in about half a second. Count the legs — 14 legs (7 pairs). Compare with a centipede nearby.

confidence_note: The tight pyramid shape of the flowerhead at the top of the spike is distinctive. Deep pink to bright magenta colour, with unspotted leaves.
summary: One of the most elegant of the chalk grassland orchids — a dense pyramid of deep pink flowers on a tall stem, with a surprisingly strong vanilla and fox scent. Pollinated by moths.
full_description:
The Pyramidal Orchid is one of the easier UK orchids to identify: the dense, rounded pyramid of deep pink to magenta flowers at the top of the stem is distinctive and instantly recognisable. The spike grows 20–50cm and carries dozens of small flowers packed together, opening from the bottom upwards. Each individual flower has a three-lobed lip and two guide ridges that direct visiting insects to the nectar. The leaves are unspotted (unlike Common Spotted Orchid) and grey-green, clasping the stem.

The scent is extraordinary and easy to miss unless you get close — a strange combination of vanilla and fox. This is specifically designed to attract moths and butterflies, which are the main pollinators. On summer evenings, look for moths hovering at Pyramidal Orchid flowers — they hover rather than land, inserting their long probosces for nectar, and pollen masses (pollinia) stick to their eyes or head.

Pyramidal Orchid grows from an underground tuber and reappears each year, though it may disappear for several years if conditions aren't right. Like all native orchids it is protected by law — it is illegal to pick, uproot, or deliberately damage it.
native_info: Native to southern England and Wales. Most common on chalk and limestone grassland. Has spread to road verges and sand dunes, particularly in southern England.
wildlife_value: Pollinated primarily by day-flying butterflies (especially Burnet moths, Common Blue, and Marbled White) and by moths at dusk and night. The flowers produce nectar but the pollen masses stick to visiting insects' heads — an efficient pollination mechanism. The plant is associated with rich chalk grassland communities that support dozens of specialist insects. All native orchids are protected by the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

life_stages.description: Through autumn and winter, Pyramidal Orchid exists as a pair of underground tubers, with no above-ground growth at all. The tubers store energy for the following year's flowering.
In spring, unspotted grey-green leaves emerge and clasp the rising stem. At this stage it cannot be confused with Common Spotted Orchid, which has distinctly spotted leaves.

The pyramid-shaped flowerhead is unmistakeable — a tight cone of deep pink flowers that opens from the bottom up. Get close and sniff: the strange vanilla-fox scent is strongest in the evening when moths are active. Each flower has a three-lobed lip and a long spur that contains nectar.

photos.caption: Pyramidal Orchid in full flower — the classic pyramid shape
Pyramidal Orchid spike on chalk grassland

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are pink orchids of chalk grassland
similar_species.key_difference: Common Spotted Orchid has spotted leaves and a more elongated, cylindrical spike that is open at the top. Pyramidal Orchid has unspotted leaves and a tight, rounded pyramid shape.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Common Spotted Orchid flowers slightly earlier (May–June vs June–July for Pyramidal)

photos.caption: Pyramidal Orchid in flower

confidence_note: The dangling, egg-shaped, flattened spikelets are completely unmistakeable — they tremble and quake in even the slightest breeze. No other British grass has this shape. Spikelets are purplish-green, arranged on fine, hair-like stems.
summary: The most delicate and beautiful grass on the chalk — Quaking Grass trembles constantly in the breeze, its heart-shaped spikelets dancing like tiny lanterns. Finding it confirms you're on genuinely old, never-fertilised grassland.
full_description:
Quaking Grass is one of the most distinctive and beautiful grasses in Britain, and one of the most reliable indicators of ancient, unimproved chalk grassland. It grows in rosettes of flat basal leaves, sending up flowering stems in June and July that carry clusters of small, flattened, heart- or egg-shaped spikelets on hair-fine branching stalks. The spikelets are purplish-green, about 6–9mm across, and the slightest movement of air sets them trembling and quaking — catching the light and appearing to dance. In a gentle breeze, a patch of Quaking Grass is one of the most enchanting sights in British grassland.

As an ancient grassland indicator, Quaking Grass tells you something important about Old Down: this has been grassland for a very long time, without ploughing or heavy fertilisation. It is a slow-growing perennial that cannot re-establish on recently disturbed or fertilised ground. Wherever you find Quaking Grass, you're standing on a piece of landscape history.

Dried stems with spikelets retain their shape and movement for months — they have been used in dried flower arrangements for centuries. The folk name 'totter grass' also refers to the trembling motion.
native_info: Native throughout Britain and Ireland on chalk and limestone grassland. An ancient grassland indicator species.
wildlife_value: The seeds are eaten by seed-eating finches including Linnet and Yellowhammer. The dense tussock structure provides shelter for grassland invertebrates. Most importantly, Quaking Grass indicates the presence of high-quality, ancient chalk grassland that supports a rich community of specialist plants and animals.

life_stages.description: June–July: slender stems 20–50cm tall carry the distinctive egg-shaped spikelets that tremble in the breeze. The spikelets are purplish-green, flattened side-on, and hang from hair-fine stalks. Get down low and watch them catching the light.

Quaking Grass spikelet close-up — flattened, heart-shaped, purplish-green

summary: One of the most ecologically important animals at Old Down — rabbits graze the chalk grassland short, which is exactly what rare wildflowers and butterflies need to survive. Without rabbits, coarser grasses would take over and the delicate chalk grassland plants would be smothered. Look for their warrens in the sunny slope banks.
full_description:
The Rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) was introduced to Britain by the Normans around 1100 AD and is now so thoroughly naturalised that it functions as a native species ecologically. At 40–50cm long, rabbits are easily recognised — brown-grey fur, long ears with black tips, large hind legs, and the distinctive white 'scut' (tail) that flashes as they flee. They are most active at dawn and dusk, though visible throughout the day at undisturbed sites like Old Down.

Rabbits are ecosystem engineers at Old Down. By grazing the chalk grassland very short and evenly, they prevent coarser, more competitive grasses from overwhelming the fine-leaved chalk grassland species that rare plants and butterflies depend on. Without rabbit grazing, the grassland at Old Down would gradually be colonised by rank grass, then Bramble and Hawthorn scrub, and the chalk grassland community — including Cowslip, Bird's-foot Trefoil, Small Blue butterfly, and Marbled White — would decline and eventually disappear. Myxomatosis can severely reduce rabbit populations, and when this happens the grassland quality changes noticeably within a few years.

Signs of rabbits are easy to find at Old Down. Warrens — networks of burrows — are visible as holes 10–20cm across with fresh-dug soil around the entrance, often on south-facing slopes where the chalk is near the surface. Round black droppings (about 1cm across) are scattered widely, often in latrine piles. Grazing marks on plants — clean-angled cuts on grass stems and shrub shoots — are also characteristic. Rabbits are important prey for Red Kite, Buzzard, Stoat, Fox, and Kestrel on the site.
native_info: Introduced to Britain by the Normans c.1100 AD. Now fully naturalised and one of the most widespread mammals in the UK. Most abundant on chalk, limestone, and sandy soils where burrowing is easy.
wildlife_value: Critical ecosystem engineer for chalk grassland — grazing maintains the short, diverse sward that rare plants and butterflies depend on at Old Down. Burrows provide shelter for other species including Rabbits obviously, but also Shelduck, Bumblebee queens, and various invertebrates. Major prey species for Red Kite, Buzzard, Kestrel, Fox, Stoat, and Weasel.

life_stages.description: Brown-grey fur above with pale buff underside; large ears 7–8cm long; powerful hind legs; white 'scut' (tail) that flashes when the animal runs. The white tail is a warning signal to other rabbits. Eyes are large and positioned on the sides of the head, giving a wide field of vision. Look for them in the early morning and evening, sitting up and alert before moving to feed.

photos.caption: Rabbit on chalk grassland — a key ecosystem engineer at Old Down
European Rabbit — brown-grey adult showing characteristic large ears
Rabbit showing alert posture and white tail (scut)

life_stages.description: Warrens are systems of interconnected burrows with entrance holes 10–20cm across, usually on sunny slopes or in hedgerow banks. Fresh soil (spoil) at the entrance indicates active use. Round dark droppings, about 1cm across, are scattered widely around the warren and in latrine piles on prominent spots. Gnawed grass and bark at ground level shows where rabbits have been feeding. Footprints show large hind feet landing in front of the smaller front feet.

Young rabbits (called kittens or kits) are born underground from February onwards and emerge at about 3 weeks old. They are miniature versions of adults but rounder, slightly fluffier, and with proportionally larger ears and eyes. Several litters are produced each year — rabbits can breed rapidly when conditions are good.

similar_species.similarity_note: Both medium-sized brown mammals with long ears in open grassland
similar_species.key_difference: Brown Hare is much larger (50–70cm), with longer black-tipped ears, longer hind legs, and a distinctly black-and-white tail (black on top, white below). Hares live entirely above ground — no warrens — and rely on speed. Hares have a wilder, more powerful look than Rabbits.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both present year-round; Hares are less common at Old Down than Rabbits

photos.caption: Rabbit — essential grazer of Old Down's chalk grassland
European Rabbit adult portrait
Rabbit showing the white scut (tail) that flashes as a warning signal

confidence_note: Multiple burrow entrances (10–20cm wide) with bare, scratched earth and soil heaps. Latrine piles of small round dark droppings nearby. Well-worn paths radiating from entrances. Close-cropped 'lawns' of grass around the warren.
summary: An active rabbit warren is a miniature landscape all of its own — bare soil, close-cropped grass, worn paths, and the distinctive small round droppings that tell you exactly who lives here. Look for the hopping tracks in wet mud.
full_description:
A rabbit warren is one of the easiest wildlife signs to find at Old Down. The warren itself is a network of underground burrows, with multiple entrance holes about 10–20cm wide. Around each entrance, the ground is bare and scratched, with a mound of loose soil to one side. Well-worn paths connect the entrances to each other and radiate outwards to feeding areas.

The most abundant sign is the droppings: small (7–10mm), round, dark, and fibrous pellets, often in large piles (latrines) near the warren entrance. Rabbits use latrines for territory marking — the piles can be enormous if the warren is long-established. The grass immediately around the warren is close-cropped, almost like a lawn, from constant grazing. In wet conditions, look for the distinctive hopping tracks — two large hind feet that land in front of the two smaller front feet, creating a characteristic paired pattern.

Other signs include: fur snagged on bramble or wire, clean diagonal cuts on grass stems and small plant shoots (rabbits make a clean cut; deer leave a ragged tear), and small scrapes in soft ground where rabbits have been digging. The warren provides habitat for many other species: foxes enlarge entrances for dens, Wheatear and Shelduck nest in disused burrows, and some invertebrates colonise the bare ground around entrances.
native_info: Rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) is non-native — introduced by the Normans in the 12th century for food and fur. Now completely naturalised.
wildlife_value: Rabbit warrens create important open habitat: the close-cropped lawns around warrens are some of the best places for short-turf specialist plants and insects. Bare soil around entrances provides nesting habitat for solitary bees and wasps. Abandoned burrows are used by foxes, Badgers, Shelduck, Wheatear, and many invertebrates.

life_stages.description: Look for burrow entrances (10–20cm wide) with fresh, loose soil at the entrance. Fresh digging looks dark and moist. Look for droppings, worn paths, and close-cropped grass. Activity is highest at dawn and dusk.

photos.caption: Rabbit burrow entrance — bare earth, worn path, approximately 15cm wide
Rabbit warren — multiple entrances with bare earth and worn paths
Rabbit burrow entrance

confidence_note: Unmistakeable: black wings with bold red bands and white spots at the wingtips. No other UK butterfly has this combination.
summary: One of Britain's most familiar and beautiful butterflies — jet black with bold red bands and white spots. Often one of the last butterflies seen in autumn, feeding on fallen fruit and ivy flowers.
full_description:
The Red Admiral is one of the most striking and recognisable British butterflies. The bold combination of jet black wings with bright red bands crossing the forewings and hindwings, plus white spots near the forewing tips, is completely unmistakeable — there is nothing else like it in the UK. Underneath, the wings have a beautiful complex pattern of brown, black, and orange that provides excellent camouflage when roosting on tree bark.

Red Admirals are primarily migrants from southern Europe and North Africa — vast numbers move north each spring, and the British population is reinforced by these arrivals each year. Some individuals are now known to overwinter successfully in southern England, emerging on warm winter days. The caterpillars feed on Stinging Nettles, making any patch of nettles in a sunny, sheltered spot potentially important for breeding.

In late summer and autumn, Red Admirals are drawn to ripe and rotting fruit — orchards, blackberries, fallen windfall apples, and garden ivy flowers are magnets for them at this time of year. They bask with wings spread flat in the autumn sunshine, soaking up warmth before their long flight south. At this time, they can also be seen roosting motionless on sun-warmed fence posts, tree trunks, and walls.
native_info: Resident and migrant. Breeds in the UK using Stinging Nettles, but many individuals are migrants from mainland Europe. Increasingly overwinters in the south of England.
wildlife_value: Caterpillars feed on Stinging Nettles, making nettles a key resource for this species. Adults are important pollinators of late-season flowers — especially ivy flowers in autumn, which are one of the most important late nectar sources for many insects. Red Admirals are among the most mobile of UK butterflies, linking habitats across large distances.

life_stages.description: The caterpillar lives in a tent of folded nettle leaves, sewn together with silk. It is black or dark brown with yellow spots along the sides. Peel back a folded nettle leaf on a sunny nettle patch in summer and you may find one.
The chrysalis hangs from a stem near the nettle patch, dark brown with small metallic-gold patches.
Fresh adults in summer are vividly coloured — jet black, red, and white. They nectar on a wide range of flowers including knapweed, thistles, bramble, and marjoram.

photos.caption: Red Admiral butterfly — the bold red bands and white spots are unmistakeable

life_stages.description: In late summer and autumn, Red Admirals feed intensely on rotting fruit and ivy flowers to build up energy reserves. At this time of year they often bask with wings fully spread on warm surfaces, and can be approached very closely.

photos.caption: Red Admiral basking in autumn sunshine
Red Admiral showing the beautiful underwing pattern
Red Admiral butterfly
Red Admiral basking
Red Admiral underwing

confidence_note: Orange-red fur with white underparts, black legs, and a bushy tail (brush) with a white tip. The pointed muzzle and large, alert, pointed ears are distinctive. Dog-like but slimmer and more alert-looking than a domestic dog.
summary: Britain's only wild member of the dog family — clever, adaptable, and absolutely everywhere. Foxes are most often heard at night in January when they scream to find mates, but can be seen at any time of day, especially at dawn and dusk.
full_description:
The Red Fox is one of Britain's most familiar wild mammals — its orange-red fur, bushy white-tipped tail, pointed nose, and large ears make it instantly recognisable. It has spread from countryside to every city and town, and is now as much an urban animal as a rural one. In towns it has learned to exploit bins, gardens, and food waste; in the countryside it hunts rabbits, voles, and mice, eats insects, earthworms, berries, and carrion, and is one of nature's most generalist opportunists.

At Old Down, foxes are most often seen at dawn and dusk, moving along the hedgerow base or crossing open grassland. In January, listen at night for the eerie, blood-curdling scream of the vixen — often heard from a long distance away — and the short, sharp bark of the dog fox. The screaming is part of the mating season (December–February). In March–April, the cubs are born underground in an earth (den), usually in a bank, among tree roots, or in a rabbit burrow.

Foxes are solitary hunters but live in social groups of one male (dog fox) and one or two females (vixens), occupying a territory. Young foxes (cubs) are dark brown-grey at birth and gain adult colouring over several weeks. By late summer the cubs disperse to find their own territories — this is when foxes are seen most often in unusual places.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. One of the commonest and most widespread wild mammals in Britain. Highly adaptable to urban and rural environments.
wildlife_value: Foxes are important predators of rabbits, voles, and Wood Mice, helping control herbivore populations. They also eat large numbers of earthworms, beetles, and invertebrates. The fox earth provides habitat for other animals when abandoned. Fox scat is an important scent-marking signal in the ecosystem, influencing the behaviour of other species.

life_stages.description: Cubs are born underground in March–April, dark brown-grey at birth, gaining the orange-red adult coat over a few weeks. They begin to play outside the earth by May, and are among the most entertaining wildlife to watch on a spring evening.

photos.caption: Fox cub exploring outside the earth — cubs appear above ground from May onwards

life_stages.description: Adults are orange-red with a white chin and underparts, black legs, and a distinctive bushy tail with a white tip. The vixen screams in January–February during mating season — a sound that regularly causes alarm to people who've never heard it before.

photos.caption: Red Fox — orange-red fur, bushy white-tipped tail, alert pointed ears
Red Fox pausing in grassland — most often seen at dawn and dusk
Red Fox
Red Fox in grassland
Fox cub exploring outside the earth — cubs appear above ground from May onwards

confidence_note: The deeply forked chestnut-red tail is unique among British raptors. Once seen, a Red Kite is unmistakable.
summary: One of Britain's greatest conservation success stories — nearly extinct by the 1980s, now soaring over southern England. The deeply forked chestnut tail is unmistakable.
full_description: The Red Kite (Milvus milvus) is one of Britain's most dramatic conservation successes. Nearly hunted to extinction by the early 20th century, with only a tiny relict population surviving in Wales, it was reintroduced to the Chilterns in 1989 and has since spread across much of England, Scotland, and Wales. A large, graceful raptor with a wingspan of 175–195cm, the Red Kite is unmistakable: warm russet-red plumage contrasts with a paler whitish-grey head, dark wingtips, pale patches on the underwings, and — most distinctively — a deeply forked, chestnut-red tail that is constantly twisted and angled in flight for manoeuvrability. It soars on thermals with effortless elegance, quite unlike the heavier-flapping Common Buzzard. Red Kites are opportunistic feeders, taking live prey including rabbits, hares, small mammals, and birds, but also readily eating carrion such as roadkill — a role that earns them the status of nature's waste disposal service. Their haunting mewing call can often be heard before the bird is seen.
native_info: Native to the UK. Reintroduction programme began in the Chilterns in 1989 and Scotland/Wales in the early 1990s. Now a resident breeding bird across much of southern and central England, spreading northward naturally.
wildlife_value: As a top predator and scavenger, Red Kites play an important role in the ecosystem by removing carrion and controlling populations of rabbits, voles, and other small animals. Their recovery is an indicator of improving raptor conservation and reduced persecution. Their presence is culturally significant — a powerful symbol of wildlife recovery.

life_stages.description: When perched, Red Kites show their full plumage clearly: russet-red body, streaked paler breast, whitish-grey head with dark streaks, and yellow bill and legs. The eyes are pale yellow. Their large size is apparent when perched on a fence post or telegraph pole. At rest, the forked tail is less obvious but the warm reddish-brown plumage is distinctive.

photos.caption: Red Kite portrait showing the pale head and russet plumage
Red Kite perched, showing full plumage detail

life_stages.description: In flight, the deeply forked chestnut-red tail is the most obvious identification feature — no other common British raptor has a forked tail. Red Kites are elegant soarers, using thermals to gain height while scanning below for food. The long, angled wings show pale patches on the undersides near the wingtips. The tail is constantly twisted and flexed to adjust direction, giving the bird a strikingly fluid quality in the air.

photos.caption: Red Kite in flight clearly showing the deeply forked tail
Red Kite soaring, UK — note the forked tail
Red Kite banking in flight showing the underwing pattern
Red Kite in soaring flight

life_stages.description: Red Kites build large stick nests (eyries) in the forks of tall trees, adding new material each year until the nest becomes massive. They often incorporate odd human-made materials — plastic bags, scraps of clothing — into the nest lining, a quirk noted since medieval times. The female incubates 1–3 eggs for about 31–32 days. Adults can be seen making regular long-range hunting flights from the nest throughout the breeding season.

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are large soaring raptors over open countryside
similar_species.key_difference: Common Buzzard has a short, broad, squared-off tail (not forked). It is stockier with shorter, broader wings. Usually darker brown plumage with a pale breast band. Flaps more frequently than Red Kite and lacks the russet-red colouring.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both year-round residents; confusion most likely when distant or in poor light

summary: The common grassland plant with dark, oval flower heads on tall wiry stems. It can survive heavy trampling because its tough, ribbed leaves grow flat to the ground. Look for the circle of creamy white stamens as the pollen is released.
full_description:
Ribwort Plantain (Plantago lanceolata) is one of the most abundant wildflowers in British grasslands — easy to overlook, but fascinating once you know it. The leaves form a flat rosette, each leaf narrow-oval with three to five prominent parallel ribs (veins) running along their length — the 'ribwort' of its name. The flower stems are long, slender, and deeply ridged, reaching 10–50cm, and are topped by a dark, oval-cylindrical spike.

The flowers themselves are tiny but beautiful at close range: as the spike matures, a ring of cream or pale yellow stamens emerges from the bottom of the spike and works its way upward, giving the head a halo-like appearance. The plant is wind-pollinated and releases clouds of pollen — important to know for hay fever sufferers. Seeds are enclosed in a papery capsule that splits to release two seeds.

Ribwort Plantain has been used in traditional medicine for centuries — the leaves were applied to wounds as a poultice and contain compounds that may have mild anti-inflammatory properties. The tough, flat rosette survives trampling better than most plants, which is why it appears along well-used paths and in lawns as well as in pristine meadows. At Old Down it grows throughout the chalk grassland and is an important caterpillar food plant for several moth species.
native_info: Native throughout the UK in almost all grassland, path-side, and disturbed habitats. One of the most widespread plants in temperate climates globally.
wildlife_value: Caterpillar food plant for the Heath Fritillary, Glanville Fritillary, and several moth species. Seeds are eaten by Goldfinch and other finches. Pollen is wind-dispersed and very abundant. The plant provides shelter and climbing structure for many small invertebrates in grassland.

life_stages.description: The distinctive flat rosette of narrow-ribbed leaves lies close to the ground. Each leaf has 3–5 prominent parallel veins — run your finger along the leaf and you can feel the ribs clearly. The leaves are tough and slightly hairy, which is why they survive being trodden on.

photos.caption: Ribwort Plantain rosette of ribbed leaves

life_stages.description: Long ridged flower stems rise from the rosette, each topped with a dark oval spike 1–4cm long. As each flower matures, a circle of pale cream stamens appears and moves up the spike — this gives the head a halo effect and is the easiest way to see that the plant is in flower. On still days you can see pollen dusting from the anthers.

photos.caption: Ribwort Plantain flower spike showing the ring of cream stamens

life_stages.description: The spike dries and turns brown. Small papery seed capsules each hold two seeds. Goldfinches and linnets pick at the dried heads through late summer and autumn.

similar_species.similarity_note: Another common plantain often growing in the same locations
similar_species.key_difference: Greater Plantain (Plantago major) has broad oval leaves and a long narrow cylindrical spike on a stout, un-ridged stem. Ribwort Plantain has narrow lance-shaped leaves and an oval stubby spike on a furrowed stem.

photos.caption: Ribwort Plantain — narrow ribbed leaves and flower spikes
Ribwort Plantain flower spike with stamens

summary: Britain's unofficial national bird and one of the most familiar — the orange-red breast is visible from a long way off. Robins are unusually confiding and will often follow people digging or clearing vegetation, waiting for disturbed worms and insects.
full_description:
The Robin (Erithacus rubecula) is one of Britain's most recognisable birds, with its warm orange-red breast, white belly, brown back, and large, expressive dark eyes. Both male and female have identical plumage — unusually for British birds. Adults are about 14cm long, rounded in shape, and tend to perch upright with a slight lean forward. The song is a rich, wistful, melodic warble, heard in every month of the year including winter, when Robins sing at night under streetlights.

Robins are famously territorial and will vigorously defend their patch against other Robins — a puffed-up chest display to show off the red breast is a threat display, and physical fights do occur. They are also unusually confiding around humans, having evolved alongside animals that disturb soil — historically wild boar, now gardeners and walkers. This is why a Robin will often appear when you dig the garden, perching nearby and darting in for earthworms and beetles.

At Old Down, Robins inhabit the hedgerows, scrub, and woodland edge around the site perimeter. They nest in low hedgerow, in crevices, or on the ground in dense vegetation, building a cup of dead leaves and moss. Young Robins look completely different to adults — they are brown and heavily spotted, with no red breast at all, which confuses many people who encounter them in summer.
native_info: Resident throughout the UK, one of the most abundant birds. Found in almost all habitats with some shrub or tree cover. Partially migratory — UK Robins are mostly resident but are joined by Continental Robins in winter.
wildlife_value: Insectivore, earthworm specialist, and berry-eater in autumn and winter. Controls populations of soil invertebrates. Nest sites and territorial patterns shape the spatial use of hedgerows and scrub at Old Down.

life_stages.description: The classic Robin — orange-red breast (the colour is technically orange, not red), brown back, large dark eyes, and white belly. Posture is upright with a slight forward lean. Often bobs up and down nervously. The song is a wistful, cascading warble, quite different from any other garden bird.

photos.caption: Robin showing the iconic orange-red breast
Robin with characteristic alert posture and head tilt

life_stages.description: Young Robins fledge in May–June and look completely different from adults. They are warm brown all over with pale buff spots on the breast and back — no orange-red at all. The spots are gradually replaced by adult plumage through a moult in late summer. Many people mistake juvenile Robins for a different species entirely.

photos.caption: Juvenile Robin — no red breast, spotted brown plumage for camouflage

similar_species.similarity_note: Both small, brown, ground-foraging birds that can appear similar at a glance
similar_species.key_difference: Dunnock is grey on the face and breast with brown streaked back, no orange breast at all. Dunnock creeps mouse-like along the ground; Robin stands more upright. The Dunnock's bill is finer and more pointed.

Robin in characteristic alert pose
