confidence_note: Small deer (knee-height to a person). Reddish-brown in summer, grey-brown in winter. Distinctive white or cream rump patch. Males (bucks) have short, rough-textured antlers with 3 points each (April–December). No visible tail — the white rump shows instead.
summary: A small, elegant deer — about the size of a large dog. Roe Deer are usually seen alone at field edges at dawn and dusk. The bounding white rump patch is the classic sight as one disappears into cover.
full_description:
Roe Deer are Britain's most common native deer and among its most elegant animals. Small and neat — about the size of a large dog — they are a warm reddish-brown in summer and greyish-brown in winter. The most distinctive feature in all seasons is the prominent white or cream rump patch that flares when alarmed — this is the most common view you'll get at Old Down as a deer bounds away into cover.

Unlike Fallow or Red Deer, Roe are solitary: they live in small territories rather than herds, and a single adult in a field edge at dawn is the typical sighting. Males (bucks) carry short, rough, upright antlers with three points each, grown from March and shed in December. Does (females) have no antlers. From late July the bucks begin the rut — chasing females in tight circles, creating 'roe rings' of worn vegetation around a bush or tree, and making a rasping bark. The alarm call — also given by does — is a loud, sharp 'bark,' startlingly like a dog's.

Roe Deer have a remarkable reproductive adaptation: fertilised eggs in late summer are kept dormant (delayed implantation) and don't develop until January, so although mating is in July–August, the one or two spotted kids aren't born until May–June.
native_info: Native throughout Britain and Ireland. The most common native deer in the UK. Absent from most of Wales and some parts of Scotland.
wildlife_value: Roe Deer browse on a wide range of woodland edge plants including Bramble, Hawthorn, and young tree shoots. Their browsing helps maintain structural diversity at woodland edges. The disturbed scrapes and fraying created by bucks provide habitat for invertebrates. Roe Deer are preyed upon by Fox (kids) and occasionally Badger.

life_stages.description: Roe kids are born May–June, usually twins. They are spotted (like a Bambi) for the first few weeks — the spots break up the outline and camouflage them in dappled woodland. Kids lie still in vegetation while the mother feeds nearby. If you find a spotted kid lying alone, leave it alone — it is not abandoned.

In summer the coat is warm reddish-brown. The buck carries antlers with up to 3 points each. Both sexes show the distinctive white rump patch when alarmed. Alert, cautious, usually seen alone at field edges.

photos.caption: Young male Roe Deer buck with velvet antlers
Female Roe Deer (doe) — no antlers, white rump patch visible

life_stages.description: In winter the coat changes to grey-brown. Bucks shed their antlers in December and regrow them through spring. The white rump patch is larger and more obvious in winter.

photos.caption: Roe Deer in winter — grey-brown coat with prominent white rump
Roe Deer buck
Roe Deer doe
Roe Deer in winter

confidence_note: Roe slots (footprints) are small (3–4cm long), heart-shaped, pointed at the front — like two crescents facing each other. Fraying (bark scraped from young trees) is at 50–100cm height. Droppings are small, cylindrical, dark pellets in loose clusters.
summary: Roe Deer leave a rich record of signs if you know what to look for — neat cloven hoof prints in mud, frayed and battered young trees where bucks mark territory, and trails of small cylindrical droppings along deer paths.
full_description:
Roe Deer are creatures of routine — they follow the same paths, visit the same feeding spots, and use the same resting areas — so their signs concentrate along predictable routes. Learning to read deer signs builds a fascinating picture of the animals' lives even when you can't see them directly.

Footprints (slots) are the first thing to look for. Roe Deer have small cloven hooves — the print is two roughly crescent-shaped halves (cleaves), pointed at the front and rounded at the back, 3–4cm long. In soft mud they show the cleaves clearly; in firmer ground only the pointed tip may print. The gait is a neat walk when calm; a bounding gait when alarmed, sometimes showing dew claws (small extra hooves) in a spring.

Fraying is the most dramatic sign: bucks mark their territories in spring and summer by rubbing and scoring their antlers against young trees and shrubs, stripping the bark in rough vertical scratches at 50–100cm height. The stripped wood and tattered bark are unmistakeable. Look for additional scent glands at the base of antlers that leave smell-marks on the frayed tree. Fraying can kill young trees and is a significant factor in woodland regeneration. Roe rings — circular worn tracks around a bush — are made during the rut (July–August).
native_info: Signs found throughout Roe Deer range in the UK.
wildlife_value: Deer paths through scrub create corridors used by other wildlife. Fraying creates open wounds on trees that are colonised by saproxylic beetles and fungi. Deer droppings redistribute plant nutrients. Roe rings and scrapes create small areas of disturbed bare ground used by certain invertebrates.

life_stages.description: Look in soft mud at field edges, pond margins, and path edges. Roe slots are small (3–4cm), heart-shaped, and pointed at the front. Compare with rabbit prints (four toes, no cloven hoof) and Fox prints (four toes with pads). A clean diagonal cut on nibbled vegetation indicates deer browsing (vs. ragged rabbit gnawing).

photos.caption: Roe Deer slots (footprints) in mud — small heart-shaped cloven prints

life_stages.description: Bucks fray (rub and score) young trees to mark their territory and polish their growing antlers. Look for vertical scrape-marks on smooth-barked young trees and shrubs at 50–100cm height, with shredded bark and exposed pale wood. The frayed tree often has a characteristic 'beaten-up' look.
Small, dark, cylindrical or oval pellets, 1–1.5cm long, usually in loose clusters along deer paths or at feeding sites. May be pointed at one end. Much smaller than Fallow or Red Deer droppings.

photos.caption: Roe Deer slots (footprints) in mud — small heart-shaped cloven prints
Deer tracks showing the cloven hoof print pattern

confidence_note: Pinnate leaves with pairs of small round toothed leaflets. Crush a leaf and it smells strongly of cucumber — the most reliable ID. Round flower heads on long stems: top half red (female flowers), bottom half yellow-green (male flowers). Very common on chalk.
summary: The best fun plant on the chalk — crush a leaf of Salad Burnet and smell your fingers. It smells exactly like cucumber. An ancient chalk grassland indicator that was eaten in salads and herb gardens for centuries.
full_description:
Salad Burnet is one of the most engaging plants to show children on the chalk. It looks modest at first — pairs of small round toothed leaflets arranged along a central stem — but crush a leaf between your fingers and the smell is immediate and striking: fresh cucumber, unmistakeable and pleasant. This smell is what made Salad Burnet a popular salad herb in Tudor and medieval times; Francis Bacon recommended it for garden paths because 'it perfumes the air most delightfully, being trodden on and crushed.'

The flowers are unusual. Each small round flower head has a two-part structure: the top half bears the red female flowers (which receive pollen), while the lower half bears the drooping yellow-green male flowers (which release pollen). Wind carries pollen from the male flowers upward to the female flowers above. Watch carefully on a breezy day and you can see the male flowers releasing their pollen in clouds.

Like Quaking Grass, Salad Burnet is an indicator of ancient, unimproved chalk grassland — it colonises slowly and can't re-establish on disturbed or fertilised ground quickly. Its presence at Old Down is a sign of the site's age and the quality of its management. It grows low and keeps growing even when grazed or cut — the leaf rosette survives close cutting and produces new growth.
native_info: Native throughout England on chalk and limestone grassland. An ancient grassland indicator.
wildlife_value: Salad Burnet flowers are wind-pollinated but also visited by small insects. The leaves are eaten by rabbits and some invertebrates. As an ancient grassland indicator, its presence at Old Down confirms the quality of the chalk grassland for other specialist species.

life_stages.description: Stems 20–40cm with round flower heads — the top half red (female flowers), bottom half yellow-green (male). Crush a leaf and smell: strong cucumber. Once you know this smell you'll find Salad Burnet everywhere on chalk.

photos.caption: Salad Burnet on chalk downland — crush a leaf and it smells of cucumber
Salad Burnet flowers — top half red female flowers, lower half yellow-green male
Salad Burnet on chalk downland
Salad Burnet flowers

confidence_note: Six red spots on metallic blue-green wings — count the spots carefully. Five-spot Burnet has only five spots. The red hindwings are visible in flight.
summary: A day-flying moth that looks like a jewel — metallic blue-green wings with six vivid red spots. It flies slowly in sunshine and doesn't care if you approach closely, because it's actually toxic to birds.
full_description:
The Six-spot Burnet is one of Britain's most distinctive moths, and the only moth you're likely to see flying confidently in bright sunshine. Most moths are night-flying and cryptic — this one is bold, slow, and brightly coloured, because it has nothing to fear. Both the caterpillar and adult moth contain hydrogen cyanide, absorbed from its foodplants, which makes it unpalatable to birds. The vivid red-on-metallic-green colouring is a warning: 'I taste terrible, don't eat me.' This warning colouring is called aposematism.

At Old Down, look for Six-spot Burnets nectaring on knapweed, scabious, and thistles alongside the butterflies in July. They are unhurried and approachable — you can get very close to photograph them. The larvae feed on Bird's-foot Trefoil and Kidney Vetch, so good populations of both plants support good numbers of this moth. The cocoons — papery golden-yellow tubes attached to grass stems — can sometimes be found in late spring.

Mating pairs often stay together for extended periods on flowerheads. The female lays eggs in neat batches on the underside of foodplant leaves. The caterpillar is yellow with black spots and is equally well-defended chemically — birds quickly learn to leave them alone.
danger_note: The moth contains hydrogen cyanide and is toxic if eaten, but is completely harmless to touch or handle. It cannot sting or bite.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. Most abundant on chalk and limestone grassland in southern England. One of several UK Burnet moth species.
wildlife_value: Adults are pollinators of chalk grassland wildflowers, particularly knapweed, scabious, and Bird's-foot Trefoil. The caterpillars feed on Bird's-foot Trefoil and Kidney Vetch, making the presence of both plants important for the species. The chemical defence of both larva and adult means they are not eaten by birds — making them unusual in the food web. Their boldness and slow flight makes them excellent for introducing children to moths.

life_stages.description: Eggs are laid in neat batches on the undersides of Bird's-foot Trefoil or Kidney Vetch leaves. They are pale yellow and hatch within 2–3 weeks.

The caterpillar is fat, yellow-green with black spots. It feeds on Bird's-foot Trefoil and Kidney Vetch. The caterpillar overwinters in a state of reduced activity and resumes feeding in spring. Like the adult, it contains hydrogen cyanide and is left alone by birds.

In late spring, the caterpillar spins a papery, golden-yellow or white cocoon high up on a grass stem or plant stalk. These are distinctive and can be found by careful searching. The cocoon is elongated and pointed at both ends.

Adults emerge in late June and fly through August. The metallic blue-green forewings with six vivid red spots are unmistakeable. Adults fly slowly in sunshine and frequently visit flowers to nectar. They are completely approachable — their toxic chemistry means they have no need to flee.

photos.caption: Six-spot Burnet Moth — metallic green wings with six red spots
Six-spot Burnet Moth side view showing wing shape
Six-spot Burnet Moth on grass — often found on grass seed heads before nectaring

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are day-flying red-spotted moths of chalk grassland
similar_species.key_difference: Count the red spots: Six-spot has six, Five-spot has five. They can fly together at the same sites.

photos.caption: Six-spot Burnet Moth

confidence_note: The song flight is unmistakable — a tiny bird hovering hundreds of feet up, singing continuously. On the ground it can look like a plain brown bird, but the small crest and streaky plumage are distinctive.
summary: Famous for its spectacular song flight — males rise vertically to 100m+ and sing continuously for minutes on end. A declining farmland bird, but still heard and seen on chalk grassland like Old Down.
full_description: The Skylark (Alauda arvensis) is one of the most celebrated birds of the British countryside, famed above all else for the extraordinary song flight of the male. A medium-sized songbird (16–18cm), it has streaky brown and buff plumage on the upperparts — the typical camouflage of a ground-nesting bird — with paler, streaked underparts, a small but distinctive crest on the crown (raised when singing or alarmed), and white outer tail feathers visible in flight. The Skylark is most often identified by sound: from March to August, males rise from the ground, ascending vertically to 50–100m or more, and deliver a continuous, complex, liquid warbling song lasting minutes or even hours without pause. This song flight — one of the finest sounds in British nature — serves to defend territory and attract mates. Unfortunately, the Skylark is in serious decline in the UK, having lost over 50% of its population since the 1970s due to intensification of arable farming, loss of wildflower meadows, and removal of the weed-rich field margins that young birds depend on for insect food.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. Partially migratory — some birds remain in the UK year-round; others migrate south to southern Europe and North Africa for winter. Populations at sites like Old Down are year-round residents on chalk grassland.
wildlife_value: Adult Skylarks eat seeds (particularly weed seeds) and insects. Chicks are fed almost exclusively on insects, grasshoppers, beetles, and invertebrate larvae from dense herbage — making insect-rich grassland and field margins essential for breeding success. Skylarks are themselves food for Sparrowhawk, Hobby, Peregrine, and occasionally Merlin in winter. Their presence on chalk grassland indicates a healthy, botanically rich ecosystem.

life_stages.description: In winter, Skylarks are quiet and inconspicuous. They gather in loose, shifting flocks of 10–50 birds on open farmland, grassland, or arable fields, foraging for seeds on the ground. In hard weather or cold spells, birds may move in larger flocks. The crest is often flattened at this time. Without the song to draw attention, winter Skylarks can easily be overlooked.

As days lengthen, male Skylarks establish territories on open grassland. The first tentative song flights begin in March — shorter and lower than the full summer performance, but unmistakably Skylark. Males begin competing for the best territories. Early spring is a good time to watch them at close range as they walk and run across the grassland with their characteristic upright posture.

photos.caption: Skylark on the ground in grassland, Lake District, UK — note the small crest

life_stages.description: From April to June, male Skylarks perform their most famous behaviour: spectacular song flights high above the grassland. Rising vertically while singing continuously, the male becomes a tiny speck against the sky at heights of 50–100m. The song is a rapid, bubbling, liquid warble — endlessly variable and extraordinarily sustained. A male may hold his position 100m up, singing, for 5–10 minutes or longer before parachuting back to earth. On still days at Old Down, a singing Skylark is one of the defining sounds of the site.

photos.caption: Skylark — perched male showing streaky plumage and raised crest
Skylark male, showing the characteristic upright stance

life_stages.description: Skylark nests are simple cups of grass, woven into a hollow scraped in the ground — usually well concealed in a grass tussock or clump of vegetation. The female incubates 3–4 speckled eggs for 11 days. Nests are highly vulnerable to agricultural operations (mowing, rolling) and predation from foxes, crows, and stoats. Successful pairs may raise 2–3 broods in a season.

Young Skylarks fledge at just 9–10 days old — before they can fly well — and are then fed on the ground for a further 2–3 weeks by both parents. During this period, the chicks are entirely dependent on insects: grasshoppers, beetles, flies, and caterpillars from dense grassland vegetation. The availability of insect-rich grassland margins is absolutely critical for chick survival — their loss to intensive farming is the primary cause of the Skylark's decline.

photos.caption: Juvenile Skylark — scaly-looking buff-brown plumage, no song yet

life_stages.description: By August, the breeding season is over. Family groups and then larger flocks form, moving across farmland and grassland foraging for seeds. Some birds begin to drift southward, and Scandinavian birds arrive to winter in Britain. Song flights become rare, though you may still hear brief bursts on warm September days.

photos.caption: Skylark in late-season grassland, UK

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are brown, crested ground-nesting birds of open habitats
similar_species.key_difference: Woodlark is smaller with a shorter tail and more rounded wings. It has a distinctive black-and-white stripe over the eye. Its song is also different — a beautiful liquid descending phrase, not the Skylark's sustained warble. Prefers woodland edges and heath rather than open grassland.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Woodlark is resident year-round but much less common in the UK

similar_species.similarity_note: Another small, streaky brown bird of grassland habitats
similar_species.key_difference: Meadow Pipit is smaller and slimmer, with a much finer bill. It has no crest. Its song flight is shorter and the call is a thin 'seep seep seep'. It bobs its tail frequently when walking, unlike Skylark.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Meadow Pipits are common year-round on chalk grassland alongside Skylarks

confidence_note: Smooth, shiny, coppery-brown skin with no visible legs, blinking eyes (snakes have no eyelids), and a rounded snout. Much smaller and more slender than any UK snake.
weather_note: Only active in warm weather. Most easily seen on sunny mornings when they bask under flat stones or corrugated metal sheets.
summary: Not a worm. Not a snake. The Slow-worm is a legless lizard — and it's completely harmless. It has eyelids (snakes don't), smooth coppery skin, and a superpower: it can detach its own tail to escape a predator.
full_description:
The Slow-worm is one of Britain's most misunderstood animals. It looks like a snake but is actually a legless lizard — it just lost its legs over millions of years of evolution. You can tell it from a snake because it has eyelids (you can see it blink), ear openings, and a body that is more cylindrical and uniform — snakes have a distinctly wider belly. The skin is smooth and shiny, usually bronze-coppery in males, browner in females (which often have a dark stripe along the back). Both are beautiful in the right light.

Slow-worms are shy and secretive, spending much of their time underground or under cover. At Old Down, look for them under flat stones, pieces of corrugated metal, or in warm grassy tussocks. They are particularly active on warm mornings when they bask briefly before retreating to cover. Their diet is specialised: they eat mainly slow-moving prey that they can catch without a chase — slugs, slow worms (despite the name confusion), small snails, earthworms, and woodlice.

Slow-worms give birth to live young in late summer — unusual for a reptile. The babies are tiny (5–10cm), golden-bronze with a dark back stripe, and look like miniature adults. Like all UK reptiles, the Slow-worm is fully protected by law. If you find one, observe it from a distance — replace any cover exactly as you found it.
danger_note: Slow-worms are completely harmless to people — they cannot bite effectively. However, they are fully protected under Schedule 5 of the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981. It is a criminal offence to intentionally kill, injure, or take a Slow-worm. Please observe without handling.
native_info: Native throughout the UK, including Scotland and Wales. Protected under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981. One of the UK's six native reptile species.
wildlife_value: Slow-worms are important predators of slugs and earthworms, making them valuable in gardens and grassland ecosystems. They are preyed upon by Adders, Kestrels, Buzzards, and domestic cats. The eggs of Slow-worm young are a food source for some ground beetles. As a protected species they are an indicator of undisturbed, structurally diverse habitat.

life_stages.description: Baby Slow-worms are born in late summer, usually 6–12 at a time. They are tiny (5–10cm) and strikingly golden or bronze, with a sharp dark stripe along the back and belly. This bold pattern fades as they grow. They are independent from birth.
Adult females are typically brown or bronze-brown, often with a dark stripe along the back and dark sides. They reach 30–50cm in length. Females give birth to 6–12 live young in August–September.

photos.caption: Adult Slow-worm — smooth, coppery skin and blinking eyes distinguish it from snakes

life_stages.description: Adult males are often more uniformly bronze-grey, with fewer dark markings than females. Blue spots may develop on older males — these are thought to be attractive to females. Males can reach 45–50cm, though most are shorter.

photos.caption: Slow-worm — note the blinking eyes (a lizard feature, not a snake feature)
Slow-worm — legless lizard, not a snake
Adult Slow-worm on chalk grassland

confidence_note: Very small and fast-flying, easy to miss. Size (14–18mm wingspan) is the best first clue — smaller than any other blue butterfly you are likely to encounter.
summary: Britain's smallest butterfly — barely larger than a thumbnail. Males are bright silvery-blue; females brownish. Found only where Bird's-foot Trefoil grows on chalk or limestone grassland.
full_description: The Small Blue (Cupido minimus) is Britain's smallest butterfly, with a wingspan of just 14–18mm — about the size of a large fingernail. Despite its name, males are silvery-blue rather than vivid blue, and females are predominantly brown with just a dusting of blue at the wing base. Both sexes have pale grey-white undersides with small but neat black spots. They fly in a single generation each year (May–July), with a brief peak in June. Small Blues fly low and fast over short chalk grassland, making them easy to overlook unless you specifically search the knee-high vegetation. The species has an absolute dependence on its sole larval food plant, Bird's-foot Trefoil (Lotus corniculatus), and will only breed where this plant is present in sufficient quantity on well-drained, short-sward grassland. This makes the Small Blue an excellent indicator of chalk grassland health — its presence confirms a botanically rich, traditionally managed site.
native_info: Native to the UK. Found mainly in southern England and Wales on chalk and limestone grasslands. Colonies are typically small and localised. Old Down is excellent habitat.
wildlife_value: Adults feed on the nectar of Kidney Vetch, Bird's-foot Trefoil, and other small flowers. Caterpillars feed exclusively on Kidney Vetch (Anthyllis vulneraria) — this is the sole larval foodplant, and Small Blue will only breed where Kidney Vetch grows on well-drained chalk or limestone grassland. Caterpillars have a remarkable relationship with ants (myrmecophily) — they secrete a sweet honeydew from a special gland, which ants drink greedily; in return the ants protect the caterpillar from parasitic wasps and predators. Their presence reliably indicates high-quality chalk grassland.

life_stages.description: Female Small Blues lay tiny white eggs singly on the flower buds of Bird's-foot Trefoil (Lotus corniculatus). The eggs are so small they are almost impossible to spot without a magnifying glass. Each female may lay 30–60 eggs across her short adult life. Eggs hatch within about a week.

Caterpillars are tiny, green, and slug-like — quite different from the butterfly they will become. They feed on the flowers and developing seed pods of Bird's-foot Trefoil. From early in their development, caterpillars attract ants by secreting a sweet liquid from a special gland on their back. The ants tend them carefully, protecting them from parasitic wasps and other predators in exchange for this sugary reward.

photos.caption: Small Blue caterpillar

life_stages.description: The caterpillar pupates on or near the Bird's-foot Trefoil plant, forming a small brown chrysalis that is exquisitely camouflaged against dead vegetation. This is the overwintering stage — the chrysalis remains dormant through autumn, winter, and into the following spring before the adult emerges in May or June of the following year.

Adults emerge in late May to early June and can be seen fluttering low over chalk grassland. Males are the first to emerge and can be seen patrolling their small territories. Females are slightly smaller and browner, spending more time at ground level searching for egg-laying sites on Bird's-foot Trefoil. Adults are short-lived — typically 2–3 weeks — but during warm weather can be seen in good numbers. At rest on a grass stem, the silvery underside with neat black spots is most visible.

Male Small Blue showing silvery-blue upperside

similar_species.key_difference: Common Blue is almost twice the size (26–34mm wingspan). Males are vivid violet-blue, not silvery. Females are brown with orange spots near wing edges. The size difference alone is usually enough to tell them apart.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Common Blue has two broods (May–June and August–September); Small Blue is single-brooded (May–July)

similar_species.similarity_note: Both associated with chalk grassland

confidence_note: Orange-red wings with black patches at the front edge and a row of blue spots around the outer margins. The inner edge (near the body) is dark brown. Underside is dark brown-grey with paler outer half — excellent dead-leaf camouflage.
weather_note: Like the Peacock, it overwinters as an adult and may be seen flying in late February on warm sunny days.
summary: Once one of Britain's most common garden butterflies, the Small Tortoiseshell has declined sharply in the south. Its larvae feed on Stinging Nettles — so every sunny nettle patch is potential butterfly habitat.
full_description:
The Small Tortoiseshell is one of Britain's most familiar butterflies — or was. It has declined significantly in southern England over recent decades, for reasons not fully understood. Possible causes include a parasitic fly (Sturmia bella, introduced from Europe) that lays its eggs on nettles near the caterpillars, warmer winters affecting hibernation, and changes in nettle patch quality. It remains common in northern Britain.

The butterfly overwinters as an adult, often in cool dark spots — including inside houses where they may be found torpid behind curtains or in loft spaces. They need to be left alone or carefully moved to a cool dark outbuilding, not brought into warm rooms where they will waste their fat reserves. In spring they emerge hungry and feed on early flowers before laying eggs.

Caterpillars are bright yellow-green with black spines, and like Peacock caterpillars they live communally in silk webs on Stinging Nettles. The best habitat is sunny nettle patches along south-facing hedgerow bases. Unlike the Peacock, the Small Tortoiseshell has two broods in good years — a spring brood and a summer brood — so adults can be seen from March to October.
native_info: Native throughout Britain and Ireland. Has declined in southern England but remains widespread.
wildlife_value: Adults are pollinators of knapweed, buddleia, thistles, and late-summer wildflowers. Caterpillars are food for Blue Tit chicks and ground beetles.

life_stages.description: Orange-red with bold black-and-yellow patches on the forewing, and a row of blue crescents on the outer margin. The underside is superb camouflage — dark brown-grey with a paler outer half, like a dead leaf when resting with wings closed.

photos.caption: Small Tortoiseshell — orange-red with black patches and blue marginal spots
Small Tortoiseshell with wings spread showing full colour pattern

similar_species.similarity_note: Both orange with dark markings, and both overwinter as adults
similar_species.key_difference: Comma has very ragged, notched wing edges (unique) and is a purer orange. Small Tortoiseshell has smooth wing edges and a darker pattern near the body.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both fly in spring and late summer

Small Tortoiseshell underside — camouflaged like a dead leaf

confidence_note: Bright green with dense tiny purple-black speckles all over. Very long antennae (much longer than the body). Females have a long, curved ovipositor (egg-laying tube). Almost entirely wingless. Found on bramble and other shrubs late summer.
summary: A beautifully speckled green cricket found on bramble and hedgerow from late summer. Almost flightless, it calls at such a high frequency that most adults can barely hear it — a bat detector brings its song into earshot.
full_description:
The Speckled Bush Cricket is one of the most beautifully marked insects in Britain. Bright green, covered in a dense constellation of tiny dark purple-brown speckles, it looks like a leaf flecked with dew. The extremely long, thread-like antennae distinguish it immediately from grasshoppers. It is found on bramble, hedgerow shrubs, and rough vegetation from late July through to November.

The song is produced by wing-rubbing (stridulation), but unlike grasshoppers, crickets rub their wings together rather than leg against wing. The Speckled Bush Cricket calls at around 20–30kHz — at the very top edge of most adults' hearing range, and completely inaudible to anyone over about 40. Children often hear it as a very faint, high-pitched tick; adults typically need a bat detector set to 20–25kHz to detect it. Bring a detector on an evening walk in August and the hedgerows will be full of invisible crickets.

Females have a long, curved, sabre-shaped ovipositor (egg-laying tube) that sticks up behind the abdomen — this makes them easy to distinguish from males. The species is almost entirely flightless, spending its life climbing slowly through vegetation. Eggs are laid into bark crevices and overwinter.
native_info: Native throughout England and Wales. Common in hedgerows and scrub.
wildlife_value: Speckled Bush Crickets are eaten by bats (which detect them easily), spiders, and insectivorous birds. They eat pollen, plant material, and small invertebrates.

life_stages.description: Bright green with dense speckles, found climbing slowly through bramble and hedgerow in late summer. Look in late afternoon on bramble leaves in sheltered hedgerows. The female's curved ovipositor is distinctive. Almost never jumps — instead it freezes or moves slowly.

photos.caption: Speckled Bush Cricket — bright green with dense dark speckles, very long antennae
Speckled Bush Cricket on vegetation

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are green jumping insects
similar_species.key_difference: This cricket has antennae far longer than its body; grasshoppers have short antennae. Crickets are mostly nocturnal; grasshoppers active by day.

photos.caption: Speckled Bush Cricket
Speckled Bush Cricket on leaf

confidence_note: Brown with cream or pale yellow spots, including a distinctive row of eye-spots near the wing edges. The dappled-shade habitat and habit of basking in patches of sunlight is a strong clue.
summary: The butterfly of dappled sunlight and woodland edges — warm brown with cream spots, and a habit of spiralling upward in fierce territory battles. One of the few UK butterflies that can be seen in every month from March to October.
full_description:
The Speckled Wood is a medium-sized brown butterfly with a distinctive pattern of pale cream spots on a warm dark-brown background, and a row of small eye-spots around the wing edges. It is strongly associated with dappled shade — woodland rides, hedgerows, and scrubby edges where patches of sunlight filter through to the ground. Males defend individual spots of sunlight on the ground or a leaf, rising in spiralling aerial battles with rival males before one retreats and the winner returns to his sunlit patch.

Speckled Wood is one of the longest-season butterflies in Britain — you can see it in every month from March to October in a warm year. This is partly because it has multiple broods, and partly because it can overwinter as either a caterpillar or a chrysalis — uniquely flexible among British butterflies. The caterpillars feed on a range of grasses and are bright green with cream stripes, perfectly camouflaged on a grass blade.

At Old Down, look for Speckled Wood along the edges where scrub or hedgerow meets the open grassland. Adults bask with wings open or half-open on sunny leaves, and are remarkably easy to approach when basking.
native_info: Native throughout England, Wales, and southern Scotland. Has expanded its range northward significantly in recent decades. One of the more common and widespread UK butterflies.
wildlife_value: Caterpillars feed on a range of coarse grasses (Cock's-foot, Yorkshire Fog, False Brome), making areas of long grass at woodland and scrub edges important for breeding. Adults take nectar from bramble, ragwort, and other flowers. The species rarely visits open grassland flowers but is an important link between woodland-edge and grassland habitats.

life_stages.description: Bright green with a pale stripe, perfectly camouflaged on a grass blade. May overwinter as a caterpillar — the only UK butterfly that can overwinter in two different life stages (as either caterpillar or chrysalis).

Adults bask with wings spread in dappled sunlight. The pattern of cream spots and eyespots on dark brown wings is distinctive. Males rise in fierce spiralling chases to defend sunlit patches. Multiple broods mean adults can be seen from March to October.

photos.caption: Speckled Wood basking in dappled sunlight
Speckled Wood showing underside pattern
Speckled Wood
Speckled Wood underside

confidence_note: Britain's largest beetle — up to 7.5cm long including the male's enormous antler-like mandibles. Shiny dark brown to black body with red-brown wing cases. Females are smaller and have much smaller mandibles. Unmistakeable.
weather_note: Most active on warm evenings in June–July. Males fly at dusk looking for females, making an impressive buzzing flight.
summary: Britain's largest and most spectacular beetle — the male's enormous antler-like mandibles look fearsome but are actually used to wrestle other males, not to hurt people. The larvae spend up to seven years eating rotting wood underground before becoming the beetle you see.
full_description:
The Stag Beetle is the largest beetle in Britain and one of its most dramatic insects. The male's extraordinary mandibles — enlarged jaws resembling a stag's antlers — are used exclusively in combat with other males for the right to mate with females. They look terrifying but can only very rarely pinch a finger, and even then it is not painful. The females have much smaller, functional jaws.

The adult beetles live for only a few weeks and do not feed as adults (they may sip tree sap or fruit juice). The real life is underground: the larvae spend 3–7 years feeding on rotting wood — old tree stumps, buried roots, and dead wood in soil. This long larval period in rotting wood makes the Stag Beetle entirely dependent on old trees and dead wood habitat. Loss of old trees and over-tidying of gardens and woodlands has reduced populations significantly — the Stag Beetle is a UK Priority Species.

Males fly at dusk in June and July, making a distinctive loud buzzing flight as they cruise low over the ground searching for females. It's an incredible sight. If you find one on the ground, move it gently to the nearest piece of old wood or log pile — do not move it far from where you found it.
danger_note: The male's antler-like mandibles look alarming but are almost always too weak to pinch meaningfully. Handle with care if you must, but they are harmless and should not be feared.
native_info: Native to Britain. UK Priority Species — has declined significantly due to loss of dead wood habitat. Mainly southern England.
wildlife_value: Stag Beetle larvae are major decomposers of dead wood, breaking down old tree stumps and buried roots. This decomposition is essential for woodland soil health. Adults are eaten by Foxes, Badgers, and crows. The species depends entirely on the presence of old trees and dead wood — a Stag Beetle population is a reliable indicator of long-established woodland or veteran trees.

life_stages.description: Creamy-white C-shaped grubs, up to 10cm long, found in rotting wood and soil. They spend 3–7 years underground eating dead wood before pupating. They are harmless and an important part of dead wood decomposition.

photos.caption: Stag beetle family larva — large white C-shaped grub found in rotting wood and buried roots. Stag beetle larvae (Lucanus cervus) look identical to this. They can spend 3–7 years as a larva before emerging as an adult.

life_stages.description: The male's enormous red-brown mandibles (up to 3cm long) are used only in wrestling contests with other males. Males fly low at dusk in June–July, making a distinctive loud buzzing. Look on the ground near old tree stumps and at the base of old oaks.

photos.caption: Stag Beetle male — the spectacular antler-like mandibles are used for wrestling
Male Stag Beetle at ground level near old wood

life_stages.description: Females are smaller than males with much smaller but functional mandibles. They spend more time on the ground searching for a spot to lay eggs near rotting wood. Can actually give a mild pinch if handled.

confidence_note: Unmistakable. The stinging hairs on square stems and heart-shaped leaves are unique. You will know if you have misidentified it.
summary: The humble nettle is arguably the most ecologically important 'weed' in Britain. Caterpillar food plant for over 40 butterfly and moth species including Red Admiral, Peacock, and Small Tortoiseshell.
full_description: The Stinging Nettle (Urtica dioica) is the plant most people have an instinctive relationship with — usually an uncomfortable one. Growing 30–120cm tall with distinctive square stems, it forms dense clonal patches via underground rhizomes in hedgerows, field margins, woodland edges, and disturbed ground. The heart-shaped, deeply serrated leaves grow in opposite pairs. The entire plant — stems, leaves, and even the veins — is covered in hollow stinging hairs (trichomes) that inject a mixture of formic acid, histamine, and serotonin when touched, causing burning irritation that typically lasts 5–30 minutes. Dock leaves (Rumex obtusifolius), which commonly grow nearby, provide alkaline relief. Nettles are dioecious — male and female flowers grow on separate plants. Male flowers hang in long, drooping catkin-like clusters; female flowers are shorter and more upright. Its ecological importance is extraordinary: over 40 species of butterfly and moth caterpillar depend on it, including some of our most beloved garden butterflies.
danger_note: Stinging hairs cause temporary skin irritation lasting 5–30 minutes. Applying dock leaves (Rumex obtusifolius), which often grow nearby, provides relief. Not toxic — irritation only.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. One of the most common plants in Britain, found wherever there is nutrient-rich disturbed soil. An indicator of high-nitrogen soils.
wildlife_value: One of the most important plants in Britain for invertebrates. Over 40 butterfly and moth species use it as their caterpillar food plant, including Red Admiral, Peacock, Small Tortoiseshell, and Comma. Dense nettle patches provide shelter for beneficial insects, spiders, and small mammals. Finches eat the seeds in late summer. The plant's ecological value far outweighs the inconvenience of the sting. The seeds are nutritionally dense and considered adaptogenic — traditionally used as a tonic food, rich in fatty acids, protein, and minerals.

life_stages.description: In spring, Nettles emerge with fresh bright green shoots. Young plants have the same heart-shaped, serrated leaves as the adult but smaller and more tender. At this stage they are 10–30cm tall. Spring nettle tips were traditionally harvested for nettle soup — they are edible after thorough cooking destroys the sting. Still prickly though.

By late spring, nettle plants are 30–60cm tall with dense, lush foliage. Each square stem is clothed in opposite pairs of large, serrated leaves. At this stage the stinging hairs are fully developed — the lesson of not touching nettles becomes clear to young naturalists quickly.

photos.caption: Stinging Nettle plant showing typical growth form and square stems
Stinging Nettle leaf detail showing serrated edges and stinging hairs

life_stages.description: Nettles flower in summer and are wind-pollinated — they produce no nectar or showy petals. Male plants have long drooping clusters of small greenish flowers (catkins). Female plants have shorter, upright, more tightly clustered flowers. After pollination, female plants produce tiny seeds. During the flowering period, the plant is at its tallest, sometimes reaching 1.2m.

photos.caption: Stinging Nettle in full growth showing dense foliage
Stinging Nettle patch in typical hedgerow habitat, UK
Peacock butterfly caterpillars feeding on Stinging Nettle — a perfect illustration of the nettle's ecological importance

life_stages.description: By late summer, nettle plants produce and disperse their tiny seeds. The leaves become tougher and darker green, and the plants begin to die back as temperatures drop. Dense stands turn yellow-brown in autumn. The dead stems remain standing through winter and provide hollow stem habitat for overwintering insects.

similar_species.similarity_note: Has similar leaf shape and growth habit — the name 'dead nettle' comes from its nettle-like appearance
similar_species.key_difference: White Dead-nettle (Lamium album) does NOT sting at all. It has white tubular flowers and a different stem structure. Touching it is the easiest test — no sting means it is not a Stinging Nettle.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Dead-nettle flowers throughout spring and summer

confidence_note: Most often heard rather than seen. The classic 'twit-twoo' is actually a duet: the female calls 'kee-WICK,' the male replies with a long, wavering 'hoooo.' Round head with no ear-tufts. Rich brown, streaked plumage. Large dark eyes. If you see one perched in a tree, look for the hunched, bark-like posture.
summary: The owl of classic ghost stories — its wavering hoot carries far on still autumn nights. The famous 'twit-twoo' is actually two owls calling to each other. Look for owl pellets under trees: neat parcels of compacted fur and bones coughed up after every meal.
full_description:
The Tawny Owl is Britain's most common owl and the one behind almost every owl hoot heard at night in the countryside. But the famous 'twit-twoo' is a lie — or rather, a duet. The female calls 'kee-WICK' (the 'twit' half); the male responds with his long, wavering, hollow 'hoooooo' (the 'twoo' half). When you hear both calls together in the darkness, a pair of owls is calling to each other across their territory. Tawny Owls are strictly nocturnal and almost never seen in daylight — but they roost in trees during the day, and if you find one it is usually mobbed loudly by small birds (Blue Tits, Robins, Chaffinches) giving alarm calls — a reliable sign that a predator is roosting nearby.

Tawny Owls hunt by listening. Their hearing is extraordinary — they can locate a mouse in total darkness by sound alone. The disc-shaped face channels sound to the asymmetrically placed ears, giving them a three-dimensional sound picture of the ground below. They hunt mainly Wood Mice, voles, and shrews, but also take small birds, large beetles, earthworms, and occasionally frogs. They hunt from a perch, watching and listening, then dropping silently onto prey.

Tawny Owls need old trees with cavities for nesting — they don't build nests, just lay eggs in a tree hole, old crow nest, or nest box. Look under old trees for owl pellets: grey, oval parcels about 4–5cm long, compressed fur and bones coughed back up after digesting a meal. Dissecting a pellet reveals the skull and bones of whatever the owl ate — usually Wood Mouse or Field Vole.
native_info: Native throughout mainland Britain. Absent from Ireland (no native owls breed there). Common wherever there are old trees with cavities.
wildlife_value: An important predator of Wood Mouse, Field Vole, and Common Shrew. Tawny Owls regulate small mammal populations in woodland. Nest cavities are often used by other species when vacated. Owl pellets deposited under roost trees contribute to the nutrient cycling of the woodland floor.

life_stages.description: Fluffy white owlets hatch in April from eggs laid in a tree hole or nest box. They are fed by both parents and begin to leave the nest (branch) before they can fly — these 'branchers' are sometimes found on the ground. If you find a young owl on the ground, leave it alone unless it is in immediate danger: the parents are almost certainly nearby.

photos.caption: Owl pellet — the compacted fur and bones coughed up after a meal. Dissect one and find the skull and bones of a wood mouse or vole.

life_stages.description: Rich chestnut-brown, intricately streaked with dark brown and buff. The round head and large dark eyes are distinctive. Almost always seen roosting motionless in a tree, looking like part of the bark. Strictly nocturnal — most reliably detected by its calls on autumn and winter nights.

confidence_note: The vivid blue funnel-shaped flowers with protruding red stamens are unlike any other common UK wildflower. Pink buds and blue open flowers often appear on the same plant at the same time.
summary: One of Britain's most striking wildflowers — tall spikes of vivid blue funnels with red stamens poking out. Bees absolutely love it, and the blue is so intense it almost doesn't look real.
full_description:
Viper's Bugloss earns its dramatic name from the spotted stem that can resemble a snake's skin, and the seed that resembles a viper's head. But the plant is completely harmless — in fact, it's one of the best wildflowers you can find for bees, butterflies, and hoverflies. The tall spike of vivid blue, funnel-shaped flowers with long red-purple stamens is one of the most eye-catching sights of summer on chalk grassland. The flowers open pink and turn brilliant blue as they mature — so a single spike carries both colours at once.

It is a biennial: in its first year it produces only a leafy rosette, then in its second year it sends up a tall flowering stem (30–90cm), sets seed, and dies. Look for the rough, bristly leaves with white spots (these are the swollen bases of hairs, not disease) and the hairy, sometimes spotted stem. It favours disturbed and well-drained ground — chalk grassland, roadsides, cliffs, and shingle banks.

Viper's Bugloss is exceptionally rich in nectar and pollen. On a warm day it will be covered in bumblebees, solitary bees, and butterflies competing for the deep nectaries. Even at a distance you can often locate it by the buzzing.
native_info: Native to southern and central Britain. Locally common on chalk, limestone, coastal cliffs, and disturbed ground. Rare in Scotland and Ireland.
wildlife_value: One of the most insect-rich wildflowers in Britain. Produces abundant nectar and pollen accessible to a wide range of bees and butterflies. Particularly valued by long-tongued bumblebees and solitary bees, as well as Small Tortoiseshell and Painted Lady butterflies. Several moth species lay eggs on the leaves. The rough, hairy stems provide shelter for small invertebrates.

life_stages.description: In the first year, Viper's Bugloss produces only a low, flat rosette of rough, bristly leaves. These have distinctive white spots (the bases of stiff hairs) and lie close to the ground through winter.

In the second year, a tall bristly spike grows rapidly to 30–90cm. Flowers open from the bottom upwards — pink buds at the top, vivid blue open flowers below, with red stamens protruding beyond the petals. This gives each spike a wonderful gradient of pink-to-blue.

photos.caption: Viper's Bugloss flowers — vivid blue with protruding red stamens
Viper's Bugloss spike showing pink buds and open blue flowers
Viper's Bugloss in flower
Viper's Bugloss flower spike

confidence_note: The distinctive thyme scent when leaves are rubbed is the clincher. Low, creeping habit with tiny oval leaves and tight clusters of small pink-purple flowers.
summary: The tiniest herb in the chalk grassland — crush a leaf and that unmistakeable thyme scent tells you exactly what it is. The tight mats of pink-purple flowers are a magnet for bees and butterflies.
full_description:
Wild Thyme creeps low across the chalk grassland surface, forming dense, flat mats only a few centimetres high. The tiny oval leaves are aromatic — give one a gentle rub and you'll get that familiar thyme scent immediately. This is the easiest way to confirm the ID. The small clusters of pink-purple flowers are held at the tips of the stems from June to August and are a magnet for bees, butterflies, and hoverflies on warm days.

Wild Thyme (Thymus polytrichus) is the native British species found on chalk and limestone grassland — it's different from the garden thyme (Thymus vulgaris) used in cooking, though they're closely related. It favours very short, well-drained turf where the grass is kept low by grazing or mowing, and cannot compete with tall vegetation. Finding it at Old Down indicates that the short-turf areas are being managed correctly.

Wild Thyme is the larval food plant of the Large Blue butterfly — though that species is not found at Old Down. The plant's main role in the local ecosystem is as a nectar source: it may be tiny, but a mat of flowering thyme on a warm June day will have more insects visiting it per square centimetre than almost any other plant.
native_info: Native to the UK. Found on chalk, limestone, and rocky grassland throughout Britain and Ireland. Requires short, well-drained turf.
wildlife_value: An important nectar source for bumblebees, solitary bees, butterflies, and hoverflies in short chalk grassland. The larvae of several specialist moths feed on Wild Thyme, and it provides shelter for ants and other small invertebrates within its creeping mats. As a plant of short turf, its presence indicates that the grassland has not been over-grown or left unmanaged — it disappears quickly when grass grows too tall.

life_stages.description: Wild Thyme grows as a low, dense mat of tiny oval aromatic leaves, creeping across bare chalk or short turf. In spring it begins to grow new shoots from the woody stems.

photos.caption: Wild Thyme growing as a low mat on chalk grassland

life_stages.description: Small clusters of pink-purple flowers appear at the tips of the stems. The flowers are tiny — only 4–6mm — but a whole mat in flower is highly visible and heavily visited by insects. The aroma is strongest on warm sunny days.

photos.caption: Wild Thyme in flower — pink-purple clusters on chalk grassland
Wild Thyme mat on chalk grassland
Wild Thyme in flower

summary: Britain's largest and most common pigeon — the clattering rush of wings as a flock launches from the treetops is an unmistakable countryside sound. Look for the distinctive white neck patches that flash in flight. The cooing call is one of the most soothing sounds of the British countryside.
full_description:
The Woodpigeon (Columba palumbus) is Britain's most abundant pigeon and one of the most numerous birds in the country, with a population of around 5.4 million breeding pairs. It is substantially larger than Feral Pigeon or Stock Dove — 41cm long with a wingspan of 75–80cm — blue-grey above, with a pinkish-grey breast, and the diagnostic white patches on each side of the neck (absent in young birds). In flight, the white crescents on each wing are very visible. The soft, repetitive cooing call — 'coo-COO-coo, coo-coo' — is one of the most characteristic sounds of British countryside and woodland edge.

Woodpigeons are almost entirely herbivorous, eating an enormous variety of plant material including grain, berries, seeds, leaves, and buds. They have a crop — a pouch in the throat — that allows them to carry large volumes of food back to their nest. Young Woodpigeons (squabs) are fed 'crop milk' — a protein-rich liquid produced by both parents from cells lining the crop — which is unusual among birds and means they can breed at almost any time of year when food is available.

At Old Down, Woodpigeons feed in the open grassland and field edges, and roost and nest in the hedgerows and scrub. They are an important prey item for Peregrine Falcon, which hunts over the site, and for Goshawk in nearby woodland. Large flocks gather on farmland near the site in autumn to feed on harvested fields.
native_info: Abundant resident throughout the UK. Found in almost all habitats with trees or hedgerows. Has increased significantly in population since the 1960s. One of Britain's most common birds.
wildlife_value: Major prey item for Peregrine Falcon, Goshawk, and Sparrowhawk. Seeds passed through the gut are dispersed widely. Nest sites used by other species. Provides a substantial food source for raptors — the presence of large Woodpigeon flocks near Old Down partly explains the regular Red Kite and occasional Peregrine sightings.

life_stages.description: Large, heavy-bodied pigeon with blue-grey plumage. The white neck patches are the most distinctive feature — white crescents on each side of the neck with iridescent green-purple plumage below them. The breast is pinkish-grey. In flight, white wing bars flash across each wing. Eyes are pale yellow.

photos.caption: Woodpigeon adult showing the distinctive white neck patches

life_stages.description: Young Woodpigeons lack the white neck patches entirely and are slightly duller brown-grey overall. They are often seen in summer following adults and begging for food. The white neck patches develop gradually through the first autumn.

photos.caption: Fledgling Woodpigeon — no white neck patch yet, scruffier plumage
Young Woodpigeon — juvenile plumage before the white neck patch develops

similar_species.similarity_note: Both medium-large grey pigeons in similar habitats
similar_species.key_difference: Stock Dove is smaller and compact, with no white neck patches and no white wing bars. It has two small black wing bars instead. Frequents old trees with nest holes; less common than Woodpigeon.

photos.caption: Woodpigeon — the largest and most common UK pigeon
Woodpigeon — the large white neck patch and pink breast are the best ID features
Woodpigeon perched — note the iridescent green and purple neck sheen
Fledgling Woodpigeon — no white neck patch yet, scruffier plumage

confidence_note: The inflated yellow-green seed pod rattles audibly when ripe — shake the stem gently. Yellow snapdragon-like flowers and opposite toothed leaves are distinctive.
summary: The gardener of the meadow — Yellow Rattle steals food from grass roots, weakening them and making space for wildflowers to grow. Shake a ripe plant and you'll hear the seeds rattling inside the pods.
full_description:
Yellow Rattle has a clever trick: it is hemiparasitic on grasses, meaning it taps into the roots of nearby grass plants and steals water and nutrients from them. This weakens the grasses, stops them from dominating, and makes space for smaller, slower-growing wildflowers to thrive. It is one of the most important plants in traditional hay meadows and is used deliberately in meadow restoration — sowing Yellow Rattle seed is often the first step in creating a new wildflower meadow.

The plant itself has yellow, two-lipped flowers emerging from an inflated green-yellow calyx, and opposite pairs of toothed leaves. It's annual — it germinates in autumn, flowers the following summer, and dies by August. But the seeds are remarkable: as the plant dries out, the seeds rattle audibly inside the papery inflated pods. This is both the origin of the name and a handy ID feature — shake a plant in July and you'll hear the rattle clearly.

Finding Yellow Rattle at Old Down is a good sign — it indicates the grassland has not been heavily fertilised and is being managed traditionally. It's an indicator of ancient, unimproved grassland that has never been ploughed.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. Most abundant in traditionally managed hay meadows and chalk grassland. An annual that needs bare soil patches to germinate.
wildlife_value: By parasitising grasses, Yellow Rattle reduces grass dominance and creates the diverse, low-fertility sward that supports dozens of chalk grassland wildflowers and the insects that depend on them. The flowers are visited by long-tongued bumblebees, particularly Buff-tailed and Garden Bumblebees. Its decline mirrors the loss of traditional hay meadows — the plant cannot survive in heavily fertilised or frequently mown grassland.

life_stages.description: Yellow Rattle germinates in autumn, producing a small rosette of toothed leaves. It immediately starts parasitising nearby grass roots, even at this tiny size.

The plant grows to 20–50cm, with opposite pairs of toothed leaves and yellow two-lipped flowers emerging from inflated green calyces. Look for the yellow flowers poking out of the swollen pod-like calyx — it looks almost like a tiny snapdragon.

photos.caption: Yellow Rattle flowers — note the inflated green calyx
Yellow Rattle in bloom in a chalk grassland meadow

life_stages.description: By July the flowers fade and the calyces puff up into papery inflated pouches. Inside, seeds loosen from the pod walls and rattle when you shake the plant — give it a try! The plant dies completely after setting seed.

photos.caption: Ripe Yellow Rattle seed pods — shake them to hear the rattle

confidence_note: The male is unmistakeable — a brilliant lemon-yellow head and underparts with a chestnut back. Females are streakier but still show yellow. Both sexes have a distinctive chestnut rump in flight.
summary: The brightest bird of the chalk farmland — the male's lemon-yellow head and chest glow like sunshine on the hedgerow. Listen for his song: 'a little bit of bread and no cheeeeese.'
full_description:
The Yellowhammer is one of Britain's most strikingly coloured farmland birds — the male's vivid lemon-yellow head and underparts, contrasting with a rich chestnut back and white outer tail feathers, are unmistakeable. Females are more streaked and less yellow, but still show enough yellow to be distinctive. In flight, watch for the chestnut rump — both sexes have it.

The Yellowhammer's song is one of the most famous in British birdsong: a series of short notes accelerating to a long, thin, buzzing final note, traditionally transcribed as 'a little bit of bread and no cheeeeese.' Males sing persistently from hedgerow tops, fence posts, and scrub from April through July. The call — a sharp 'twick' — can be heard year-round from flocks in winter fields.

Yellowhammers are on the Red List of Birds of Conservation Concern — their population has crashed by over 50% since the 1970s, mainly due to the loss of weedy arable fields and winter stubbles that once provided seeds. Old Down's scrubby chalk grassland, with nearby farmland, is exactly the type of habitat this species needs, making every sighting especially significant.
native_info: Native resident throughout the UK, though rarer in western Scotland and Ireland. Red List species. Population has declined by more than 50% since the 1970s due to agricultural intensification.
wildlife_value: Yellowhammers eat seeds (especially grass seeds and weed seeds) year-round, and feed their chicks almost entirely on insects and caterpillars during the breeding season. They nest low in dense scrub or hedgerow bases, and require uncut field margins and weedy stubble for winter foraging. Their decline mirrors the loss of these traditional farming features.

life_stages.description: The nest is built low in a hedgerow, bramble patch, or tussock of grass — sometimes on the ground. The eggs are pale with distinctive dark scribbly streaks and blotches, as if written in ink, which gives the old folk name 'writing lark.' Clutch size: 3–4 eggs, 2–3 broods per year.
Chicks hatch after about 13 days and fledge around 13 days after that. Both parents feed them almost exclusively on insects and caterpillars, making insect-rich grassland essential in summer.

The male Yellowhammer in summer is one of the most vividly coloured of British birds — brilliant lemon-yellow head and underparts, rich chestnut back with dark streaks. In winter the colours are slightly duller. He sings from exposed perches throughout summer.

photos.caption: Male Yellowhammer — brilliant lemon-yellow head and underparts
Male Yellowhammer on a perch

life_stages.description: In winter, Yellowhammers form flocks, often mixing with other buntings, finches, and sparrows. They visit stubble fields and weedy margins searching for seeds. The flock includes both males and the duller females and juveniles.

photos.caption: Yellowhammer in winter plumage
Male Yellowhammer
Yellowhammer on perch
Yellowhammer, winter

confidence_note: White papery bark and delicate drooping branches are unmistakable. Young trees can be confused with Downy Birch — check the hairless twigs (Silver Birch) vs hairy twigs (Downy Birch).
summary: Slender tree with brilliant white bark and weeping branches. A pioneer species that colonises open ground quickly. Vital for wildlife — over 300 insect species depend on it.
full_description: Silver Birch (Betula pendula) is one of Britain's most elegant native trees, instantly recognised by its brilliant white, papery bark that peels in horizontal strips and develops dark diamond-shaped cracks with age. It has a slender, graceful form with pendulous (drooping) branches and small, triangular leaves with a double-toothed edge that flutter in the breeze. In autumn the leaves turn a clear, clean yellow before falling. Silver Birch is a pioneer species — one of the first trees to colonise bare or disturbed ground. It thrives on acid, sandy or poor soils, making it ideal for the sandy, acidic conditions at Sholing. Despite its delicate appearance it is a powerhouse for wildlife: over 300 species of insect have been recorded using it, including the Birch Polypore fungus, which grows exclusively on birch. Its seeds — tiny winged nutlets — are produced in huge quantities and dispersed by wind, and are a key winter food for finches such as Redpoll and Siskin.
native_info: Native to Britain and found throughout, but most at home on acid, sandy soils in the south and east, and across upland areas in the north.
wildlife_value: Exceptional wildlife value. Supports over 300 insect species including many moths (Buff-tip, Pebble Hook-tip). Birch Polypore and other fungi grow on its bark and dead wood. Seeds eaten by Redpoll, Siskin and other finches. Provides nesting habitat for many birds in holes and branches.

life_stages.description: In early spring, long male catkins (yellow-green, 2–4cm) hang from the branches, releasing clouds of pollen. Smaller, upright female catkins are pollinated by wind. This happens before or as the leaves emerge.
Leaves are small, triangular, and mid-green with a double-toothed margin. They tremble in the lightest breeze. By October they turn clear yellow before falling.
The white bark and fine, drooping purple-brown twigs are beautiful in winter. Look for the bark at any time of year — it is the most reliable identification feature.

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are native birches with white bark
similar_species.key_difference: Downy Birch has hairy twigs and rounder leaves; Silver Birch has hairless, warty twigs and more pointed, triangular leaves with a more pendulous habit.

photos.caption: Silver Birch showing white bark and delicate canopy

confidence_note: Round, slightly notched leaves and small, dark woody cone-like fruits (persistent on the tree) are diagnostic. Usually found right beside water.
summary: The tree of the waterside. Round leaves and dark, cone-like fruits. Its roots fix nitrogen and stabilise stream banks — and its waterlogged wood lasts for centuries.
full_description: Alder (Alnus glutinosa) is Britain's waterside tree, almost always found growing with its feet in or near water — along stream banks, pond margins, marshes and wet woodland. At Miller's Pond and along the Shoreburs Greenway, look for it wherever the ground is persistently wet. It has round-to-oval leaves, slightly notched at the tip, that are sticky when young (hence 'glutinosa'). Its most distinctive feature is the small, dark woody fruits that look like miniature cones and persist on the tree through winter long after the leaves have fallen. In late winter, before any other tree, Alder's purple-red male catkins hang in clusters, a sign that spring is approaching. Its roots host nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Frankia), enriching poor, waterlogged soils. The wood is unusually rot-resistant when permanently waterlogged — Venice was built on Alder piles.
native_info: Native throughout Britain. Most abundant in wet, lowland areas. A key species of wet woodland (alder carr).
wildlife_value: Catkins provide early pollen for bees. Seeds eaten by Redpoll, Siskin and Goldfinch in winter. Supports many specialist insects including the Alder Moth. Dead alder in water is important for invertebrates. Roots stabilise riverbanks and provide habitat for water voles and otters.

life_stages.description: One of the first trees to flower. Long, dangling male catkins (purple-red then yellow) appear from February. Smaller, egg-shaped female catkins become the distinctive woody 'cones'.
Round-oval, dark green leaves, slightly sticky when young. Old woody cones from the previous year often still visible alongside new growth.
The small dark woody cone-like fruits persist on bare branches through winter. A key identification feature. Look for them dangling in clusters at the waterside.

photos.caption: Alder catkins and last year's woody cones

confidence_note: Shiny, dark green, spiny leaves are unmistakable. Upper branches of mature trees often have smooth-edged leaves. Red berries in winter on female plants only.
summary: Evergreen with spiny, glossy leaves and red winter berries. One of only three native British evergreen trees. Berries are vital food for thrushes and other winter birds.
full_description: Holly (Ilex aquifolium) is one of Britain's best-known native trees and one of only three native evergreen broadleaved trees (alongside Box and Yew). Its dark, waxy, spiny leaves are unmistakable. Interestingly, the spines are primarily a defence against browsing by deer and cattle — on mature trees where branches are beyond reach, the leaves often become smooth-edged. Holly is dioecious (separate male and female plants), and only female plants bear the bright red berries, provided a male plant is nearby for pollination. The berries ripen in autumn and are a critical winter food source for thrushes — particularly Fieldfare and Redwing — Blackbirds, and Mistle Thrushes, which guard berry-laden bushes fiercely against rivals. Holly grows slowly and can live for hundreds of years, developing into a tall tree in woodland or remaining as dense, impenetrable scrub in hedgerows.
danger_note: Holly berries are toxic to humans (especially children) and dogs, causing vomiting and diarrhoea. Do not eat them.
native_info: Native throughout England, Wales and southern Scotland. Common in woodland and hedgerows.
wildlife_value: Berries are a critical winter food for Blackbird, Mistle Thrush, Fieldfare and Redwing. Dense evergreen foliage provides roosting and nesting cover year-round, especially in winter. Flowers provide nectar and pollen for bees. Holly Blue butterfly lays eggs on Holly in spring.

life_stages.description: Small, white, four-petalled flowers appear in clusters in May and June. They are scented and attractive to bees. Male and female flowers are on separate plants.
Female plants bear clusters of bright red berries from October onwards, persisting through winter until eaten by birds. A vital wildlife resource in the lean winter months.

photos.caption: Holly with typical spiny leaves and red berries

confidence_note: Broad, rounded leaves (unlike most willows which are narrow), and silky grey catkins ('pussy willow') in early spring before leaves. Damp or wet ground.
summary: The pussy willow of early spring — silky grey catkins appear before the leaves. One of the most important early-spring pollen sources for bees. Broad leaves distinguish it from most willows.
full_description: Goat Willow (Salix caprea) is one of the earliest trees to flower in spring, and its familiar fluffy grey catkins — long known as 'pussy willow' — are a welcome sight in late February and March, appearing before the leaves and providing one of the most important early pollen sources for bumblebee queens emerging from hibernation. Unlike most willows, which have narrow, lance-shaped leaves, Goat Willow has broad, oval leaves with a rounded tip, making it one of the easier willows to identify. It grows as a large shrub or small tree in damp or disturbed ground, woodland edges and scrub — exactly the kind of habitat found along the Shoreburs Greenway. Male plants bear yellow catkins (pollen-producing) and females bear green catkins that develop into cottony seed heads. The Purple Emperor butterfly — one of Britain's most magnificent insects — depends almost exclusively on Goat Willow for its larvae.
native_info: Native throughout Britain. Common in damp ground, woodland edges, roadsides and scrub.
wildlife_value: Exceptionally important for early-spring pollinators — one of the best pollen sources when little else is in flower. Supports over 150 insect species. Larval food plant for the Purple Emperor butterfly. Catkin pollen important for early queen bumblebees.

life_stages.description: Silky grey oval catkins appear on bare branches from late February. Male catkins turn yellow as pollen is released. Female catkins are more slender and turn green, later producing cottony seeds.
Broad, oval leaves, dark green above and grey-green and downy below. Very different from the narrow leaves of most willows. Twigs are grey-brown and may be downy.

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are willows growing near water
similar_species.key_difference: Crack Willow has very long, narrow lance-shaped leaves (10–15cm). Goat Willow has broad, rounded-oval leaves. Crack Willow is a large tree; Goat Willow usually a smaller shrub.

photos.caption: Goat Willow 'pussy willow' catkins in early spring

confidence_note: Tiny white flowers with yellow centres at ground level, on short stalks, with a rosette of spoon-shaped leaves. One of Britain's most familiar wildflowers.
weather_note: Flowers open in sunshine and close at night or in dull weather (hence 'day's eye' — the origin of 'daisy').
summary: Britain's most familiar wildflower. White petals around a yellow centre, hugging the ground in lawns and meadows. Flowers almost all year round and is a key early nectar source.
full_description: The Common Daisy (Bellis perennis) is arguably Britain's most recognisable wildflower. Its simple, cheerful white-petalled flowers with bright yellow centres need no introduction. The name 'daisy' comes from 'day's eye' — the flowers open in sunshine and close at dusk or in overcast weather. It is a perennial plant that forms low rosettes of spoon-shaped, slightly hairy leaves, with flowers on short stems (2–10cm). It grows in short, grazed or mown grassland — lawns, meadows, parks — and is one of the few wildflowers that actually benefits from mowing, as it keeps competition low. Despite its humble reputation, it is an important early nectar source, particularly in spring, flowering almost continuously from February to November. It is also a food plant for several moth species, and its seeds are eaten by small birds. In meadows managed for wildlife, daisies can form impressive drifts.
native_info: Native throughout the British Isles. Extremely common.
wildlife_value: Important early and late-season nectar source for bees, hoverflies and small butterflies. Leaves eaten by various moth caterpillars. Seeds eaten by sparrows and finches. One of the most accessible wildflowers for pollinators in urban and suburban settings.

similar_species.similarity_note: Both have white petals and yellow centres
similar_species.key_difference: Oxeye Daisy is much larger (flowers 3–6cm across on tall stems to 70cm). Common Daisy is tiny (1–2cm flowers) at ground level on very short stems.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Common Daisy flowers almost year-round; Oxeye Daisy peaks May–September

photos.caption: Common Daisy — white petals and yellow disc florets

confidence_note: Shiny, bright yellow flowers on tall, branched, hairless (or slightly hairy) stems. No reflexed sepals (unlike Creeping Buttercup). Leaves deeply divided into 3–7 lobes.
weather_note: Flowers open in sunshine; petals have a waxy coating that reflects UV light, making them attractive to insect pollinators.
summary: The classic buttercup of summer meadows — tall, branching stems with shiny yellow flowers. The most upright of the common buttercups, creating golden drifts in uncut grassland.
full_description: Meadow Buttercup (Ranunculus acris) is the stately, tall buttercup of traditional hay meadows and uncut grassland, reaching 30–80cm. Its shiny, bright yellow flowers (2–3cm across) sit on long, branching stems. The leaves are deeply divided into 3–7 lobes, themselves further divided, giving a lacy appearance — the stem leaves become progressively simpler and narrower towards the top. Unlike Creeping Buttercup, Meadow Buttercup does not produce runners (stolons) and unlike Bulbous Buttercup it has no reflexed (bent-back) sepals. The polished petals have a glossy, waxy surface that strongly reflects UV light — visible to insects as a bright signal. Meadow Buttercup is an indicator of old, unimproved grassland and its presence in good numbers at Sholing is a positive sign. In meadow management, it is one of the species that flowers before a traditional July hay cut.
danger_note: All buttercups contain protoanemonin, an irritant sap. Avoid contact with eyes or prolonged skin contact. Toxic if eaten in large quantities. Livestock avoid it when fresh but may eat it when dried in hay — though potency reduces when dried.
native_info: Native throughout the British Isles.
wildlife_value: Important pollen and nectar source for bees, beetles and hoverflies. Seeds eaten by finches and buntings. Part of traditional meadow flora supporting a wide range of invertebrates.

similar_species.similarity_note: Very similar yellow buttercup in similar habitats
similar_species.key_difference: Creeping Buttercup produces creeping runners (stolons) along the ground. Meadow Buttercup is taller and more upright with no runners. Creeping Buttercup prefers wetter, muddier ground.

photos.caption: Meadow Buttercup — shiny yellow flowers on tall branching stems

confidence_note: Flat-topped clusters of tiny white (occasionally pink-tinged) flowers. Finely feathery, aromatic leaves are distinctive — rub a leaf for a pungent, herby smell.
summary: Flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers above finely feathery, aromatic leaves. A tough meadow plant important for hoverflies and small beetles. Leaves smell strongly of herbs when crushed.
full_description: Yarrow (Achillea millefolium) is a tough, aromatic perennial of grassland and meadows, instantly identifiable by its finely divided, feathery leaves that smell pungent and herby when crushed — the genus name honours Achilles, who legendarily used it to staunch wounds. The flowers are borne in flat-topped clusters (corymbs) of many tiny individual flower heads, usually white but sometimes pink-tinged. The plant grows 20–60cm tall and spreads by both seed and underground rhizomes, forming patches in grassland. It is one of the key 'matrix' species of traditional meadows, providing a flat landing platform for a huge variety of invertebrates — particularly hoverflies, small beetles, and solitary wasps. It is extremely drought-tolerant and thrives in dry, sunny grassland, but will grow almost anywhere. Yarrow has a very long folk medicine tradition and is still used in herbal medicine.
native_info: Native throughout the British Isles. Very common.
wildlife_value: One of the top plants for invertebrate diversity. The flat flower-head is easily accessible to many small insects. Supports hoverflies, solitary wasps, beetles, small butterflies and moths. Leaves eaten by several moth caterpillars.

photos.caption: Yarrow — flat-topped white flower clusters

confidence_note: Short plant with a dense, oblong spike of small violet-purple flowers. Grows in short grassland and lawns. Leaves oval and slightly toothed.
summary: Low-growing plant with dense spikes of violet-purple flowers in short grassland and lawns. An important nectar plant for bumblebees, and one of the few wildflowers that thrives in mown lawns.
full_description: Self-heal (Prunella vulgaris) is a neat, low-growing perennial that occurs in short grassland, lawns, woodland rides and disturbed ground. Its dense, oblong flower spikes carry small two-lipped flowers of rich violet-purple, each with a hooded upper lip and a fringed lower lip, in whorls around a tight, barrel-shaped head. It grows 5–30cm tall and can survive regular mowing by keeping low. The plant has a very long history in herbal medicine — its common name refers to its traditional use in wound-healing and as a treatment for sore throats. It is an important nectar source for bumblebees, particularly Buff-tailed and White-tailed Bumblebees, and is also visited by other bees and butterflies. In lawns managed with a light touch — cutting less frequently and slightly higher — Self-heal will quickly establish itself.
native_info: Native throughout the British Isles. Very common.
