summary: Larger, wartier cousin of the Common Frog. Dry, bumpy skin and golden eyes with horizontal pupils. Walks rather than hops. A garden ally that eats slugs and other pests. Migrates to ponds in spring.
full_description: The Common Toad (Bufo bufo) is larger and more robust than the Common Frog, with dry, warty, rough-textured brown or olive-brown skin (never the smooth, moist skin of the frog). It has distinctive copper-gold or amber eyes with horizontal slit pupils. It moves by walking or short hops rather than the frog's longer leaps. Outside the breeding season, Toads are terrestrial, living in gardens, woodland, rough grassland and scrub — often far from water. They are nocturnal for most of the year, sheltering under logs, stones and plant pots by day. In late February to March, Toads undertake remarkable migrations to breeding ponds, often crossing roads — toad patrols (where volunteers carry toads across roads) are an important conservation activity. Males arrive first and grasp females in amplexus, sometimes forming 'mating balls'. Spawn is laid in long strings (frog spawn is in clumps). Toads are remarkable in that they are largely immune to the toxins of many invertebrates (such as ants and woodlice) that frogs cannot eat, making them important controllers of a wide range of invertebrate pests.
danger_note: Toads produce mild toxins from parotoid glands behind the eyes — dogs that mouth them may foam briefly. Wash hands after handling. Do not eat (mildly toxic). Not dangerous to healthy humans who handle them carefully.
native_info: Native throughout Britain. Absent from Ireland. Declining — on the Biodiversity Action Plan list due to loss of ponds and road mortality during breeding migrations.
wildlife_value: Important controller of slugs, beetles, ants and many other invertebrate garden pests. Prey for Grass Snake, Hedgehog, Badger, Heron and Corvids. Declining — loss of garden ponds is a major threat.

similar_species.similarity_note: Both native amphibians at ponds
similar_species.key_difference: Common Frog has smooth, moist skin and longer legs and hops. Common Toad has dry, warty skin, shorter legs and walks. Frog spawn in clumps; Toad spawn in long strings.

photos.caption: Common Toad — warty skin and golden horizontal-pupil eye

confidence_note: Large dragonfly. Male: black with bold blue and green spots. Female: black with brown-green spots. Broad, apple-green patches on the last two segments near the tail tip in both sexes. Inquisitive — often approaches people.
weather_note: Most active in warm, sunny weather. Feeds on the wing in woodland rides and gardens, not just over water.
summary: One of Britain's largest and most colourful dragonflies — black and blue-green. Famous for its inquisitive behaviour, hovering to investigate people. A regular visitor to gardens as well as ponds.
full_description: The Southern Hawker (Aeshna cyanea) is one of Britain's commonest and most familiar large dragonflies, and one of the most charismatic. Males are black with paired spots of bright blue and green running down the abdomen; females are dark with brown-green spots. Both sexes share distinctive broad, apple-green patches on the last two abdominal segments. The Southern Hawker is a powerful, direct flier that patrols territories over ponds and along woodland rides and garden hedgerows, not only over water — it feeds actively in woodland glades and gardens far from water, catching midges, flies and other small invertebrates. It is famously inquisitive and will often hover close to a stationary human, investigating them at close range. Larvae (nymphs) are aquatic, living in ponds and other water bodies for 2–3 years before emerging as adults. At Miller's Pond, Southern Hawkers should be a reliable summer species.
native_info: Native throughout England and Wales. Common in the south; rarer in the north.
wildlife_value: Important predator of flying insects — controls midge, fly and small moth populations. Larvae are important predators in pond ecosystems. Prey for Hobby, Kingfisher and larger spiders.

life_stages.description: Aquatic nymph lives in the pond for 2–3 years, hunting invertebrates and small fish. Climbs out of the water up plant stems at night to emerge as an adult.
Newly emerged adults (tenerals) are pale and soft for a few days. Mature adults patrol powerfully and inquisitively from July to October, hunting on the wing.

photos.caption: Southern Hawker male — black with blue and green spots

confidence_note: Damselfly. Male: brilliant metallic blue-green body with a dark blue-black smudge on each wing (not the whole wing, as in the Beautiful Demoiselle). Female: metallic green body with translucent greenish wings. Fluttering, butterfly-like flight.
weather_note: Flies only in warm, sunny weather. Found exclusively near slow-moving or still water with muddy or silty substrates.
summary: One of Britain's most beautiful insects — males flash iridescent blue-green with distinctive dark wing patches as they flutter like a butterfly over waterside vegetation. A signature species of slow, clean waterways.
full_description: The Banded Demoiselle (Calopteryx splendens) is one of Britain's most spectacular damselflies and arguably one of the most beautiful of all British insects. The male has a brilliant, iridescent metallic blue-green body and wings with a distinctive dark blue-black smudge covering approximately the outer half of each wing — the 'band' that gives the species its name. The female has an equally beautiful iridescent metallic green body with translucent, pale green-tinged wings and a false white 'pseudopterostigma' near the wing tip. The flight is quite unlike that of other damselflies or dragonflies — slow and fluttering, like a butterfly, the wing patches flashing as they glide over waterside vegetation. Males display to females on waterside perches. Banded Demoiselles are associated with slow-moving or standing water with a muddy or silt substrate — the larvae live in mud at the bottom of ponds and slow streams. The Shoreburs Greenway waterways are documented Banded Demoiselle habitat. They are also an indicator of water quality — their presence suggests clean, unpolluted water with a good invertebrate community.
native_info: Native throughout England and Wales. Expanding its range northward, possibly in response to climate change.
wildlife_value: Larvae are important predators in waterside mud communities. Adults feed on small flying insects. Prey for Kingfisher, Hobby and larger dragonflies. An indicator of clean, slow-moving water with good aquatic invertebrate diversity.

life_stages.description: Aquatic larva lives in silty mud at the bottom of ponds and slow rivers for one to two years, hunting small invertebrates.
Adults flutter over waterside vegetation from May to September. Males display from waterside perches, flashing their wing patches to attract females.

similar_species.similarity_note: Very similar iridescent damselfly
similar_species.key_difference: Beautiful Demoiselle has the dark wing colour covering almost the entire wing (not just a central band). It prefers faster-flowing, cleaner streams than Banded Demoiselle.

photos.caption: Banded Demoiselle male — iridescent blue-green with dark wing band

confidence_note: Males have a grey crown, chestnut-brown nape and black bib; females are plain sandy-brown with a pale stripe behind the eye and no bib. Always in noisy, chattering groups.
summary: A noisy, sociable little bird that almost always turns up in a chattering gang rather than alone. Once one of Britain's most common birds, it has declined sharply and is now on the conservation Red List.
full_description:
The House Sparrow (Passer domesticus) is a compact, big-headed finch-like bird about 15cm long. The male has a grey crown, chestnut-brown patch running back from the eye, black bib (larger in more dominant males), and streaky brown back. The female and juveniles are much plainer — sandy-brown all over with a pale buff stripe behind the eye and darker streaking on the back, and no black bib. House Sparrows are almost never seen alone: they live in noisy, gossiping colonies, feeding, dust-bathing, and roosting together in dense hedges or under eaves.

Despite being one of the most familiar birds in Britain for centuries, House Sparrow numbers have fallen by around 70% since the 1970s, and it is now Red-listed as a bird of conservation concern. The causes are debated but likely include loss of nesting sites in modern buildings, fewer garden insects to feed chicks, and changes in farming. Colonies that do survive tend to be resilient once established — a good hedge or scrubby corner with insects, seeds, and thick cover can support a thriving group for years.

At Old Down, House Sparrows favour the thick hedgerows and scrubby margins around the site, particularly where bramble and hawthorn provide dense cover for nesting and refuge from Sparrowhawks. Listen for the constant cheerful chirruping and chattering — a House Sparrow colony is rarely quiet. Children can look for their dust-bathing 'scrapes' — shallow bowls of bare earth where sparrows fluff dust through their feathers to control parasites.
native_info: Native and historically abundant throughout the UK, closely associated with human settlement for thousands of years. Now Red-listed due to a severe long-term population decline, though it remains widespread.
wildlife_value: Feeds chicks almost entirely on insects and spiders in the breeding season, making good invertebrate-rich habitat essential. Seeds and scraps form the adult diet outside the breeding season. Nest sites in dense hedges and building crevices are also used by other small birds once vacated.

life_stages.description: Grey crown, chestnut-brown band from the eye to the nape, black bib on the throat and upper breast (bigger in dominant, older males), streaky brown-and-black back, and a stout grey-brown bill (black in the breeding season, yellowish in winter).

photos.caption: House Sparrow male — grey crown, chestnut nape, black bib

life_stages.description: Plain sandy-brown overall with a pale buff stripe behind the eye, streaked darker on the back and wings, and no black bib. Juveniles resemble the female. Told apart from other 'little brown birds' by the stout bill and constant chattering flock behaviour.

photos.caption: House Sparrow female — plain sandy-brown, pale stripe behind the eye

life_stages.description: 2–5 broods a year are common. Chicks fledge after about 15 days and are fed almost entirely on insects. Juveniles look like washed-out females and beg noisily from parents in family parties well after fledging.

photos.caption: A fledgling House Sparrow, recently out of the nest
Juvenile House Sparrows, still with the duller plumage and gape marks of young birds

similar_species.similarity_note: Closely related sparrow, scarcer in southern England
similar_species.key_difference: Tree Sparrow has a solid chestnut-brown (not grey) crown, a neat black cheek spot on an otherwise white face, and both sexes look alike. House Sparrow males have a grey crown and no cheek spot.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both present year-round where they occur

similar_species.similarity_note: Often confused with a female House Sparrow at a glance
similar_species.key_difference: Dunnock is slate-grey on the head and breast with a thin, needle-like insect-eating bill, and shuffles quietly and alone at the base of hedges rather than chattering in a flock.

photos.caption: House Sparrow male — grey crown, chestnut nape, black bib
House Sparrow female — plain sandy-brown, pale stripe behind the eye
A fledgling House Sparrow, recently out of the nest
Juvenile House Sparrows, still with the duller plumage and gape marks of young birds

confidence_note: The male's vivid rose-pink breast, jet-black cap and flashing white rump in flight are unmistakable. Shy and quiet, so often heard (a soft, low 'peu' whistle) before it is seen.
summary: A shy, secretive finch that hides in dense hedges — the male's rose-pink breast and jet-black cap are stunning when finally glimpsed. Easiest to spot in winter when bare hedges give fewer places to hide.
full_description:
The Bullfinch (Pyrrhula pyrrhula) is one of Britain's most beautiful finches but also one of the shyest. The male has a rose-pink breast and cheeks, a glossy black cap and face, blue-grey back, and a brilliant white rump that flashes conspicuously as the bird flies away from you — often the only clear view you get. The female shares the same pattern but in muted grey-buff tones instead of pink. Both sexes have a distinctive stubby, rounded black bill adapted for eating buds and seeds, and a soft, low, disyllabic 'peu' whistle is often the first clue a Bullfinch is nearby, well before it is seen.

Bullfinches were once persecuted by fruit growers because they strip the flower buds from fruit trees in late winter and early spring, feeding on the developing embryo inside each bud — a single bird can remove a large number of buds from an orchard tree in a day when little other food is available. This reputation earned them a bad name historically, though numbers have actually declined significantly in farmland over recent decades, and they are now an Amber-listed species of conservation concern, largely dependent on unmanaged hedgerows and scrub.

At Old Down, Bullfinches favour the denser, taller hedgerows and blackthorn scrub around the chalk grassland, where they feed on the seeds of dock, bramble, and ash keys as well as buds. They are genuinely secretive birds, usually staying low and well hidden in cover, so winter — when hedges are bare of leaves — is by far the best time to catch a clear view of this gorgeous finch.
native_info: Resident throughout the UK, though scarcer and more local than most garden finches. Strongly associated with mature hedgerows, woodland edge and scrub; has declined on intensively managed farmland.
wildlife_value: Feeds on tree and shrub buds, seeds of bramble, dock, ash and nettle, and some insects for chicks. A good indicator of well-managed, structurally diverse hedgerows with mature shrubs left to flower and seed.

life_stages.description: Vivid rose-pink breast and cheeks, glossy black cap and face, blue-grey back, black wings with a pale wing-bar, and a brilliant white rump that shows clearly in flight. Stubby black bill built for crushing buds and seeds.

photos.caption: Bullfinch male — vivid rose-pink breast, black cap, white rump

life_stages.description: Same pattern as the male — black cap, white rump — but in soft grey-buff tones instead of pink. Told apart from other finches by the black cap, stubby bill, and white rump.

photos.caption: Bullfinch pair — pink-breasted male below, buff-brown female above

life_stages.description: 2 broods typical, nest is a flimsy twig-and-moss platform hidden deep in a hedge or conifer. Juveniles resemble the female but lack the black cap until their first autumn moult.

photos.caption: Juvenile Bullfinch, lacking the adult's black cap and grey back

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are colourful, pink-breasted finches of hedgerows
similar_species.key_difference: Chaffinch has a much paler, dusky-pink breast, a blue-grey (not black) cap, and bold white wing-bars and outer tail feathers. It lacks the Bullfinch's black face and white rump.

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are chunky, seed-eating finches with a stout bill
similar_species.key_difference: Greenfinch is olive-green with yellow flashes in the wings and tail, not pink and black, and is far more likely to be at a garden feeder than deep in a hedge.

photos.caption: Bullfinch male — vivid rose-pink breast, black cap, white rump
Bullfinch pair — pink-breasted male below, buff-brown female above
Juvenile Bullfinch, lacking the adult's black cap and grey back

confidence_note: Looks black at a distance but shimmers with green and purple iridescence up close, and is covered in pale spots in fresh winter plumage. Short tail, long pointed bill, and a whirring, direct flight are good clues even at range.
summary: A glossy, spangled bird famous for its extraordinary aerial murmurations — thousands of Starlings twisting and swirling together at dusk, especially in autumn and winter. Also a remarkable mimic, weaving other birds' calls into its own scratchy song.
full_description:
The Starling (Sturnus vulgaris) looks like an unremarkable black bird from a distance, but a close view reveals plumage that shimmers with iridescent green and purple, especially on the head and back. In fresh winter plumage the whole bird is covered in bold cream-white spots, which gradually wear away over the winter so that by the height of the breeding season in late spring the bird looks almost uniformly glossy black. It has a short tail, a long, sharply pointed bill (yellow in summer, dark in winter), and a distinctive fast, direct, whirring flight on triangular wings, quite different from the fluttering, undulating flight of a blackbird.

Starlings are famous for murmurations — vast, swirling flocks that gather at dusk in autumn and winter, sometimes tens of thousands of birds strong, twisting and pulsing through the sky in shapes before dropping suddenly into a communal roost. The behaviour is thought to help confuse predators such as Sparrowhawks and Peregrine Falcons, and to share information about good feeding areas. Starlings are also gifted mimics, weaving fragments of other birds' calls, car alarms, and mechanical sounds into their scratchy, wheezy, clicking song, often delivered from a rooftop or treetop perch with wings held slightly open.

At Old Down, Starlings feed in tight, fast-moving flocks on the short chalk turf and adjoining farmland, probing the ground with that long bill for leatherjackets (cranefly larvae) and other soil invertebrates. Winter numbers are boosted by migrants arriving from Scandinavia, Russia and eastern Europe, and small evening murmurations can sometimes be seen over the site before the flock heads off to roost. Despite still being a familiar garden bird, the UK breeding population has fallen sharply since the 1980s and Starling is now Red-listed.
native_info: Resident and breeding throughout the UK, with numbers swelled in autumn and winter by continental migrants. Once superabundant, but the UK breeding population has declined by more than 80% since the 1960s, and it is now Red-listed.
wildlife_value: An important predator of soil invertebrates, especially leatherjackets and other cranefly larvae, which it finds by probing short turf with its bill. Nests in tree holes and building cavities, competing with other hole-nesters such as Great Spotted Woodpecker.

life_stages.description: Fresh autumn plumage is densely covered in bold cream-white spots on a glossy black base, with a dark bill. This is the classic 'starling' look most people picture.

photos.caption: Adult Starling in fresh winter plumage — heavily spangled with white spots

life_stages.description: By the breeding season the pale spots have worn away, leaving the plumage looking almost solid glossy black with strong green-purple iridescence, and the bill turns bright yellow.

photos.caption: Adult Starling in summer plumage — glossy black with green-purple iridescence

life_stages.description: Nests in tree holes, building cavities and nest boxes. Juveniles are drab grey-brown all over with a pale throat and dark bill — easily mistaken for a different species until they moult into blotchy immature plumage in late summer.

photos.caption: Juvenile Starling, uniform grey-brown before moulting into adult plumage

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are common medium-sized black garden and farmland birds
similar_species.key_difference: Blackbird has a longer tail, slower fluttering flight, and hops rather than the Starling's confident upright walk. Male Blackbird has a bright orange-yellow bill and no iridescence or spotting; Starling has a shorter tail and a whirring, direct flight.

photos.caption: Adult Starling in fresh winter plumage — heavily spangled with white spots
Adult Starling in summer plumage — glossy black with green-purple iridescence
Juvenile Starling, uniform grey-brown before moulting into adult plumage

confidence_note: A chunky, olive-green finch with a heavy pale bill and bright yellow flashes in the wings and tail, especially obvious in flight. Song includes a distinctive nasal, wheezy 'dzweee'.
summary: A chunky olive-green finch with a heavy seed-cracking bill and flashes of bright yellow in the wings and tail. Once one of Britain's commonest garden finches, it has suffered a serious decline due to a parasitic disease spread at bird feeders.
full_description:
The Greenfinch (Chloris chloris) is a stocky, big-headed finch, olive-green above and yellowish-green below, with a thick, pale, conical bill perfectly shaped for cracking open seeds. In flight, and often when perched, bright yellow patches flash in the wings and at the base of the tail — a good feature for picking it out from other finches at a distance. Females and juveniles are duller and browner than the male but show the same yellow flashes. The song is a distinctive, slightly wheezy, nasal 'dzweee', often delivered from a high perch or during a slow, exaggerated, bat-like display flight over the breeding territory.

Greenfinches were once among the most familiar visitors to British garden bird feeders, but the population has more than halved since the mid-2000s due to trichomonosis, a parasitic disease spread between birds at shared feeding stations and contaminated water. Regularly cleaning feeders and bird baths, and occasionally moving feeder positions, helps reduce transmission. Despite the decline, Greenfinch remains a widespread bird of hedgerows, scrub, and woodland edge as well as gardens.

At Old Down, Greenfinches favour the taller hedgerows and scrubby margins of the chalk grassland, where they feed on the seeds of thistles, dock, and other coarse wildflowers as well as tree seeds such as yew and hawthorn. Outside the breeding season they often form loose flocks with other finches, moving between good seed sources across the site.
native_info: Resident and widespread throughout the UK in hedgerows, scrub, woodland edge and gardens. Numbers have declined sharply since around 2006 due to the spread of trichomonosis, and the species is now Red-listed.
wildlife_value: An important seed-eater, feeding on the seeds of thistles, dock, bramble, and various trees including yew and hawthorn, helping disperse some of these plants. A frequent garden feeder visitor, though good hygiene at feeders is important to limit disease spread.

life_stages.description: Rich olive-green overall with a stout, pale pinkish-grey bill and bright yellow patches in the wings and at the base of the tail, most obvious in flight.

photos.caption: Greenfinch male — olive-green with bright yellow wing and tail flashes
Greenfinch male showing the stout, pale, seed-cracking bill

life_stages.description: Duller, greyer-brown than the male with less extensive yellow, and some streaking on the back. Juveniles are streakier still. The stout pale bill remains a good identification feature at any age.

photos.caption: Adult female Greenfinch, duller and more streaked than the male
Juvenile Greenfinch, streaked brown plumage before its first moult

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are colourful finches often seen together at feeders
similar_species.key_difference: Goldfinch has a red-and-white face patch and black-and-yellow wings, quite different from the plain olive-green Greenfinch head. Goldfinch is also more slender with a finer bill for teasel and thistle seeds.

similar_species.similarity_note: A female Greenfinch can look superficially like a dull sparrow
similar_species.key_difference: Even dull female Greenfinches show a hint of yellow in the wing and tail, and have a more sharply pointed, conical bill than the House Sparrow's stubbier one.

photos.caption: Greenfinch male — olive-green with bright yellow wing and tail flashes
Greenfinch male showing the stout, pale, seed-cracking bill
Adult female Greenfinch, duller and more streaked than the male
Juvenile Greenfinch, streaked brown plumage before its first moult

confidence_note: Told apart from Song Thrush by the bold cream stripe above the eye (supercilium), rusty-red flanks and underwing, and smaller size. Usually seen in flocks, often with Fieldfares, and only present in winter.
summary: Britain's smallest thrush and a true winter visitor, arriving in October from Iceland and Scandinavia to strip hedgerows of berries. Look for the cream eyebrow stripe and warm rusty-red flanks, often in flocks with Fieldfares.
full_description:
The Redwing (Turdus iliacus) is the smallest thrush seen in Britain, a little smaller and daintier than the familiar Song Thrush. It shares a similar spotted breast but is readily told apart by a bold cream-white stripe above the eye (the supercilium), a pale stripe below the cheek, and warm rusty-red flanks and underwing that flash conspicuously in flight — the feature that gives the bird its name. Redwings do not breed in southern England; the birds seen at Old Down are winter visitors that have migrated from breeding grounds in Iceland, Scandinavia and Russia, arriving on the east and north coasts in large overnight flights from October onwards, often calling with a thin, high-pitched 'seeee' as they pass over in the dark.

Once they arrive, Redwings roam the countryside in flocks, often alongside the larger, greyer Fieldfare, searching hedgerows and fields for berries and soil invertebrates. Hawthorn, holly, and other berry-laden hedges are stripped systematically as the flock moves through, and in hard winter weather Redwings will also visit gardens and orchards for windfall apples and other fruit when their usual food is scarce or frozen.

At Old Down, look for mixed flocks of Redwings and Fieldfares working along the hedgerows and open grassland edges from late autumn through winter, particularly after a good hawthorn and holly berry crop. Their thin, high 'seeee' contact calls, often heard from birds flying over after dark during migration, are a distinctive and evocative sound of the autumn night sky in Britain.
native_info: A winter visitor to the whole of the UK from Iceland and continental Scandinavia/Russia; a very small number of pairs breed in northern Scotland. Present in Britain only from around October to March.
wildlife_value: An important consumer of hedgerow berries in autumn and winter, helping disperse seeds of hawthorn, holly and other shrubs. Also feeds on soil invertebrates such as earthworms in mild weather, switching to fruit when the ground freezes.

life_stages.description: Brown above, boldly spotted below like other thrushes, but smaller and daintier with a bold cream supercilium above the eye and warm rusty-red flanks and underwing, obvious in flight. Only present in the UK outside the breeding season.

photos.caption: Redwing — cream supercilium (eyebrow stripe) and rusty-red flanks
Redwing — Britain's smallest thrush, a winter visitor from the north

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are spotted brown thrushes seen through the colder months
similar_species.key_difference: Song Thrush is present year-round (not just winter), lacks the cream eyebrow stripe and rusty-red flanks, and is warmer buff-brown with neater, more evenly spaced spots.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Redwing only present October–March; Song Thrush present all year

similar_species.similarity_note: Frequently flocks together with Redwing in winter
similar_species.key_difference: Fieldfare is noticeably larger with a grey head and rump, chestnut-brown back, and yellowish spotted breast — lacks the Redwing's cream eyebrow stripe and rusty flanks.

photos.caption: Redwing — cream supercilium (eyebrow stripe) and rusty-red flanks
Redwing — Britain's smallest thrush, a winter visitor from the north

confidence_note: Told apart from Swallows and House Martins by its all-dark, sooty-brown plumage, longer scythe-shaped wings, shorter forked tail, and screaming calls in fast, wheeling 'screaming parties' around rooftops.
summary: A screaming, scythe-winged flier that spends almost its entire life in the air — eating, sleeping and even mating on the wing. Arrives from Africa in late April and is gone again by August, one of the shortest and most spectacular visits of any British bird.
full_description:
The Swift (Apus apus) is one of the most extraordinary birds to visit Britain. Sooty-brown all over (looking black against the sky) with long, narrow, curved wings shaped like a scythe or a boomerang, and a short forked tail, it spends almost the whole of its life airborne — feeding on airborne insects, drinking on the wing by skimming over water, and even sleeping in flight by shutting down half its brain at a time. Non-breeding young Swifts may stay continuously airborne for up to ten months without ever landing. Only the need to nest and incubate eggs brings an adult Swift down to a solid surface at all.

Swifts arrive in Britain remarkably late, usually from late April, having spent the winter over central and southern Africa, and they leave again as early as late July or August — one of the shortest stays of any British migrant bird, giving rise to the old country saying that summer 'arrives with the Swifts and leaves with them too'. On warm evenings, look and listen for 'screaming parties' — tight, fast-wheeling groups of Swifts chasing each other around rooftops at high speed with piercing screaming calls, a classic sound and sight of the British summer sky. Swifts nest almost exclusively in small gaps and crevices in old buildings, and the loss of these nest sites during renovation and new-build construction is a major cause of the species' recent decline; it is now Red-listed.

At Old Down, Swifts are seen hawking for insects high over the open chalk grassland and woodland edge on warm days, sometimes dropping low to feed just above the vegetation in cool or overcast weather when insects fly lower. They do not nest on the open site itself but commute out from nesting colonies in nearby village and town buildings to feed over the richer insect-hunting grounds here — a reminder that even a bird rarely seen perched depends on a network of habitats across the wider landscape.
native_info: A summer breeding visitor to the whole of the UK, present only from around late April to August before returning to winter in Africa. Now Red-listed due to a steep decline linked to loss of nest sites in buildings.
wildlife_value: Feeds entirely on airborne insects and spiders caught in flight, consuming huge numbers over a breeding season and helping to naturally control flying insect populations. Depends on cavities in old buildings for nesting, so is a strong indicator of traditional building stock being retained.

life_stages.description: Sooty-brown all over, appearing black against the sky, with long scythe-shaped wings, a short forked tail, and a small pale patch under the chin visible only at close range. Flies with fast, flickering wingbeats interspersed with long glides, and gives piercing screaming calls in groups.

photos.caption: Common Swift in flight — scythe-shaped wings, forked tail, all-dark plumage
A 'screaming party' of Swifts wheeling around rooftops in summer

similar_species.similarity_note: Often confused as 'the same bird' — both are aerial insect-hunters of summer
similar_species.key_difference: Swallow has a red throat, pale underparts, and long streaming tail-streamers, and is not closely related to Swift despite the superficial similarity — Swifts are more closely related to hummingbirds than to swallows and martins.

similar_species.similarity_note: Another aerial feeder often seen alongside Swifts over villages
similar_species.key_difference: House Martin is smaller, with a bright white rump and white underparts, a shorter and less deeply forked tail, and a fluttering rather than scything flight action.

photos.caption: Common Swift in flight — scythe-shaped wings, forked tail, all-dark plumage
A 'screaming party' of Swifts wheeling around rooftops in summer

confidence_note: Small, pale orange-brown, and always rests with its wings closed showing a single small eyespot near the forewing tip — it never basks with wings open like most other browns. Low, weak, bobbing flight close to the ground.
weather_note: Flies only in warm sunshine and drops immediately into the grass on a cloudy spell, vanishing from view almost instantly thanks to its camouflaged underside.
summary: A small, pale orange-brown butterfly of short, sunny grassland that never sits with its wings open — always closed, showing a single tell-tale eyespot. Easy to overlook thanks to its weak, low flight and habit of vanishing into the turf.
full_description:
The Small Heath (Coenonympha pamphilus) is one of Britain's smallest and least conspicuous butterflies, with a wingspan of only around 3–3.5cm. It is pale orange-brown with a greyish underside to the hindwing, and — unusually for a British butterfly — it never basks with its wings open. It always perches with wings closed, showing a single small black eyespot with a white centre near the tip of the forewing. This eyespot is thought to distract predators into attacking a wingtip rather than the vulnerable body.

The flight is weak, low, and bobbing, rarely rising more than a few centimetres above the grass, and the butterfly drops out of sight the instant the sun goes behind a cloud, its mottled underside blending perfectly with dry grass stems. This combination of small size, low flight, and instant camouflage means Small Heaths are very easy to overlook even where they are common — patient, close-focus looking at short turf on a sunny day is the best way to find them. Caterpillars feed on fine grasses, including fescues and meadow-grasses, and the species usually produces two broods in southern England, giving adults on the wing from May right through to September.

At Old Down, Small Heath favours the shortest, most closely grazed and driest areas of chalk grassland, where fine grasses grow low and warm quickly in the sun. It is often overlooked in favour of showier chalk grassland butterflies like the Chalkhill Blue, but a careful search of the shortest turf on a warm day will usually turn up several individuals bobbing weakly between grass stems.
native_info: Native and widespread throughout the UK, though it has declined in some intensively farmed lowland areas. Strongly associated with short, unimproved grassland, including chalk grassland, heathland and coastal turf.
wildlife_value: Caterpillars feed on fine grasses in short turf, part of the invertebrate food web supporting insectivorous birds and other predators. A good indicator of well-managed, unimproved short grassland rather than rank, overgrown swards.

life_stages.description: Small, pale, dome-shaped eggs are laid singly on fine grass blades in short turf.
Green, well camouflaged among fine grass, feeding on fescues and meadow-grasses. Overwinters as a partly grown caterpillar, resuming feeding and growth in spring.

photos.caption: Small Heath caterpillar, green and well camouflaged on fine grasses

life_stages.description: Pale orange-brown with a grey-brown underside to the hindwing; always rests with wings closed showing a single eyespot near the forewing tip. Two broods in southern England give a long flight season from May to September with peaks in June and August.

photos.caption: Small Heath — always rests with wings closed, showing a single eyespot
Small Heath resting low in short grassland

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are brown grassland butterflies of chalk grassland
similar_species.key_difference: Meadow Brown is considerably larger and darker, with a much bigger, more obvious double-pupilled eyespot, and often basks with wings partly open, unlike the Small Heath's closed-wing habit.

photos.caption: Small Heath — always rests with wings closed, showing a single eyespot
Small Heath resting low in short grassland
Small Heath caterpillar, green and well camouflaged on fine grasses

confidence_note: Britain's largest fritillary — big, powerful, deep orange with black markings, and a strong gliding flight. The underside shows distinctive streaky silver-green 'washes' rather than the discrete silver spots of other fritillaries.
weather_note: A strong-flying, sun-loving species that is most active and most easily seen on warm, sunny days, especially along sheltered, sunlit woodland rides.
summary: Britain's largest and most powerful fritillary, a big, deep-orange butterfly of sunny woodland rides with a strong, gliding flight. Named for the streaky silver-green markings washed across the underside of the wings.
full_description:
The Silver-washed Fritillary (Argynnis paphia) is the largest fritillary butterfly found in Britain, with a wingspan that can exceed 7cm. The upperside is a rich, deep orange marked with bold black spots and streaks, while the underside — particularly on the hindwing — is washed with streaky, iridescent silvery-green bands rather than the neat, separate silver spots seen in most other fritillaries, giving the species its name. The flight is powerful and confident, with long, effortless glides between wingbeats, quite different from the flappier flight of smaller fritillaries and browns. Males perform an extraordinary courtship display, looping repeatedly over and under a following female in a spiralling flight while releasing scent from special scales on the forewing.

The life cycle has an unusual twist: females do not lay eggs directly on the caterpillar foodplant (Common Dog-violet) but instead lay singly in crevices in the bark of trees, often several metres up, close to violets growing on the shaded woodland floor below. The tiny caterpillar hatches, eats its eggshell, and immediately goes into hibernation in the bark crevice for the winter without feeding at all, only descending to find violets to eat the following spring. This strategy is thought to reduce the risk of eggs or young caterpillars being found among leaf litter by predators and parasites over winter.

At Old Down, Silver-washed Fritillaries are seen gliding along sunny, sheltered woodland rides and the woodland edge bordering the chalk grassland in high summer, often nectaring on bramble blossom and thistles. Their large size, confident gliding flight and deep orange colour make them one of the most impressive and unmistakable butterflies of the site's woodland edges in July.
native_info: Native to England and Wales, strongly associated with sunny rides and glades in broadleaved woodland, particularly where Common Dog-violet grows in dappled shade. Has recovered well in recent decades in some regions after earlier declines.
wildlife_value: Adults are important pollinators of bramble blossom and other summer flowers along woodland rides. Caterpillars depend entirely on Common Dog-violet, so good populations of violets in dappled woodland-floor light are essential for the species' survival at a site.

life_stages.description: Laid singly in bark crevices of trees, often well above ground level, near violets growing below rather than directly on the foodplant.
Dark, spiny caterpillar that hatches in late summer, hibernates immediately without feeding, and only descends from the bark to find and feed on Common Dog-violet the following spring.
Large, deep orange with bold black markings above; underside washed with streaky silver-green bands. Strong, gliding flight along sunny woodland rides, peaking in July.

photos.caption: Silver-washed Fritillary male — large, deep orange with black markings
Silver-washed Fritillary underside — the streaky silver 'wash' that gives the species its name

similar_species.similarity_note: Another large orange fritillary, though more a grassland than woodland species
similar_species.key_difference: Dark Green Fritillary has green (not silver) undersides and is more typical of open grassland and coastal slopes rather than woodland rides; Silver-washed is larger with the distinctive streaky silver wash.

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are orange woodland-edge butterflies of similar size
similar_species.key_difference: Comma has deeply ragged, jagged wing edges and a small white comma-shaped mark on the dark underside, quite unlike the fritillary's smooth wing outline and silver-washed underside.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both can be seen in summer

photos.caption: Silver-washed Fritillary male — large, deep orange with black markings
Silver-washed Fritillary underside — the streaky silver 'wash' that gives the species its name

confidence_note: Males are a distinctive pale, silvery powder-blue — paler than any other British blue butterfly. Females are brown with orange spots along the wing edge, similar to other female blues, so check the male's colour and the chalk grassland habitat.
weather_note: Flies only in warm, sunny weather; large numbers can be on the wing together on a hot August afternoon but almost none visible on a dull day.
summary: A chalk grassland specialist and the palest blue butterfly in Britain — males are a distinctive silvery powder-blue, quite different from the richer blue of other species. A perfect, iconic sighting for Old Down's chalk downland.
full_description:
The Chalkhill Blue (Lysandra coridon) is one of the most characteristic and beautiful butterflies of southern English chalk grassland, and its pale, almost silvery powder-blue male upperside is unlike any other blue butterfly found in Britain — distinctly paler than the richer blue of the Common Blue or Adonis Blue. Females are chocolate-brown with a neat row of orange spots along the edge of each wing, similar in general pattern to other female blues, so habitat and the colour of accompanying males are the best clues to identification. Both sexes have a chequered black-and-white fringe to the wings.

Chalkhill Blue caterpillars feed exclusively on Horseshoe Vetch, a low-growing yellow-flowered plant restricted almost entirely to chalk and limestone grassland, which is why the butterfly itself is such a strong indicator of good, unimproved downland. Like several other blue butterflies, the caterpillars have a mutualistic relationship with ants: they produce a sugary secretion from a special gland that ants collect as food, and in return the ants guard the caterpillars from predators and parasites, sometimes even carrying them into their nest overnight for protection.

At Old Down, Chalkhill Blues are one of the signature species of high summer on the chalk grassland, appearing in good numbers on warm days in August where Horseshoe Vetch grows in short, sheep- or rabbit-grazed turf on the sunniest slopes. Watching a group of pale powder-blue males gathered at a damp patch of ground (a behaviour called 'mud-puddling', where they take up salts and minerals) is one of the most memorable sights the site's chalk grassland has to offer, and a strong sign that the grassland here is being managed well.
native_info: Native to England, almost entirely restricted to chalk and limestone grassland in southern and eastern England, where its caterpillar foodplant Horseshoe Vetch grows. A good indicator of high-quality, well-grazed downland.
wildlife_value: Adults are important pollinators of late-summer chalk grassland wildflowers such as knapweed and scabious. Caterpillars have a close mutualistic relationship with ants, which protect them in exchange for a sugary secretion, and depend entirely on Horseshoe Vetch.

life_stages.description: Laid singly on or near Horseshoe Vetch leaves. Overwinters as an egg, unusual among the British blues, hatching the following spring.

photos.caption: Chalkhill Blue egg on a Fescue grass leaf, laid near its horseshoe vetch foodplant

life_stages.description: Green and well camouflaged on Horseshoe Vetch, tended and protected by ants attracted to a sugary secretion the caterpillar produces.

Male is a distinctive pale, silvery powder-blue above; female is chocolate-brown with orange spots along the wing edges. A single generation flies from late July to September, peaking in August, often in large numbers on good chalk grassland.

photos.caption: Chalkhill Blue male — pale silvery-blue upperside, unique among British blues
Chalkhill Blue pair mating — pale blue male, brown female

similar_species.similarity_note: The most likely confusion species — both are blue butterflies of chalk grassland
similar_species.key_difference: Common Blue males are a richer, deeper violet-blue than the pale, silvery Chalkhill Blue, and Common Blue flies earlier in the summer with an additional spring/early-summer generation, while Chalkhill Blue is single-brooded and flies later, from late July.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Common Blue flies April–September; Chalkhill Blue only late July–September

similar_species.similarity_note: Another chalk grassland blue, sometimes found at the same sites
similar_species.key_difference: Adonis Blue male is a much more vivid, electric sky-blue than the pale Chalkhill Blue, with fine black lines crossing the white wing-fringe (absent or much less distinct in Chalkhill Blue).
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Adonis Blue flies May–June and August–September; Chalkhill Blue only late July–September

photos.caption: Chalkhill Blue male — pale silvery-blue upperside, unique among British blues
Chalkhill Blue pair mating — pale blue male, brown female
Chalkhill Blue egg on a Fescue grass leaf, laid near its horseshoe vetch foodplant

confidence_note: Unmistakable — glossy charcoal-black wings with two bold red streaks and a red patch, flies confidently by day. The bold yellow-and-black striped caterpillars, usually in groups on ragwort, are equally easy to identify.
weather_note: A day-flying moth that is most active and easiest to see on warm, sunny days, though it will also fly briefly at dusk.
summary: A striking black-and-red day-flying moth whose bold yellow-and-black striped caterpillars are a familiar sight stripping ragwort plants bare in late summer. Both stages advertise their foul taste with vivid warning colours.
full_description:
The Cinnabar Moth (Tyria jacobaeae) is one of Britain's most distinctive and easily recognised moths, and one of relatively few that fly confidently in daylight. The wings are glossy charcoal-black marked with two bold crimson-red streaks along the leading edge of each forewing and a red patch near the tip, with the hindwings almost entirely red edged in black. This striking red-and-black colouring is a warning to predators (aposematism): both the adult moth and its caterpillar sequester toxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids from their foodplant, ragwort, making them foul-tasting and mildly poisonous, so birds quickly learn to avoid them.

The caterpillar is, if anything, even more recognisable than the adult — boldly banded in orange-yellow and black, and usually found feeding in conspicuous groups on Common Ragwort in late summer. A group of caterpillars can strip a ragwort plant completely bare of leaves and flowers within days, sometimes moving on to a neighbouring plant when food runs out. Because ragwort is toxic to grazing livestock (particularly horses), the Cinnabar Moth is sometimes seen as a natural, welcome form of biological control in fields where the plant is a genuine concern, although ragwort is also an extremely valuable native wildflower for a huge range of other pollinating insects and should not be indiscriminately removed.

At Old Down, Cinnabar Moths and their caterpillars are closely tied to the ragwort growing on disturbed ground and grassland margins around the site. Adults fly from late May through summer, while the unmistakable striped caterpillars are one of the easiest and most rewarding invertebrates for children to find here in July and August — a quick scan of any patch of flowering ragwort will often turn up several.
danger_note: Both the caterpillar and adult moth contain toxic alkaloids absorbed from ragwort and are mildly poisonous if eaten, but are completely harmless to touch or handle. They cannot sting or bite.
native_info: Native and widespread throughout the UK wherever its foodplant, Common Ragwort, grows in reasonable quantity — grassland, waste ground, road verges, and field margins.
wildlife_value: Both adult and caterpillar are chemically defended and rarely eaten by birds, but the moth is an important pollinator of grassland flowers, and the caterpillars are food for a small number of specialist predators and parasitoid wasps that can tolerate the toxins. Entirely dependent on ragwort as a caterpillar foodplant.

life_stages.description: Yellow eggs are laid in batches of 30–60 on the underside of ragwort leaves, hatching within 1–2 weeks.

photos.caption: Cinnabar Moth eggs laid in a batch on ragwort

life_stages.description: Bold orange-yellow and black banded caterpillar, usually found feeding gregariously in groups on ragwort. Can strip a plant of leaves and flowers within days. Fully toxic like the adult thanks to alkaloids absorbed from the foodplant.

photos.caption: Cinnabar Moth caterpillar — bold yellow-and-black stripes on ragwort
Cinnabar caterpillars often strip a ragwort plant almost bare in a group

life_stages.description: Pupates in a cocoon in leaf litter or just below the soil surface, usually overwintering as a pupa before emerging as an adult the following late spring.
Glossy black wings with red streaks and a red hindwing; flies confidently by day as well as at dusk. Unmistakable among British moths.

photos.caption: Adult Cinnabar Moth with wings spread, showing the glossy black forewings with red streaks and red spots
Adult Cinnabar Moth at rest among grass, wings folded showing the red leading-edge streak

similar_species.similarity_note: Another red-and-black day-flying, chemically defended moth of similar habitats
similar_species.key_difference: Six-spot Burnet has metallic blue-green forewings with six distinct red spots, quite different from the Cinnabar's charcoal-black wings with red streaks and an all-red hindwing.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Cinnabar flies May–August; Six-spot Burnet flies June–August

photos.caption: Cinnabar Moth caterpillar — bold yellow-and-black stripes on ragwort
Cinnabar caterpillars often strip a ragwort plant almost bare in a group
Cinnabar Moth eggs laid in a batch on ragwort
Adult Cinnabar Moth with wings spread, showing the glossy black forewings with red streaks and red spots
