confidence_note: A plain, straw-coloured moth with a slim, tapering wing shape and a fine pale streak running along the centre of each forewing. One of several similar 'wainscot' moths named for grasses, so check the plain unmarked wings and pale streak carefully.
summary: A plain, straw-coloured night-flying moth of grassy places, named for the way its slim, tapering shape and pale stripe resemble a piece of wood panelling. Common and easily overlooked, but a genuine grassland specialist.
full_description:
The Common Wainscot (Mythimna pallens) is a plain but neatly marked moth, straw-yellow to pale buff in colour with a fine, pale, slightly darker-edged streak running lengthways along the centre of each forewing. The wings are held in a slim, elongated, tapering triangle at rest, quite different from the broader, rounder shape of many other moths — a shape and colouring reminiscent of dried grass stems, which gives excellent camouflage among the tall grassland vegetation where it lives. 'Wainscot' refers to wood panelling, a name given to this and related species because their streaky, straw-toned pattern was thought to resemble grain in wood panelling.

This is one of the commonest of Britain's many grass-feeding 'wainscot' moths, and one of the easier ones to identify thanks to its plain, largely unmarked wings and pale central streak — several related wainscot species have additional dots or marks that need closer comparison. The caterpillars feed low down on a wide range of coarse grasses, including cock's-foot and various meadow-grasses, usually hidden by day and feeding at night, making them rarely seen even where common.

At Old Down, Common Wainscot is a night-flying moth of the tussocky, unmown grassland margins and chalk grassland turf, readily attracted to light traps used for moth surveys on warm summer nights. Though rarely seen by day, its presence — usually confirmed through moth trapping — is a good sign of a healthy population of the coarse grasses its caterpillars depend on.
native_info: Native and common throughout lowland Britain wherever coarse grasses grow, including grassland, field margins, roadside verges and gardens.
wildlife_value: Caterpillars feed on a range of common grasses, contributing to the invertebrate food web. Adults are nocturnal and are eaten by bats and night-hunting birds; caterpillars and pupae are taken by ground-feeding birds and small mammals.

life_stages.description: Pale greyish-brown, feeding low down on the stems and leaves of coarse grasses at night. Overwinters as a partly grown caterpillar, resuming feeding in spring before pupating.

Straw-yellow to pale buff forewings with a fine pale central streak, held in a slim tapering shape at rest. Flies at night and is attracted to light. Usually two broods, giving adults from June to September.

photos.caption: Common Wainscot — straw-coloured forewings with a pale central streak
Common Wainscot at rest, wings folded in a slim, tapering shape

similar_species.similarity_note: One of several similar grass-feeding wainscot moths
similar_species.key_difference: Several related wainscots have additional dark dots or stronger streaking on the forewing; Common Wainscot is comparatively plain with just the single pale central streak, making it one of the more straightforward wainscots to identify.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Most wainscot species fly in mid-to-late summer

photos.caption: Common Wainscot — straw-coloured forewings with a pale central streak
Common Wainscot at rest, wings folded in a slim, tapering shape

confidence_note: The adult moth is genuinely almost identical to the closely related Dark Dagger and cannot be told apart reliably without examining fine details or genetics — most moth recorders log sightings as 'Grey/Dark Dagger agg.' unless the caterpillar is found. The caterpillar, black with a yellow side-stripe and a raised black hump, is much easier to identify.
summary: A mottled grey moth named for the fine, dagger-shaped black markings on its forewings — but its striking black-and-yellow caterpillar with a distinctive hump is far easier to identify than the adult, which is a near-perfect match for the similar Dark Dagger.
full_description:
The Grey Dagger (Acronicta psi) is a variably mottled grey moth, its forewings marked with fine black streaks including short, dagger-shaped marks that give the species its name (the Latin species name 'psi' refers to the Greek letter that some of the markings resemble). It is a good example of a British moth where the adult stage presents a genuine identification puzzle even for experienced naturalists: the Grey Dagger is virtually indistinguishable from the closely related Dark Dagger by sight alone, and the two species are usually only reliably separated by examining the caterpillar, the underlying wing colour beneath the scales, or genetic testing. For this reason, adult sightings are often recorded simply as 'Grey/Dark Dagger' unless a caterpillar has confirmed which species is present.

The caterpillar removes all doubt. It is one of the most striking of British moth larvae — jet black along most of its length with a bold, broken yellow stripe running down each side, a prominent raised black hump on the back near the front, and a fine reddish tuft further back. It feeds openly on the leaves of a wide range of trees and shrubs, including hawthorn, blackthorn, birch and various fruit trees, and its bold pattern and unmistakable silhouette make it a genuine highlight for children hunting for caterpillars in late summer.

At Old Down, Grey Dagger caterpillars can be found from July into September feeding openly on hawthorn and blackthorn in the hedgerows around the chalk grassland — a good example of how, in moths, the caterpillar is sometimes a far more useful and rewarding identification target than the adult.
native_info: Native and common throughout the UK wherever its broadleaved tree and shrub foodplants grow, including hedgerows, woodland edge, scrub and gardens.
wildlife_value: Caterpillars feed on a wide range of native trees and shrubs, forming part of the food supply for insectivorous birds feeding chicks in summer. Adults are nocturnal and provide food for bats.

life_stages.description: Unmistakable: black with a broken yellow side-stripe, a prominent raised black hump near the front of the body, and a fine reddish tuft further back. Feeds openly by day on hawthorn, blackthorn, birch and other trees and shrubs.

photos.caption: Grey Dagger caterpillar — black with a yellow stripe and a prominent hump

life_stages.description: Mottled grey forewings marked with fine black streaks, including short dagger-shaped marks. Virtually identical to the Dark Dagger and usually only safely told apart by the caterpillar. Flies at night and comes to light.

photos.caption: Grey Dagger — mottled grey forewings with fine black dagger-shaped marks

similar_species.similarity_note: Adults are essentially identical and cannot be reliably separated on sight
similar_species.key_difference: The two species are usually distinguished only by the caterpillar (Dark Dagger's has a red rather than yellow stripe and lacks the prominent hump) or by genetic and dissection methods. Adult sightings are commonly recorded as 'Grey/Dark Dagger agg.'

photos.caption: Grey Dagger — mottled grey forewings with fine black dagger-shaped marks
Grey Dagger caterpillar — black with a yellow stripe and a prominent hump

confidence_note: Named for its uniform dark brown, mouse-like colouring and its habit of scurrying rather than flying away when disturbed by day, hiding in low crevices. Smooth, glossy wings with faint darker kidney-shaped marks help confirm the identification.
summary: A smooth, uniform dark-brown moth that behaves like its name suggests — when disturbed in a daytime hiding place it scurries away on foot rather than flying, exactly like a small mouse.
full_description:
The Mouse Moth (Amphipyra tragopoginis) is named for both its colouring and its behaviour. The wings are a smooth, glossy, uniform dark brown with only faint, darker kidney-shaped markings, giving an overall drab appearance quite unlike the boldly patterned wings of many other moths. More distinctive still is its behaviour when found resting in a sheltered daytime hiding spot, such as under loose bark, in a shed, or among dense vegetation: rather than flying off, a disturbed Mouse Moth typically scurries rapidly away on foot with a low, scuttling gait remarkably reminiscent of a small mouse, which is exactly how the species earns its common name.

The caterpillars are much less conspicuous than the boldly marked larvae of many other moths in this family, feeding at night on a wide range of herbaceous plants including docks, goosefoot, and various garden and hedgerow plants, and hiding by day low down among the vegetation or in the soil surface litter. Adults fly at night in late summer and are readily attracted to light traps, but by day they are much more likely to be found at rest in a sheltered crevice than seen in flight.

At Old Down, Mouse Moths are found in the dense hedgerows, scrub, and sheltered vegetation margins around the chalk grassland, where their nondescript caterpillars feed unnoticed on the wide range of coarse herbaceous plants growing in these areas. It is a good example of a moth better known through its distinctive scurrying escape behaviour than through any striking pattern on its wings.
native_info: Native and common throughout lowland Britain in hedgerows, gardens, woodland edge and other sheltered vegetated habitats.
wildlife_value: Caterpillars feed on a wide range of common herbaceous plants, forming part of the invertebrate food web. Adults are nocturnal and provide food for bats and other night-hunting predators.

life_stages.description: Plain green or brownish, feeding at night on a wide range of low-growing herbaceous plants including docks and goosefoot, hiding low down by day.

Smooth, glossy, uniform dark brown wings with only faint kidney-shaped markings. When disturbed at a daytime resting place it typically scurries away on foot rather than flying, a distinctive mouse-like behaviour. Flies at night and comes to light.

photos.caption: Mouse Moth at rest — smooth, uniform dark brown, low, streamlined profile
Mouse Moth showing its faintly kidney-shaped wing marks

similar_species.similarity_note: Another plain brown night-flying moth of similar habitats
similar_species.key_difference: The Uncertain and related Rustic moths have a slightly more mottled, less glossy wing surface and lack the Mouse Moth's very smooth uniform sheen and distinctive scurrying escape behaviour.

photos.caption: Mouse Moth at rest — smooth, uniform dark brown, low, streamlined profile
Mouse Moth showing its faintly kidney-shaped wing marks

confidence_note: One of Britain's largest bumblebees, with an unusually long body and by far the longest tongue of any UK bumblebee, adapted for deep tubular flowers. Easily confused with the commoner Garden Bumblebee (Bombus hortorum) and needs a careful look at face shape and body proportions; a dark, all-black form also occurs.
summary: One of Britain's largest and scarcest bumblebees, with the longest tongue of any UK species — built for reaching deep into long tubular flowers like red clover that shorter-tongued bees cannot use. A conservation priority species found on good, flower-rich chalk grassland.
full_description:
The Large Garden Bumblebee (Bombus ruderatus) is one of the biggest bumblebees found in Britain, noticeably long-bodied compared to most other species, with black-and-yellow banding (a pale yellow collar band, a central yellow band, and a white tail) similar in general pattern to the commoner Garden Bumblebee, though an all-black form with no yellow bands also occurs and can only be told apart from other dark bumblebees by an expert. Its most remarkable feature is its extremely long tongue — the longest of any British bumblebee — which allows it to reach deep into the long, tubular flowers of plants such as red clover and comfrey that are too deep for most other bumblebee species to feed from efficiently.

This specialisation comes at a cost: because Large Garden Bumblebees rely so heavily on flower-rich grassland with plenty of deep tubular flowers, the huge decline in traditional flower-rich hay meadows and unimproved grassland across Britain during the twentieth century hit this species particularly hard, and it is now a national conservation priority, considered nationally scarce and largely confined to the least intensively farmed pockets of countryside, particularly in southern England. Its presence at a site is a strong signal of genuinely good-quality, flower-rich habitat rather than the more generalist grassland many commoner bumblebees can tolerate.

At Old Down, the chalk grassland's rich mix of clovers, vetches and other deep-flowered legumes provides exactly the kind of habitat this scarce bumblebee needs. Spotting one requires a careful look — checking the length of the tongue extended into a flower and the overall size and body proportions compared to the commoner bumblebees nearby — but finding a Large Garden Bumblebee here is a genuine sign that the site's grassland management is benefiting some of Britain's most specialised and vulnerable pollinators.
danger_note: Female bumblebees can sting if handled roughly or if their nest is disturbed, but are not aggressive when foraging on flowers. The sting is not barbed, so (unlike a honeybee) the bee is not harmed by stinging, but stings are still rare unless provoked.
native_info: Native to the UK but now nationally scarce, with a scattered and declining distribution concentrated in flower-rich grassland in southern England. Listed as a conservation priority species due to long-term decline linked to loss of traditional hay meadows.
wildlife_value: An important pollinator, especially valuable for long-tubed flowers such as red clover and comfrey that shorter-tongued bees struggle to reach, helping set seed in these plants. Its presence indicates flower-rich grassland of high conservation value.

life_stages.description: Emerges from hibernation in spring to found a new colony, usually in an underground cavity such as an old rodent burrow. Larger than the workers, with the same long-bodied shape and exceptionally long tongue.

Smaller than the queen but sharing the same distinctive long body and very long tongue. Forages on deep tubular flowers such as red clover, comfrey and vetches, often reaching much further into a flower than other bumblebee species can manage.

photos.caption: Large Garden Bumblebee — long body, long tongue, on a tubular flower
Large Garden Bumblebee foraging — note the notably long tongue

similar_species.similarity_note: The most likely confusion species, with an almost identical banding pattern
similar_species.key_difference: Garden Bumblebee (Bombus hortorum) is more common and slightly smaller with a more triangular face; Large Garden Bumblebee is bigger and longer-bodied with an even longer tongue, but the two genuinely require careful, expert comparison to separate with confidence.

similar_species.similarity_note: A much commoner bumblebee found in the same grassland
similar_species.key_difference: Buff-tailed Bumblebee is shorter and stockier with a buff (not white) tail in the queen, and a noticeably shorter tongue suited to more open flowers rather than deep tubular ones.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both fly through spring and summer

photos.caption: Large Garden Bumblebee — long body, long tongue, on a tubular flower
Large Garden Bumblebee foraging — note the notably long tongue

confidence_note: Superficially resembles the common Red-tailed Bumblebee but has smoky, dark-tinted wings, a less densely furry, slightly shinier body, and no pollen baskets on the hind legs (cuckoo bees never collect pollen). Yellow side-tufts of hair on the red tail are another good clue.
summary: A brood-parasite bumblebee that never builds its own nest or collects pollen — instead the female sneaks into a Red-tailed Bumblebee's nest, kills or subdues the resident queen, and tricks the workers into raising her own young.
full_description:
The Red-tailed Cuckoo Bee (Bombus rupestris) looks at first glance like a fairly ordinary black-bodied, red-tailed bumblebee, but it lives an entirely different lifestyle from a true bumblebee. It is a brood parasite — sometimes called a 'cuckoo bumblebee' for the obvious parallel with the cuckoo bird — that never builds its own nest, never forages for pollen to feed young, and has no worker caste of its own. Instead, a mated female Red-tailed Cuckoo Bee seeks out an established nest of the common Red-tailed Bumblebee (Bombus lapidarius), fights her way in, and either kills the resident queen outright or subdues and dominates her, before laying her own eggs and using pheromones and aggression to force the host colony's workers to raise the cuckoo's offspring instead of their own.

Because it never needs to collect pollen, the female Red-tailed Cuckoo Bee lacks the pollen baskets (the smooth, shiny, hair-fringed patch on the hind leg used to carry pollen home) that all true worker and queen bumblebees possess — a useful identification feature if a good close view is possible. The wings also tend to look darker and smokier than a true Red-tailed Bumblebee's, and the body is slightly less densely hairy, giving it a somewhat sleeker, shinier appearance overall, with tufts of yellowish hair often visible at the sides of the otherwise red tail.

At Old Down, Red-tailed Cuckoo Bees can be found nectaring on chalk grassland flowers such as knapweed, scabious and thistles wherever their host, the Red-tailed Bumblebee, is common, since a healthy population of the host species is essential for the cuckoo bee to persist at all. It is a wonderful example for children of how nature is full of surprising relationships — not every bee that looks like a bumblebee lives like one.
danger_note: Females can sting if handled, but like other bumblebees are not aggressive towards people and rarely sting unless directly provoked.
native_info: Native to the UK, found wherever its host species, the Red-tailed Bumblebee, is common — grassland, hedgerows, gardens and scrub across most of Britain.
wildlife_value: As an adult, an effective pollinator of grassland flowers such as knapweed and scabious. As a brood parasite, entirely dependent on healthy populations of its host, the Red-tailed Bumblebee, making it a species that indicates a well-functioning wider bumblebee community rather than being a threat to it.

life_stages.description: Black body with a red-orange tail, smoky dark-tinted wings, and no pollen baskets on the hind legs (a key clue that it is a cuckoo species). Emerges later in the season than true bumblebee queens, once host colonies are well established.

photos.caption: Red-tailed Cuckoo Bee — dark smoky wings and a red-orange tail
Red-tailed Cuckoo Bee nectaring on red clover

similar_species.similarity_note: Its host species and the most likely confusion — very similar black-and-red colouring
similar_species.key_difference: True Red-tailed Bumblebee workers and queens have clear pollen baskets on the hind legs, denser fur, and clear (not smoky) wings; the cuckoo species lacks pollen baskets entirely and has darker, smokier wings.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Red-tailed Bumblebee flies March–October; cuckoo females mainly seen June–September once host nests are established

similar_species.similarity_note: A common true bumblebee found in the same grassland
similar_species.key_difference: Buff-tailed Bumblebee has a buff-white (not red) tail and clear pollen baskets, quite different from the Red-tailed Cuckoo Bee's red tail and pollen-basket-free legs.

photos.caption: Red-tailed Cuckoo Bee — dark smoky wings and a red-orange tail
Red-tailed Cuckoo Bee nectaring on red clover

confidence_note: A small, neatly shield-shaped bug in bronzy-green with darker mottling, usually found sitting on or near Hedge Woundwort, its main foodplant, which gives an important habitat clue when confirming the identification.
summary: A small, neat, bronze-green shieldbug that lives almost entirely on Hedge Woundwort, the plant that gives it its name. Like all shieldbugs, it releases a defensive smell if handled, earning the family the nickname 'stink bugs'.
full_description:
The Woundwort Shieldbug (Eysarcoris venustissimus, sometimes placed in the genus Stagonomus) is a small shieldbug, around 6–8mm long, with a neat, classic shield-shaped outline and a bronzy-green body finely mottled with darker patches. Like other shieldbugs, it belongs to the true bug order Hemiptera and feeds by piercing plant tissue with a needle-like mouthpart (a rostrum) and sucking up sap, rather than chewing leaves like a caterpillar. Its common name comes from its close association with Hedge Woundwort (Stachys sylvatica), a common hedgerow and woodland-edge plant with dark maroon flowers and a distinctive, slightly unpleasant smell when its leaves are crushed, which is both the main foodplant and favourite hiding place for this shieldbug.

Like all true shieldbugs, the Woundwort Shieldbug has scent glands that release a sharp, unpleasant odour if the bug is handled or feels threatened — the reason the whole group is sometimes nicknamed 'stink bugs' in other parts of the world. This is a purely defensive mechanism against predators and is completely harmless to people; at most it is simply an unpleasant smell on the fingers, easily washed off. Immature nymphs look quite different from the adult, being rounder in outline with a more strongly contrasting pattern of pale and dark patches, gradually developing wings and the neat adult shield shape after several moults over the summer.

At Old Down, Woundwort Shieldbugs can be found on and around patches of Hedge Woundwort growing in the dappled shade of hedgerows and woodland-edge paths bordering the chalk grassland. A gentle search of woundwort leaves and flower spikes, particularly checking the undersides of leaves, is the best way for children to find both adults and the more unusually patterned nymphs.
native_info: Native and widespread across England and Wales wherever Hedge Woundwort grows, in hedgerows, woodland edges and shady field margins.
wildlife_value: Feeds by piercing and sucking sap from Hedge Woundwort and related plants. Both nymphs and adults are food for insectivorous birds, spiders and other predators, forming part of the wider hedgerow food web.

life_stages.description: Rounder in outline than the adult, with a more strongly contrasting pattern of pale and dark patches and no fully developed wings. Passes through several moults over the summer before reaching adult form.

photos.caption: Woundwort Shieldbug nymph — rounder and more patterned than the adult

life_stages.description: Neat, classic shield shape, bronzy-green finely mottled with darker patches, around 6–8mm long. Found on or close to Hedge Woundwort. Releases a defensive smell if handled, harmless to people.

photos.caption: Woundwort Shieldbug — small bronze-and-green shield shape

similar_species.similarity_note: Another small shieldbug of hedgerows and woodland edge
similar_species.key_difference: Hairy Shieldbug (Sloe Bug) is noticeably furrier in appearance with visibly hairy edges to the body, and is more strongly associated with blackthorn than with Hedge Woundwort.

photos.caption: Woundwort Shieldbug — small bronze-and-green shield shape
Woundwort Shieldbug nymph — rounder and more patterned than the adult

confidence_note: The spider itself needs a careful look at its brown-and-cream striped legs and body, but its web is completely unmistakable — a large, flat sheet of silk in grass or scrub tapering into a deep funnel retreat, spectacular when picked out by dew or morning mist.
summary: One of Britain's largest and most impressive web-builders — a funnel-web spider whose huge, flat sheet web tapering into a silk tunnel becomes spectacularly visible when picked out by morning dew, especially across chalk grassland scrub in late summer.
full_description:
The Labyrinth Spider (Agelena labyrinthica) is one of Britain's largest and most striking funnel-web spiders, with a brown body marked with pale chevron patterns and distinctive banded, striped legs. Females can reach up to 2cm in body length, making this one of the bigger spiders regularly found in grassland and scrub. But it is not the spider itself that most people notice first — it is the extraordinary web. Rather than the classic circular orb web most people picture when they think of a spider's web, the Labyrinth Spider spins a large, flat, densely woven horizontal sheet of silk draped over low vegetation such as gorse, bramble or long grass, which narrows at one end into a deep, tubular silk funnel or tunnel leading down into dense cover.

The spider waits, usually hidden just inside the mouth of the funnel, for a flying or jumping insect to land on the sheet. It detects the vibrations of the struggling prey through the silk, dashes out at extraordinary speed to bite and subdue it, then drags the prey back into the funnel to feed in safety, away from its own predators. These webs are largely invisible in dry conditions but become spectacularly obvious on a dewy or misty summer morning, when hundreds of tiny water droplets caught on the silk sheet reveal the full size and structure of the funnel and its labyrinth-like layers — a genuinely magical sight for children exploring chalk grassland scrub early in the day, and the source of both the spider's common and scientific names.

At Old Down, Labyrinth Spider webs are a highlight of the chalk grassland's scrubby, gorse- and bramble-dotted slopes in high summer. A dewy morning walk in July or August, checking low scrub and long grass for the tell-tale glistening sheet-and-funnel structure, is one of the best wildlife-watching activities the site offers — and once a web is found, patiently watching the funnel entrance often reveals the spider herself waiting just out of sight.
danger_note: Completely harmless to people. Like all UK spiders it could technically bite in self-defence if trapped against skin, but its fangs cannot easily pierce human skin and there is no venom risk to people.
native_info: Native and widespread across southern and central England and Wales, most abundant on unimproved chalk and limestone grassland, heathland and coastal scrub with plenty of low vegetation to anchor its large sheet webs.
wildlife_value: An effective predator of flying and jumping grassland insects, helping regulate invertebrate populations. Its large webs and the spider itself are, in turn, food for birds and other predators; a good example for children of a mid-level predator in the grassland food web.

life_stages.description: Spiderlings hatch from an egg sac in spring and grow through several moults over the summer, building progressively larger sheet-and-funnel webs as they mature.

photos.caption: Juvenile Labyrinth Spider on its low sheet web

life_stages.description: Brown body with pale chevron markings and clearly banded legs, up to about 2cm long in females (males are smaller). Builds the large, flat sheet web tapering to a funnel retreat that is the species' most recognisable feature. Mating and egg-laying occur in autumn, after which adults die with the first hard frosts.

photos.caption: Labyrinth Spider female sitting at the mouth of her funnel web
A dew-covered Labyrinth Spider sheet-and-funnel web in grassland

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are large, common late-summer spiders of grassland and scrub
similar_species.key_difference: Garden Spider builds a classic circular orb web and has a rounded body with a pale cross-shaped mark, quite different from the Labyrinth Spider's flat sheet-and-funnel web and elongated, banded-legged body.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both most conspicuous July to October

photos.caption: Labyrinth Spider female sitting at the mouth of her funnel web
A dew-covered Labyrinth Spider sheet-and-funnel web in grassland
Juvenile Labyrinth Spider on its low sheet web

confidence_note: A slim, long-legged brown spider with a pale stripe down the centre of the body, usually seen basking on vegetation with legs held forward in pairs rather than sitting in a web. A female carrying a large round white egg sac in her jaws, or guarding a silk 'nursery tent', confirms the identification instantly.
summary: A remarkable spider that hunts on foot rather than in a web, yet devotes enormous care to its young — the female carries her large round egg sac everywhere in her jaws, then builds a silk 'nursery tent' and stands guard over the spiderlings until they disperse.
full_description:
The Nursery-web Spider (Pisaura mirabilis) is a slim, long-legged, athletic spider, greyish-brown with a pale, often cream or yellowish stripe running down the centre of its back. Unlike web-building spiders such as the Garden Spider or Labyrinth Spider, it is a free-hunting spider that stalks and pounces on prey directly, and is most often seen basking on sunlit leaves or low vegetation with its front two pairs of legs held together and stretched forward — a resting posture that makes it look longer and slimmer than it really is.

The species' remarkable parental behaviour gives it its common name. After mating, the female wraps her eggs in a large, round, papery silk sac and carries it everywhere she goes, gripped firmly in her jaws (chelicerae) and held slightly beneath her body — a considerable physical burden she maintains for around three weeks until the eggs are ready to hatch. Just before hatching, she attaches the sac to vegetation and spins an elaborate three-dimensional silk tent or 'nursery web' around it, inside which the spiderlings hatch and spend their first few days. The female stands guard on or near the tent, fiercely defending her young from predators until they are ready to disperse and fend for themselves — an unusually devoted level of maternal care for a spider. Males also have a striking behaviour of their own: before mating, a male presents the female with a silk-wrapped 'nuptial gift', often a captured fly, to improve his chances of being accepted rather than eaten.

At Old Down, Nursery-web Spiders are common on the chalk grassland and along scrubby, sunny path-side vegetation through summer. Watching for a female carrying her conspicuous round white egg sac, or spotting the distinctive silk tent draped over a bramble or grass tussock later in the season, is a wonderful chance for children to see genuine parental care in an invertebrate up close.
danger_note: Completely harmless to people. It hunts on foot rather than biting defensively, and its fangs cannot easily pierce human skin.
native_info: Native and common throughout England, Wales and southern Scotland in grassland, hedgerows, scrub and woodland edge with plenty of low vegetation for basking and hunting.
wildlife_value: An active hunter of small flying and crawling insects, helping regulate invertebrate numbers in grassland and scrub. In turn, adults, egg sacs and spiderlings are food for birds and other predators.

life_stages.description: Carries a large, round, papery white egg sac gripped in her jaws and held beneath her body for around three weeks before hatching, defending it fiercely if disturbed.

photos.caption: Female Nursery-web Spider carrying her large round egg sac in her jaws
Close view of a female carrying her silk-wrapped egg sac beneath her body

life_stages.description: Just before hatching, the female spins an elaborate silk tent around the attached egg sac. Spiderlings hatch and remain inside this 'nursery web' for their first few days, guarded closely by the female, before dispersing to hunt independently.

photos.caption: The silk nursery tent spun to protect the spiderlings after hatching, guarded by the female

life_stages.description: Slim, long-legged, greyish-brown with a pale central stripe down the back. Hunts actively on foot rather than building a prey-catching web, often seen basking with the front legs held forward in pairs.

photos.caption: Nursery-web Spider — slim brown body with a pale central stripe

similar_species.similarity_note: Another free-hunting, non-web-building spider of grassland
similar_species.key_difference: Wolf spiders are generally stockier and more mottled/patterned than the slim, striped Nursery-web Spider, and female wolf spiders carry their egg sac attached to the rear of the abdomen rather than in the jaws, and carry newly hatched spiderlings riding on their back — a very different behaviour from the Nursery-web Spider's silk tent.

confidence_note: A dense, dark evergreen conifer with flat, short, dark green needles arranged in two rows, reddish flaking bark, and (on female trees) bright red, fleshy, cup-shaped berries in autumn. No other common British tree looks quite like it.
summary: A dense, dark evergreen conifer, deeply linked to churchyards and ancient sites, and famous for both its extraordinary longevity and its serious toxicity — one of very few British trees where almost every part is genuinely dangerous if eaten.
full_description:
Yew (Taxus baccata) is a slow-growing, long-lived evergreen conifer with a dense, dark green canopy that stays clothed in foliage all year round, casting deep, heavy shade beneath it where little else can grow. The needles are short, flat, and dark glossy green above with a paler underside, arranged in two neat rows along the twig, quite different from the rounder, prickly needles of pine or spruce. The bark is thin, reddish-brown to purplish, and flakes away in small, papery scales, often revealing patches of paler wood beneath — mature trees can develop wonderfully gnarled, fluted, and hollow trunks over time.

Yew is exceptionally long-lived; some ancient churchyard yews in Britain are estimated to be well over a thousand years old, and a handful may even predate the churches built beside them, suggesting the tree itself was already considered a sacred or significant site in pre-Christian times. Yews are usually either male or female (dioecious): male trees produce small clusters of yellow pollen cones in late winter and early spring, while female trees, if pollinated, produce distinctive fleshy, bright-red, cup-shaped structures called arils in autumn, each containing a single hard, dark seed. Confusingly, the soft red aril flesh is the one part of the whole tree that is not poisonous and is eaten safely by birds such as thrushes, which help disperse the seeds — but the hard seed inside the aril is highly toxic, along with the needles, bark, and wood of the entire tree, all of which contain dangerous taxine alkaloids that can affect the heart if eaten in any quantity. For this reason, Yew is one of the very few British native trees that genuinely needs a clear, calm safety conversation with children: admire it, but never chew, suck, or eat any part of it, including the tempting-looking red berries — always spit out and discard the hard seed even if the surrounding red flesh has been tasted.

At Old Down, ancient and more recently planted Yew trees form a distinctive, dark, evergreen presence within the woodland and along boundary hedgerows, historically linked to the wider chalk downland landscape's association with old churchyards, boundary markers and ancient trackways across southern England. Its dense evergreen cover provides valuable year-round shelter and nesting sites for birds even in the depths of winter when deciduous trees stand bare.
danger_note: Highly toxic. The needles, bark, wood and especially the hard seed inside each red berry contain taxine alkaloids that can be dangerous to the heart if eaten, even in fairly small amounts — this is one of the most poisonous common trees in Britain and has caused serious poisoning in both people and livestock. The soft red berry flesh (aril) itself is not toxic and is safely eaten by birds, but the seed inside definitely is: teach children to look but never taste any part of this tree, and to spit out the hard central seed immediately if red flesh is ever put in the mouth. Seek urgent medical help if any part of the plant, especially a seed, is swallowed.
native_info: Native throughout the UK, especially associated with chalk and limestone soils in southern England, and iconic in churchyards, hedgerows and ancient woodland. Many of Britain's oldest living trees are Yews.
wildlife_value: Dense evergreen cover provides valuable year-round shelter and nesting sites for birds, especially in winter when other trees are bare. The red aril flesh is an important autumn and winter food source for thrushes and other birds, which disperse the toxic seed unharmed through their gut without digesting it. Ancient hollow yews also provide roosting cavities for bats.

life_stages.description: Small, rounded, pale yellow pollen cones form in leaf axils on male trees in late winter, releasing clouds of fine yellow pollen carried on the wind to female trees.

photos.caption: Male Yew flowers releasing yellow pollen in early spring

life_stages.description: Bright red, soft, cup-shaped fleshy structures (arils) develop on female trees in autumn, each open at the tip to reveal a single hard, dark, highly toxic seed. The red flesh is eaten safely by birds; the seed is not.

photos.caption: Yew arils — the only non-toxic part of the tree, but the seed inside is highly poisonous

life_stages.description: Dense, dark evergreen canopy present year-round, with flat two-ranked needles and flaking reddish-brown bark. Very slow-growing but exceptionally long-lived, with the oldest British specimens estimated at over a thousand years old.

photos.caption: Mature Yew tree — dense, dark evergreen canopy
Yew bark — reddish-brown, flaking in thin scales

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are dense, dark evergreen trees/shrubs with red berries in a British hedgerow or woodland
similar_species.key_difference: Holly has glossy, spiny-edged broad leaves quite unlike Yew's soft, flat, needle-like leaves, and Holly's red berries (also toxic, but less severely so) are borne differently, in small clusters rather than as single arils each holding one large exposed seed.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both evergreen year-round; both berry in autumn/winter

photos.caption: Mature Yew tree — dense, dark evergreen canopy
Yew bark — reddish-brown, flaking in thin scales
Yew arils — the only non-toxic part of the tree, but the seed inside is highly poisonous
Male Yew flowers releasing yellow pollen in early spring

confidence_note: A low, mat-forming plant with narrow grey-green leaves and small, bright pink, five-petalled flowers, each petal finely toothed at the tip with a paler, often white-speckled ring near the centre. Confined to short, dry, sparsely vegetated chalk turf, which helps confirm the identification.
summary: A dainty, low-growing chalk grassland wildflower with vivid pink, finely fringed petals and a pale central ring — a scarce and declining specialist of the very shortest, driest turf, and a beautiful summer sight on Old Down's chalk slopes.
full_description:
Maiden Pink (Dianthus deltoides) is a low, ground-hugging perennial wildflower of dry, short grassland, forming loose mats of narrow, grey-green, grass-like leaves close to the ground from which slender flowering stems rise to around 15–30cm. Each stem carries one or a few bright, vivid pink flowers, roughly 1.5–2cm across, with five petals that are finely toothed along the outer edge and often marked with a paler pink or white-speckled ring towards the centre of the flower — a distinctive feature that helps separate it from other pink-flowered plants at a glance. The petals have a slightly deltoid (triangular) shape, giving the plant its scientific species name.

As a true specialist of short, dry, nutrient-poor chalk and sandy grassland, Maiden Pink cannot compete with taller, more vigorous plants and needs open, sparsely vegetated turf — created by grazing animals, rabbits, or naturally thin, free-draining chalky soil — to survive and reproduce. This narrow habitat requirement, combined with the loss of traditionally managed chalk grassland across lowland Britain during the twentieth century, has made Maiden Pink a genuinely scarce and declining wildflower, now largely confined to the best remaining pockets of unimproved downland turf in southern and eastern England.

At Old Down, Maiden Pink grows in the shortest, most closely grazed and sun-baked patches of chalk grassland, often alongside other classic downland specialists such as Wild Thyme and Salad Burnet. Its bright pink flowers, low growth habit and preference for the barest, driest ground make it a lovely and genuinely meaningful find for children exploring the site's chalk slopes in July — a small plant that tells a big story about how rare and precious good-quality chalk grassland has become.
native_info: Native to England, mainly in the south and east, strongly restricted to short, dry, unimproved chalk and sandy grassland. Nationally scarce and declining due to loss of traditionally grazed downland.
wildlife_value: Flowers provide nectar for bees, hoverflies and day-flying moths and butterflies able to reach the narrow floral tube. Its presence is a strong indicator of high-quality, species-rich, short chalk grassland turf.

life_stages.description: Low mats of narrow, grey-green, grass-like leaves persist close to the ground for much of the year, becoming most conspicuous once flowering stems die back after summer.

Slender stems bear one or a few bright pink, finely toothed flowers around 1.5–2cm across, each with a paler, often white-flecked ring near the centre. Flowers June to August, peaking in July on the shortest, sunniest chalk turf.

photos.caption: Maiden Pink — bright pink, five-petalled flower with a pale central ring
Maiden Pink growing low in short, dry chalk grassland turf

similar_species.similarity_note: Another common pink-flowered wildflower, though of very different habitat
similar_species.key_difference: Red Campion is a taller, softer-leaved plant of hedgerows and woodland edge with rounder, unfringed petals split into two lobes, quite unlike Maiden Pink's low, mat-forming habit and finely toothed petals restricted to short, dry chalk turf.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Red Campion flowers March–October; Maiden Pink flowers June–August

similar_species.similarity_note: A closely related, even scarcer pink-flowered relative
similar_species.key_difference: Deptford Pink has flowers in tighter clusters with narrower, less toothed petals and hairier stems and leaves; it is nationally rarer still than Maiden Pink and not currently recorded at Old Down.

photos.caption: Maiden Pink — bright pink, five-petalled flower with a pale central ring
Maiden Pink growing low in short, dry chalk grassland turf

confidence_note: Unmistakable — a pure white, heart-shaped face, golden-buff and grey upperparts, and pure white underparts. Flight is buoyant, silent and low, quartering over rough grass at dusk and dawn; the eerie screeching call is nothing like a Tawny Owl's hoot.
weather_note: Barn Owl feathers are not fully waterproof, so persistent rain stops them hunting and can cause real hardship; after a wet spell they are often forced to hunt in daylight to make up for lost time, which is when they are easiest to see.
summary: A ghostly white owl of rough grassland and field margins, hunting low and silent at dusk on long, rounded wings. The heart-shaped white face is unmistakable, and pale birds can look startlingly luminous in headlights or torchlight.
full_description:
The Barn Owl (Tyto alba) is one of Britain's most recognisable and beautiful birds of prey, with a pure white, heart-shaped facial disc, golden-buff and dove-grey upperparts finely speckled with black and white, and gleaming white underparts. Unlike the more familiar Tawny Owl, Barn Owls hunt largely by sound as well as sight — their facial disc funnels sound to asymmetrically positioned ears, allowing them to pinpoint a vole rustling in grass even in total darkness. Flight is slow, buoyant and almost completely silent, thanks to soft, comb-edged flight feathers that break up turbulence.

Barn Owls are specialist hunters of short-tailed field voles and other small mammals, and their fortunes rise and fall with vole populations and the amount of rough, unmown grassland margin available to hunt over. They nest in tree hollows, old barns, and specially provided nest boxes, and pairs will often use the same territory for years. Because they hunt low over open ground at dusk, dawn, and sometimes in broad daylight when provisioning owlets or after bad weather, they are one of the most likely owls for a careful, quiet observer to actually see hunting rather than just hear.

At Old Down, Barn Owls hunt the rough grass margins and field edges around the chalk grassland, particularly at dusk in the golden light of a summer evening or on damp mornings after a run of wet weather. Watch quietly from field edges rather than approaching — a hunting owl that is disturbed wastes valuable hunting time.
native_info: Resident and native throughout lowland Britain wherever suitable rough grassland hunting habitat and nest sites remain; Amber-listed due to long-term declines linked to loss of rough grassland margins and nest sites.
wildlife_value: A specialist predator of field voles, wood mice and shrews — a single breeding pair and their brood can account for several thousand small mammals in a season, making them a valuable natural check on rodent numbers around farmland.

life_stages.description: Heart-shaped pure white facial disc, golden-buff and grey speckled upperparts, and white underparts. Hunts low over rough grassland with slow, silent, buoyant flight, mainly at dusk and dawn.

photos.caption: Barn Owl hunting low over rough grassland at dusk
Barn Owl at Old Down, showing the heart-shaped white facial disc
Barn Owl in flight, golden-buff upperparts and white underparts

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are owls seen or heard around Old Down at dusk
similar_species.key_difference: Tawny Owl is chunkier and mottled rich brown all over with dark eyes and a rounded (not heart-shaped) face, is almost entirely nocturnal, and gives a hooting call rather than the Barn Owl's eerie screech.

photos.caption: Barn Owl hunting low over rough grassland at dusk
Barn Owl at Old Down, showing the heart-shaped white facial disc
Barn Owl in flight, golden-buff upperparts and white underparts

confidence_note: A winter finch closely related to the Chaffinch. Look for the orange-buff breast and shoulder patch, white rump conspicuous in flight, and mottled black-and-orange back (males more strikingly marked than females). Often mixed into Chaffinch flocks, so check flocks carefully.
summary: A close relative of the Chaffinch that arrives from Scandinavia each winter, told apart by its orange-buff breast, mottled black back, and the bright white rump that flashes as it flies off. Often found feeding on beech mast under trees.
full_description:
The Brambling (Fringilla montifringilla) is the Chaffinch's northern cousin, breeding in the birch and conifer forests of Scandinavia and Russia and arriving in Britain purely as a winter visitor. Adult males in fresh winter plumage are strikingly patterned, with a mottled black-and-buff back, deep orange-buff breast and shoulders, and a blue-grey nape that becomes glossy black by spring; females and young birds are duller and browner but share the same orange breast tone. In flight the long, gleaming white rump — brighter and more extensive than the Chaffinch's — is the most reliable feature at a distance.

Bramblings are strongly associated with beech trees in winter, since beech mast (the small triangular beech nuts) is their preferred food, and huge continental flocks will gather wherever a good mast year coincides with cold weather pushing them further west and south. In Britain, numbers vary enormously from year to year depending on the beech mast crop on the continent — some winters bring only scattered individuals mixed into Chaffinch flocks, others bring much larger numbers. They also feed on other seeds and, in hard weather, will come to bird tables.

At Old Down, Brambling are best looked for from late autumn through winter among Chaffinch flocks feeding on the ground below beech and other seed-bearing trees, or passing over calling with a distinctive nasal 'tswoo-eek'. A good beech mast year is the best time to find them in numbers.
native_info: A winter visitor to the whole of the UK from breeding grounds in Scandinavia and Russia; does not breed in Britain. Numbers vary greatly year to year depending on the continental beech mast crop.
wildlife_value: Feeds mainly on beech mast and other tree and weed seeds in winter, supplementing with insects in the breeding season on its northern breeding grounds; part of the winter finch flocks that make use of Old Down's beech trees.

life_stages.description: Orange-buff breast and shoulders, mottled black-and-buff back, and a bright white rump obvious in flight. Males are more boldly marked than females. Only present in the UK as a winter visitor.

photos.caption: Brambling feeding, showing the orange-buff breast and mottled back
Brambling, a winter visitor from Scandinavia

similar_species.similarity_note: Close relatives, often flock together in winter
similar_species.key_difference: Chaffinch is present year-round and has a blue-grey crown with a pinkish (not orange) breast and a double white wing bar rather than the Brambling's bright white rump.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Brambling only present October–March; Chaffinch present all year

photos.caption: Brambling feeding, showing the orange-buff breast and mottled back
Brambling, a winter visitor from Scandinavia

confidence_note: Grey above with a long tail and pointed wings, superficially hawk-like in flight — but the unmistakable, far-carrying 'cuck-oo' call of the male is by far the easiest way to confirm one is present. Females are sometimes rufous-brown ('hepatic' form).
summary: A summer migrant famous for laying its eggs in the nests of other birds and for the male's unmistakable two-note call. Grey and long-tailed, superficially resembling a small hawk in flight, but its voice is what gives it away.
full_description:
The Cuckoo (Cuculus canorus) is one of Britain's most famous but most rarely actually seen summer visitors, better known by its voice than its silhouette. Adults are slate-grey above with a long, barred tail and pointed wings that give them a fleeting resemblance to a Sparrowhawk in flight — a resemblance that may help them intimidate small host birds away from their nests. The male's far-carrying, two-note 'cuck-oo' call, delivered from an exposed perch, is one of the classic sounds of the British spring and gives the bird its name in dozens of languages.

Cuckoos are brood parasites: females never build a nest of their own, instead watching host species such as Reed Warbler, Meadow Pipit, or Dunnock, then slipping in to lay a single egg in the host's nest while the owners are away, often removing one of the host's own eggs at the same time. The cuckoo chick hatches quickly and instinctively ejects the host's remaining eggs or chicks from the nest, monopolising the host parents' feeding effort until it fledges — dramatically larger than its foster parents. Adult Cuckoos leave Britain remarkably early, often by July, having spent barely three months here; Sub-Saharan Africa is their wintering ground.

At Old Down, listen for the male's calling from scattered perches around the woodland edge and chalk grassland from late April, peaking through May and into June — one of the most reliable and evocative signs that spring has properly arrived, even though catching sight of the bird itself takes patience and luck.
native_info: A summer migrant to the whole of the UK, present April to July before returning to sub-Saharan Africa for the winter; Red-listed owing to significant population declines linked to changes on the African wintering grounds and en route.
wildlife_value: A brood parasite of small songbirds including Reed Warbler, Meadow Pipit and Dunnock; the caterpillars it favours as food (including hairy, chemically defended species most other birds avoid) make it an unusual predator within the food web.

life_stages.description: Slate-grey above with a long, barred tail and pointed wings, superficially hawk-like in flight. Best confirmed by the male's unmistakable 'cuck-oo' call from an exposed perch. Only present in the UK from April to July.

confidence_note: A large, upright thrush with a distinctive grey head and rump contrasting against a chestnut-brown back and boldly spotted yellowish breast. Usually in flocks, often with Redwings, and gives a harsh 'chack-chack-chack' flight call.
weather_note: Hard frost that freezes the ground pushes Fieldfares away from earthworm-hunting on open turf and onto berry-laden hedges instead, and heavy snow can force large flocks into gardens for windfall fruit.
summary: Britain's largest common thrush and a true winter visitor, arriving in noisy flocks from Scandinavia to strip hedgerows of berries. The grey head and rump contrasting with a chestnut back make it unmistakable among the winter thrushes.
full_description:
The Fieldfare (Turdus pilaris) is a big, bold thrush, noticeably larger than a Blackbird, with a distinctive combination of a blue-grey head and rump, a rich chestnut-brown back, and a warm yellowish breast boldly marked with dark spots and streaks. It is a gregarious bird, almost always seen in flocks that can number from a handful of birds to several hundred, often travelling and feeding alongside the smaller Redwing. In flight, the flocks give a harsh, chattering 'chack-chack-chack' call that is one of the classic sounds of the British winter countryside.

Fieldfares do not breed in Britain in any numbers; the birds seen here are winter visitors from Scandinavia and further east, arriving from October as the weather turns colder on the continent. They feed on open fields and short turf for earthworms and other invertebrates in mild weather, switching to hawthorn, holly and other hedgerow berries — and eventually windfall apples and orchard fruit — as the ground hardens with frost. A flock stripping a berry-laden hedge can move on almost as quickly as it arrived.

At Old Down, look and listen for chattering Fieldfare flocks working the hedgerows and open chalk grassland from late autumn through winter, especially in the company of Redwings after a good hawthorn crop, and watch for large numbers appearing suddenly during cold snaps as continental birds are pushed further west and south in search of food.
native_info: A winter visitor to the whole of the UK from Scandinavia and further east, present October to March; a very small number occasionally breed in northern Britain. Red-listed as a winter visitor of conservation concern.
wildlife_value: A major consumer of hedgerow berries and orchard windfalls in winter, helping disperse hawthorn and holly seed; also takes earthworms and soil invertebrates from open turf when the ground is unfrozen.

life_stages.description: Large thrush with a blue-grey head and rump, chestnut-brown back, and boldly spotted yellowish breast. Usually seen in noisy flocks, often with Redwings. Only present in the UK as a winter visitor.

confidence_note: A small, glossy blue-black and white swallow relative with a distinctive bright white rump, obvious in flight, and pure white underparts. Shorter, more forked tail than a Swallow, and builds mud-cup nests under eaves.
weather_note: Cold, wet spells that suppress flying insect activity can force House Martins to feed low over water or open ground, and prolonged bad weather in spring can delay their return or cause breeding failures.
summary: A small, glossy blue-black and white swallow relative, instantly told apart from a Swallow by its bright white rump. Builds distinctive mud-cup nests under eaves and feeds on the wing, often at height over open ground.
full_description:
The House Martin (Delichon urbicum) is a small hirundine — a member of the swallow family — with glossy blue-black upperparts, a short, only shallowly forked tail, and pure white underparts. Its most distinctive feature, visible even at a distance and in poor light, is the bright white rump that contrasts sharply with the dark back and tail, immediately separating it from the similarly aerial but longer-tailed Swallow. Like other hirundines it feeds entirely on the wing, snapping up flying insects in fast, agile flight that is often higher and more circling than the low, dashing flight of Swallows.

House Martins build distinctive enclosed mud-cup nests with a small entrance hole, tucked under the eaves of buildings, bridges, and other structures with a suitable overhang — the original nest sites were sea cliffs and crags, which some populations still use. Nests are built from hundreds of small mud pellets carried in the bill, often refurbished and reused year after year, and colonies of several nests together are common on suitable buildings. They arrive in Britain from Africa in April and leave again by September or October, one of the last summer migrants to depart.

At Old Down, House Martins can be seen hawking for insects high over the open chalk grassland and woodland edge on warm days throughout the summer, sometimes gathering in loose, wheeling flocks before roosting or migrating — a reminder that even birds that nest on nearby buildings depend on open countryside like this to find enough insect food to raise their young.
native_info: A summer migrant to the whole of the UK, present April to September/October before wintering in Africa. Amber-listed owing to declines linked to loss of nest sites and reduced flying insect abundance.
wildlife_value: An aerial insectivore taking large numbers of flying insects on the wing, helping to keep local insect populations in balance; its mud nests are themselves used by House Sparrows and other species once vacated.

life_stages.description: Glossy blue-black above with a bright white rump and pure white underparts, and a short, shallowly forked tail. Feeds on the wing, often high over open ground. Only present in the UK from April to September/October.

confidence_note: A large, upright, pale grey-brown thrush with bold, rounded dark spots on a whitish breast, an obvious white belly, and white underwing flashes visible in its bounding flight. Bulkier and greyer than a Song Thrush, with a loud, far-carrying song often delivered from a treetop in windy weather.
weather_note: Mistle Thrushes are famous for singing loudly from an exposed treetop perch in blustery, stormy weather when most other birds fall silent, earning the old country name 'stormcock'.
summary: Britain's largest common thrush, bulkier and paler grey-brown than the Song Thrush, with bold round spots and a habit of singing loudly from a treetop even in stormy weather — earning it the old nickname 'stormcock'.
full_description:
The Mistle Thrush (Turdus viscivorus) is the largest of Britain's common thrushes, notably bulkier than a Song Thrush and with a more upright, confident stance. Plumage is pale grey-brown above with a whitish breast marked by bold, rounded dark spots — larger and less neatly arranged than the Song Thrush's — and white underwing flashes and outer tail corners that are conspicuous in its strong, bounding flight. Pairs are often fiercely territorial, vigorously chasing off crows, magpies and other potential nest predators from around their nest and favourite feeding trees.

The species' old country name, 'stormcock', comes from its habit of singing its loud, far-carrying, slightly melancholy song from an exposed treetop perch even in blustery, wet weather when most other birds have fallen silent — one of the earliest songs of the year, sometimes beginning in January. True to its scientific name viscivorus ('mistletoe-eating'), it has a particular fondness for mistletoe berries along with holly, yew and hawthorn berries in winter, and a single bird will often defend a berry-laden tree as a private larder against all comers.

At Old Down, listen for the stormcock's loud, fluty song from treetops on blustery days from midwinter onwards, and watch for its strong, bounding flight and white underwing flashes as it moves between feeding trees around the woodland edge and chalk grassland.
native_info: Resident and native throughout the UK, present year-round; Red-listed owing to significant population declines in recent decades.
wildlife_value: Feeds on berries (mistletoe, holly, yew, hawthorn) in winter and earthworms and invertebrates in the breeding season, helping disperse the seeds of the berries it eats, including mistletoe.

life_stages.description: Large, pale grey-brown thrush with bold, rounded dark spots on a whitish breast and white underwing flashes in flight. Sings loudly from treetops even in stormy weather. Present all year.

confidence_note: A small, streaky yellow-green finch with a forked tail and, in males, a black crown and chin. Yellow wing bars and yellow-edged tail feathers show well in flight. Often acrobatic, hanging upside-down on alder or birch cones like a small tit.
summary: A small, streaky yellow-green finch that feeds acrobatically on alder and birch cones, often hanging upside down like a tit. Numbers are boosted hugely in winter by continental birds, and flocks can appear suddenly at garden feeders in hard weather.
full_description:
The Siskin (Spinus spinus) is a small, lively finch, noticeably smaller than a Greenfinch, with streaky yellow-green plumage, a neatly forked tail, and bold yellow wing bars and tail-edges that flash in flight. Breeding males have a smart black crown and chin that females and young birds lack, giving them a slightly more contrasty look. Siskins are highly acrobatic feeders, often hanging upside down from the tips of alder or birch catkins and cones — much like a tit — to extract the tiny seeds, a habit that quickly gives them away even in a mixed finch flock.

A small resident population breeds in Britain's conifer forests, particularly in Scotland and Wales, but numbers seen across the rest of the country are hugely boosted in winter by birds arriving from Scandinavia and further east. Wintering Siskins form flocks that roam widely in search of alder and birch seed crops, and in years when the wild seed crop fails they will readily turn up at garden feeders, particularly for nyjer seed, sometimes in large, restless, chattering flocks.

At Old Down, look for Siskins feeding acrobatically in streamside alders and birches from autumn through to early spring, often mixed with Lesser Redpolls, and listen for their thin, wheezy twittering calls given almost constantly as the flock moves between trees.
native_info: A small resident breeding population in Britain's conifer forests, greatly boosted in winter (October–March) by migrants from Scandinavia and further east.
wildlife_value: A specialist feeder on alder and birch seed in winter, also taking conifer seed where available; an important part of the mixed finch and redpoll flocks that use streamside and woodland-edge trees through the colder months.

life_stages.description: Small, streaky yellow-green finch with a forked tail and bold yellow wing bars; breeding males have a black crown and chin. Often feeds acrobatically, hanging upside down on cones. Present as a small resident population, greatly boosted in winter.

confidence_note: An unobtrusive, streaky grey-brown bird best identified by its distinctive hunting behaviour: perching upright on an exposed twig, sallying out in a fast looping flight to snatch a flying insect, then returning to the same or a nearby perch.
weather_note: Cold, wet spells that ground flying insects can make hunting very difficult for this aerial-insect specialist, sometimes causing breeding failures in poor summers.
summary: An unobtrusive summer visitor best known for its hunting style: perching upright on an exposed twig, darting out in a looping sally to snatch a flying insect, then returning to the same perch — a behaviour that gives it away far more than its plain grey-brown plumage.
full_description:
The Spotted Flycatcher (Muscicapa striata) is one of the least flashily plumaged of Britain's summer migrants — grey-brown above, streaky grey-white below, with only fine dark streaking on the crown and breast (the 'spots' of the name are subtle, not bold) — but its behaviour makes it unmistakable once noticed. It perches upright and alert on an exposed twig or fence wire, watching for passing insects, then makes a fast, agile, looping sally out into the air to snatch its prey with an audible snap of the bill, before returning to the same perch or one nearby to eat and watch again.

This 'sally and return' hunting technique, repeated over and over from a favourite perch, is by far the easiest way to pick out a Spotted Flycatcher among the summer birdlife of a woodland edge or garden. They arrive in Britain late, typically in May, among the last of the summer migrants, and nest in loose cups tucked into ivy, wall crevices, or open-fronted nest boxes, often close to human habitation. Numbers have declined very sharply in Britain in recent decades, likely linked to a combination of pressures on the African wintering grounds, migration hazards, and reduced flying insect abundance here.

At Old Down, look for Spotted Flycatchers perched upright on exposed dead twigs or fence posts around the woodland edge from late May through summer, watching for their characteristic darting sallies after passing insects — patience at a likely perch is usually rewarded better than active searching.
native_info: A summer migrant to the whole of the UK, present May to September before wintering in sub-Saharan Africa. Red-listed owing to very steep population declines in recent decades.
wildlife_value: A specialist aerial insectivore, taking flies, moths, beetles and other flying insects on the wing; its steep decline is considered an indicator of wider pressures on flying insect populations and long-distance migrants.

life_stages.description: Streaky grey-brown above and greyish-white below with fine dark streaking, best told by its hunting behaviour: perching upright then sallying out to snatch flying insects before returning to the same perch. Only present in the UK from May to September.

confidence_note: Extremely variable — can be orange with up to 21 black spots, black with two or four red spots, or many patterns in between, which makes colour alone unreliable. Size (larger than most native ladybirds), a domed shape, and a pale area behind the head with a distinctive 'M' or 'W'-shaped black mark are more consistent clues.
summary: A large, extremely variable, non-native ladybird first recorded in Britain in 2004 and now one of the most widespread ladybird species, of serious conservation concern because it outcompetes and preys on native ladybirds.
full_description:
The Harlequin Ladybird (Harmonia axyridis) is a large, strikingly variable ladybird native to eastern Asia that was introduced to parts of Europe and North America for aphid control before spreading, or being accidentally introduced, into Britain, where it was first recorded in 2004. Colour and spot pattern vary enormously between individuals — some are orange with up to 21 black spots, others glossy black with two or four large red or orange spots, with many intermediate forms — making pattern alone an unreliable guide. More consistent features are its relatively large size, strongly domed shape, and a pale, often orange-brown patch behind the head marked with a black shape resembling the letters 'M' or 'W'.

Since its arrival, the Harlequin Ladybird has spread rapidly across Britain and is now a serious concern for native ladybird conservation: it is a voracious predator that will eat the eggs, larvae and pupae of native ladybird species, including the familiar 7-Spot Ladybird, in addition to aphids, and out-competes native species for food in many habitats. Several native ladybird species have declined significantly in areas where Harlequins have become established, making this one of the clearest examples in Britain of a non-native invertebrate causing measurable harm to native wildlife.

At Old Down, Harlequin Ladybirds can be found year-round on trees, shrubs and garden vegetation, often in large aggregations seeking shelter in autumn. Recording sightings helps track its spread and impact on the site's native ladybird species, including the 7-Spot Ladybird.
native_info: Non-native, introduced from eastern Asia via continental Europe; first recorded in Britain in 2004 and now widespread and often abundant across England and Wales.
wildlife_value: A generalist predator of aphids, but also preys heavily on the eggs, larvae and pupae of native ladybirds and other insects, making its overall impact on native wildlife strongly negative despite also consuming pest aphids.
invasive_impact: Preys on and outcompetes native ladybird species, including the 7-Spot Ladybird, and has been linked to measurable declines in several native ladybird populations across Britain since its arrival in 2004.
removal_advice: Not required or practical to remove individuals — this is a well-established, widespread species in Britain. Recording sightings (e.g. via the UK Ladybird Survey) is more useful than attempting control, which has no meaningful effect on the wider population.

life_stages.description: Large, strongly domed ladybird with extremely variable colour and spot pattern — orange with many black spots, or black with a few large red spots. A pale patch behind the head with a black 'M' or 'W' mark is a more reliable feature than colour alone. Present year-round.

confidence_note: An elongated, soft-bodied beetle with orange-red wing cases and a small dark patch at the very tip. Extremely common on flat-topped summer flowers such as hogweed and other umbellifers, very often seen mating in pairs, giving it its cheerful country nickname.
weather_note: Most active and abundant in warm, sunny summer weather when umbellifer flowers are in full bloom.
summary: A common orange-red beetle with soft, elongated wing cases, swarming over hogweed and other flat-topped summer flowers — very often seen mating in pairs, earning it the affectionate nickname 'hogweed bonking beetle'.
full_description:
The Red Soldier Beetle (Rhagonycha fulva) is one of the most conspicuous and easily recognised beetles of the British summer, with soft, elongated, orange-red wing cases (unlike the hard, glossy cases of most beetles) and a small dark patch right at the wing tips. It swarms in large numbers on flat-topped umbellifer flowers — hogweed, cow parsley and wild carrot in particular — where it is extremely often seen paired up mating, a habit so noticeable and so consistent that the species has earned the cheerful country nickname 'hogweed bonking beetle'.

Both adults and the soil-dwelling larvae are useful predators, feeding on aphids and other small, soft-bodied insects in addition to visiting flowers for nectar and pollen as adults, making the species a beneficial presence in gardens and grassland alike. It is entirely harmless to handle and, unlike some soldier beetle relatives, poses no threat to people, pets or garden plants.

At Old Down, Red Soldier Beetles are unmissable on hogweed and other umbellifer flowerheads through the summer, often in large numbers and frequently paired up — one of the easiest and most rewarding insects for children to spot on a warm July day.
native_info: Widespread and abundant throughout the UK on flowery grassland, hedgerows and gardens.
wildlife_value: Both larvae and adults are useful predators of aphids and other small insects; adults are also frequent visitors to umbellifer flowers, contributing to pollination.

life_stages.description: Elongated beetle with soft orange-red wing cases and a small dark patch at the tips. Swarms on hogweed and other umbellifer flowers in summer, very often seen mating in pairs.

confidence_note: A pale sandy-brown to tan beetle, smaller and slimmer than the familiar Cockchafer ('May bug'), with a covering of fine hairs giving it a slightly fuzzy look. Flies at dusk on warm summer evenings, often in swarms around the crowns of trees, with a loud, buzzing flight.
weather_note: Flies at dusk on warm, still summer evenings; swarms are much reduced or absent in cool or windy conditions.
summary: A smaller, paler relative of the familiar Cockchafer or 'May bug', flying in noisy dusk swarms around tree crowns on warm summer evenings, a little later in the year than its larger cousin — hence the name.
full_description:
The Summer Chafer (Amphimallon solstitiale) is a pale sandy-brown to tan beetle, smaller, slimmer and paler than the well-known Cockchafer or 'May bug', with a fine covering of short hairs that gives the whole body a slightly fuzzy texture. It shares the Cockchafer's general chunky chafer-beetle shape and its habit of flying at dusk with a loud, buzzing drone, but appears about a month later in the year — late June into July rather than May — which is reflected in its common name and its scientific name solstitiale, referring to the summer solstice.

On warm, still summer evenings, male Summer Chafers can form large, noisy swarms around the crowns of oak and other trees at woodland edges, searching out females, and both sexes are strongly attracted to light, sometimes appearing at lit windows on warm nights. Larvae are typical fat, C-shaped white grubs living in the soil, where they feed on grass and plant roots for one or two years before pupating — like other chafer grubs, they are an important food source for birds such as rooks and gulls when turned up by cultivation or grazing animals.

At Old Down, listen and look for the loud, buzzing dusk flight of Summer Chafers swarming around tree crowns at the woodland edge on warm evenings in late June and July — a distinctive and easily overlooked sound of the summer dusk.
native_info: Widespread across England and Wales in woodland edges, grassland and gardens with light or sandy soils; more local in Scotland.
wildlife_value: Larvae feed on grass and plant roots in soil and are an important food source for birds; adults are eaten by bats and nightjars during their dusk-flying swarms.

life_stages.description: Pale sandy-brown to tan chafer beetle, smaller than the Cockchafer, with a fine fuzzy hair covering. Flies at dusk on warm summer evenings, often swarming around tree crowns with a loud buzzing flight.

confidence_note: A slender, elongated, brilliant metallic green (sometimes coppery or bronze) beetle commonly seen on open summer flowers. Males have distinctively swollen, thickened hind 'thighs' (femora) that give the species its name and are unmistakable once noticed; females lack the swelling.
weather_note: Most active on warm, sunny days, when it can be found basking and feeding openly on flowers.
summary: A slender, brilliant metallic green beetle, common on open summer flowers, whose males sport distinctively swollen, thickened hind thighs — a feature so obvious once noticed that it gives the species both its English names.
full_description:
The Thick-kneed Flower Beetle (Oedemera nobilis), also widely known as the Swollen-thighed Beetle or False Oil Beetle, is a slender, elongated beetle with a brilliant, iridescent metallic green sheen (occasionally showing coppery or bronze tones in some light), commonly found basking and feeding openly on the flowers of ox-eye daisy, buttercups, and other open summer blooms. Males have unmistakably swollen, bulging hind 'thighs' (femora) — a feature so distinctive that it gives the species both of its common English names, though its exact function (likely related to gripping females during mating, or simple display) is not fully settled. Females lack the swelling and have more slender legs throughout.

Adults feed on pollen rather than the flower petals themselves, and are frequent, easily observed visitors to a wide range of open, accessible summer flowers, making them one of the more approachable beetles for a child to watch closely without disturbing it. Wing cases are notably narrow and slightly gaping at the rear, a family trait shared with other false blister beetles, and the whole beetle has a delicate, elongated build quite different from the bulkier shape of most other flower-visiting beetles.

At Old Down, Thick-kneed Flower Beetles are easy to find basking and feeding on open flowers such as ox-eye daisy and buttercup across the chalk grassland through early to mid-summer — check any shiny green beetle on a flowerhead for the male's telltale swollen thighs.
native_info: Widespread and common across southern and central England and Wales on open, flower-rich grassland and gardens; more local further north.
wildlife_value: Adults feed on pollen and are frequent flower visitors, contributing modestly to pollination of open-flowered plants such as ox-eye daisy and buttercup.

life_stages.description: Slender, elongated, brilliant metallic green beetle. Males have distinctively swollen, thickened hind thighs. Feeds openly on pollen from summer flowers.
